It was asserted that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 105 of 1983 filed suit showing wrong address of the defendants by fraudulent suppression of the facts and obtained a decree dated  17-11-1984. It was specifically stated that the defendant- appellants were not residing at the addresses shown in the plaint rather they were residing at Dhaka. There was no proper service upon them as summons were fraudulently suppressed.

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying material allegation made in the plaint and asserted that the summons upon the defendants in Other Suit No. 105 of 1983 were duly served and that the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest in the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge, after examining 4 PWs on behalf of the plaintiffs and 7 DWs, on behalf of the defendant and after considering the Exhibits, dismissed the suit by the impugned judgment and decree.

4. Heard Mr KZ Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for appellants and Mr Rafiq-ul-Huq with Mr Zaforullah, the learned Advocates appearing for the respondent, perused the paper book including plaint, written statement and deposition of the PWs and DWs and the impugned Judgment and decree and the memo of appeal, Mr KZ Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, submits that the trial Court ought to have considered from the records of Other Suit No. 105 of 1983 whether the summons were served upon the defendants of that suit properly and legally in accordance with the mandatory provisions of Order V, rules 15, 19 and 20 of the CPC and, in addition, the trial Court ought to have considered whether the plaintiffs of the present suit were, in fact, residing at the addresses shown in the plaint of Other Suit No. 105 of 1983 and in view of the evidence on records the trial Court ought to have decreed the suit but the failure of the Judge has caused a miscarriage of justice. He next submits that the finding of the Court below are based on misreading of evidence and non-consideration of evidence. He also submits that there was no substituted service upon the defendants of that suit in accordance with law.

5. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, submits that the trial Court has rightly disbelieved the evidence on record which failed to make out a case of fraud or fraudulent suppression of service of summons upon the defendants of Other Suit No. 105 of 1983 and there has been sufficient compliance of Order V, rules 17 and 20 of CPC.

<u>6. In order to prove the case the plaintiffs examined 4 PWs. PW 1 is Noor Jahan Ahmed the plaintiff No. 1 of other suit No. 130 of 1986. She stated that previously they used to live at 'Lalkuti' but after 9th of December 1994 it was let out to the Jibon Bima Corporation and they were living at Dhaka addresses. The other part of the Lalkuti of the suit land of Title suit No. 105 of 1983 was already let out to one Dr Aziz. She asserted that the decree in other suit No. 105 of 1983 was obtained by suppression of summons. It was obtained fraudulently and neither Ashraf Ali Khan nor Mokbul Hossain has any authority to represent them in the suit and no summons was served upon her. PW 2 is Tasiruddin Ahmed. He is the plaintiff No. 2 and son of plaintiff No. 1 and the brother of other 3 brothers. He asserted that no summons was served upon him or other plaintiffs in Title suit No, 105 of 1983 and they were not residing at the addresses shown in the plaint of that suit. He also asserted that Ashraf Ali Khan had no authority to represent them in the suit and Moqbul Hossain had no authority to depose in the suit on their behalf and in fact, defendants had no authority in the suit. The decree of that suit is not binding upon them and by the fraudulent means they obtained the decree. PW 3 is Shamsuzzaman Manik. He supported the plaint case that the plaintiffs were not residing at Lalkuti. PW 4 is Motahar Rahman Khan. He stated that he did not depose on the points of suppression of summons. However, he stated that the suit building belongs to the plaintiffs and defendant had no possession therein. The relevant evidence for the purpose of disposing of this appeal is of DW 7. DW 5 is Isar Ali Sarker. He was process server at the relevant time and he was authorised to cause service of summons of other suit No. 105 of 1983 and he served the same on 17-3-1984 in presence of witnesses. In his cross-examination he admitted that there was no date below. the signature of the other witnesses and he did not know all the Mokabila witnesses and they were present at the time of service. DW 7 is Shafiqur Rahman. He was the Mokabila witness of the service by DW 5. He stated that he was the tenant under Mokbul Saheb and then he was the tenant under Tarifuddin and after the Tarifuddin left the country he became the tenant under Ashraf Ali Khan, Noorjahan Begum asked him to vacate the land and thereafter he filed the case against her. He stated that the notice was served by hanging. He admitted his signature was wanted by the process server and the notice was hung on a tree by the process server. In his cross- examination he admitted that he haild from Noakhali District but he had been living at Dinajpur for 25 years. He further admitted that the notice was hung on the tree before it was signed by him. He voluntary stated that the tree was within the boundary of the suit house. He admitted that he had no knowledge about the writing below his signature. He denied the defence suggestion that the service was collusive and fraudulent at the instance of Mokbul Saheb and was done at the instance of Mokbul Saheb. Thus it appears that although the PWs 1-5 asserted that they were not residing at the address as shown in the other suit No. 105 of 1983 at the relevant time and they were staying in Dhaka there is no contrary evidence to show otherwise. Further, it appears that process server admittedly hung the notice on a tree allegedly within the boundary of the suit house. It is further seen that there is no date below the signature of Mokabila witnesses. There is nothing on record that anybody identified the house in which allegedly the defendants of other suit No. 105 of 1983 lastly resided and therefore it does not appear that the service of the summons upon the defendants was in compliance of Order V, rules 17 and 20, CPC. In this connection the learned advocate Mr KZ Alam has referred to the case of Upendra Chandra Rishi and others vs Sufia Begum and others reported in 42 DLR (AD) 285 wherein it was held-it is obligatory upon the process server to mention in his report the name and address of the person if any by whom the house in question was identified and in whose presence the copy of summons was affixed. The learned Advocate has further referred to the case of Kedar Mull Agarwala and another vs Wazifunnessa and another reported in 1935 (Cal) 745 in support of his contention that service under Order V, rule 20 CPC and cl(2) does not preclude the defendants from afterwards showing that in fact there had been no service on him at all and the order for substituted service was procured on misrepresentation of facts. The plaintiffs in this suit have proved that they were not residing at Lalkuti Mohammadpur since December, 1984 and Since the plaintiffs and the defendant are relations it is expected that the plaintiffs had knowledge about the address of the defendants of Title Suit No. 105 of 1983 but even then it appears that at the relevant time tenants of the plaintiffs, namely Jibon Bima Corporation, was holding and possessing the suit building. Therefore if the summons were served even under Order V, rules 17 and 20, CPC the service cannot be construed as sufficient in view of wrong addresses shown in the plaint of Title Suit No. 105 of 1983. The learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the contention of the plaintiffs that they were not residing at Mohammadpur at the relevant time on the ground that in a previous suit No. 172 of 1973 Mohammadpur address was shown by the plaintiff in the plaint of that suit. This finding of the learned Subordinate Judge does not stand to reason.</u>

<u>7. It is evident from the Judgment of the Court below that the record of Other Suit No.105 of 1983 was called for and was before the Court but the Court did not come to any finding about the sufficiency of service and satisfaction of the earlier Court on that point in the Judgment. He proceeded on the assumption that there was due service on the other defendants other than defendant No.5 whereas that was the main issue the Court was called upon to decide. The learned Court ought to have come to a finding whether of not there was sufficient service under Order V, rule 17 and 20, CPC upon other defendants other than defendant No.5. So far the substituted service upon defendant No. 5 is concerned, it appears that admittedly the notice was hung on a tree but Order V, rule 20 contemplates that it must be hung in the Court house and also upon some conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant is known to have last resided. A tree within the suit land cannot be construed as a conspicuous part of the house and therefore the learned Subordinate ought to have held that even substituted service under Order V, rules 17 and 20 was not in accordance with law. Moreover, it appears that PW 5 admitted that the signature of the Mukabila witnesses were not dated and the Mukabila witness PW 7 admitted that he had no knowledge as to the writing below his signature and who wrote it. The trial Court also found that there are over-writings in the report. PW 7 appears to be hostile towards the plaintiff of the suit inasmuch as he admitted that there was litigation between him and Noor Jahan Begum. No permanent resident of Mohammadpur appears to be witness in the report and PW 7 appears to be a chance witness. His testimony does not inspire any confidence. In such circumstances we are constrained to hold that there was no service upon the defendant of Other Suit No. 105 of 1983. Now, the facts of this case is that despite order of this Court the record of the other suit No. 105 of 1983 was not sent to this Court by the trial Court and after this Court sent the order by special messenger a report has been sent by the presiding Judge to the effect that the records of other suit No.1 05 of 1983 is missing. In such circumstances we could not get the opportunity to satisfy ourselves whether or not there was sufficient compliance of law which could be gathered from the record itself. Mr KZ Alam, the learned Advocate submits that the reasons for this disappearance of the records is obvious and inference may be drawn under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act that it could have shown that there was no service at all if the record was produced. It is difficult for us to hold anyone responsible for disappearance of the records unless inquiry is done and the culprit is brought to took. In such circumstances not useful purpose, will be served by sending the case back on remand to the trial Court in absence of the records. Moreover, we are satisfied that the plaintiffs proved their address to be different from what was shown in the plaint of other suit No. 105 of 1983 at the relevant time.</u>

8. In view of the finding and discussion as stated above we hold that the trial Court committed error of law in dismissing the suit holding that there was sufficient service upon the defendants.

9. Now it appears that although the issue before the Court was whether the decree of Other Suit No. 105 of 1983 was obtained by fraudulent suppression of summons the Court decided the title anti possession of the parties in this suit which is uncalled for. Mr KZ Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, has drawn our attention to the ordering portion of the impugned Judgment and decree where the learned Subordinate Judge awarded exemplary costs upon the plaintiffs on a finding that the suit was filed to harass the defendants. This finding is also uncalled for and deprecated by us.

10. In the result this appeal is allowed and the impugned Judgment and decree are set aside and the ex parte Judgment and decree passed in other suit No. 105 of 1983 dated 27-11-1984 are set aside and the other suit No. 105 of 1983 is restored to its original file and number and the trial Court is directed to decide the suit after giving the defendants of that suit who are the appellants, time to file written statement in the suit and then to decide the suit in accordance with law. If the record is traced out, it is well and good and even if it is not traced out the parties shall take steps for reconstruction of the record of the other suit No.105 of 1983. There shall be no order as to cost.

Send down the records at once.

End.

caseno: Writ Petition Nos. 4083 of 2002 and 4084 of 2002
lawyer:
Mahmudul Hoque for Rokonuddin Mahmud, Advocate------For the Petitioners.
Kazi Waliul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General------For Respondent No.2 in WP No, 4084 of 2002,
parties:
Ashique Jeans Apparels Ltd and another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
National Board of Revenue and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J: In both these Rules, the parties and the fact in issue being the same and similar, both are taken up for hearing together and now disposed of by this single judgment. In Writ Petition No. 4083 of 2002, the Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why Memos being file No. 11(302) Anu;1/2000/2563 dated 21-12-2000 (Annexure-A) (wrongly stated in the prayer as well as in Rule issuing order as file No. 11(302) Anu:1/2000/2653), File No. 11(302) Anu: 1/2000/571 dated 4-4-2001 (Annexure-B) and File No. 11 (307) Anu: 1/2000/933 dated 31-5-2001 (Annexure-B 1) should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and why respondent Nos.1-2 should not be directed to withdraw, cancel, revoke and/or rescind the same and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. In Writ Petition No. 4084 of 2002, the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memos being file No. 11(301) Anu: 1/2000/2566 dated 21-12-2000 (Annexure-A) (wrongly written in the prayer as well as in the Rule issuing order as file No. 11(302) Anu:-1/2005/2653), file No. 11(301) Anu: 1/2000/568 dated 4-4-2001 (Annexure-B) (wrongly stated in the prayer as well as in the Rule issuing order as file No.11(302)/Anu: 1/2000/571 dated 4-4-2001 and file No. 11(301) Anu: 1/2000/936 dated 31-5-2001 (Annexure-B 1) (wrongly stated in the prayer as well as in the Rule issuing order as. file No.11 (302) Anu: 1/2000/933 dated 31-5-2001) shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 shall not be directed to with draw, cancel, revoke and/or rescind the same and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. Both the petitioners are the limited companies incorporated under the companies laws of Bangladesh and are engaged in the business of producing and manufacturing various types of garments and apparels since their incorporation on 26-5-1999. Both the companies are 100% exportoriented garment industries which have been set up at the addresses given in the cause title by importing machineries and other equipment from abroad, While importing the capital machineries for the factory the petitioners opened Letters of Credit in September, 1999 and May, 1999 respectively. On arrival of the capital machineries the same were installed part by part and by January, 2000 major parts of the machineries were set up. The companies went into commercial production on and from 1st April, 2000. The petitioners obtained Tax Identification Number and VAT registration number from the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT and also obtained Bonded Warehouse Licence, CCI & E registration. BOI registration from the concerned authorities for the purpose of running the business. Under section 46A (1) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 (hereinafter referred to as the said Ordinance) the petitioners made an application to the National Board of Revenue for tax holiday on 24-9-2000 furnishing all the necessary information supported by documents for the said purpose. The National Board of Revenue by letter dated 28-11-2000 requested the petitioner to furnish further documents which the petitioner duly furnished through its letter dated 10-12-2000. The National Board of Revenue then by letter dated 21-12-2000 regretted and expressed its inability to grant tax holiday to the petitioners contending that the applicant has installed at its factory 45 old machines in violation of section 46A(2)( d) of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984 and the pre-production electricity bills were so high that it indicates that the commercial production of the companies commenced 3 or 4 months earlier and, as such, the condition for filing application for tax holiday within 180 days of commencement of commercial production has not been fulfilled. The petitioners stated in the writ petitions that the National Board of Revenues on receipt of the application noted in the file on 25-9-2000 that the application was filed within 180 days as stipulated in section 46A of the Ordinance. The National Board of Revenue by order dated 17-12-2000 also noted the explanation of the petitioner that due to installation works of the machineries the electricity bill of the petitioner prior to commencement of the commercial production was high and after commencing commercial production the same was higher and the said explanation of the petitioner was found by the National Board of Revenue as acceptable. The National Board of Revenue in its said note dated 17-12-2000 recommended for tax holiday in favour of the petitioner. It also appeared from note dated 18-12-2000 and 19-12-2000 respectively that the petitioner had satisfactorily explained the use of the machines borrowed from a sister concern for a period of one month only and therefore the petitioner was totally surprised and taken aback by the impugned letter dated 21-12-2000 refusing to grant tax holiday to the petitioner. The petitioner then wrote to the respondent No.1 for reconsideration of its decision stating that eight machines borrowed from a sister concern for 1 month were not old and on similar circumstances the National Board of Revenue had earlier granted tax exemption to one Satarupa Weaving Mills, Ltd, despite having partly used old machines therein. In reply to the said letter, the National Board of Revenue by its letter dated 16-1-2001 asked the petitioner to attend to a hearing on 5-2-2001 which the petitioner duly abided by. Thereafter, when the petitioner found delay in getting the reply from the National Board of Revenue on its application for review, wrote another letter dated 7-5-2001 to the respondent No.1 to grant tax exemption to the petitioner upon reviewing its earlier decision. By letter dated 31-5-2001, (Annexure-B 1) the National Board of Revenue informed the petitioner that the decision of the review committee is final and conclusive under rule 59A(6) of the Income Tax Rules. The petitioner alleged that no decision was ever passed by any review committee under rule 59A(6) as mentioned by the National Board of Revenue in the letter dated 31-5-2001. The earlier letter refusing tax exemption to the petitioner dated 21-12-2000 was issued by the respondents and then the subsequent letter dated 4-4-2001 in response to the prayer for review was also issued by the respondents. Finally, the letter dated 31-5-2001 was also issued by the respondent though the decision of the review committee was mentioned as final. Actually, there was no decision ever passed by the review committee and even the hearing held on the application dated 5-2-2001 was also not held before the Review Committee but held before the Member (Tax Policy) of the National Board of Revenue.

4. However, being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the decision dated 21-12-2000 (Annexure-A), 4-4-2001 (Annexure-B) and 31-5-2001 (Annexure-B) the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rules in both the writ petitions.

5. The respondent No.2 entered appearance and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegation of the writ petitions contending, inter alia, that after receiving the application praying for tax holiday, the National Board of Revenue went for inspection of the factory and found that the petitioner company installed 45 units of used and old machineries along with 94 new machineries and did not produce the material documents during inspection of the same before the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Companies Circle- 3, Taxes Zone-1, Dhaka. It is further contended that the petitioner's declaration in respect of the Letter of Credit opened in September, 1999 is not correct because the petitioner opened Letter of Credit on 31-5-99 and 17-8-99 and the declaration as to installation of machineries in January, 2000 and commercial production stated from 1st of April, 2000 are also not correct, because the petitioner commenced its commercial production through old and new machineries at least 3/4 months earlier than the disclosed date of commencement of commercial production and hence the National Board of Revenue was legally justified to reject the prayer for tax exemption under section 46A of the IT Ordinance, 1984. It is further contended by the respondent that the petitioner's company neither submitted application praying for tax holiday in the prescribed form furnishing all the necessary information and documents in this regard for installation of the factory nor disclosed the actual date of commencement of commercial production. The petitioner failed to submit application before the NBR within 180 days as stipulated time limit for praying for tax holiday. Since the .petitioners submitted application after the expiry of 180 days, the NBR was legally justified to reject the prayer of tax holiday. The respondent further contended that the petitioner did not fulfil the condition of section 46(2)(d) and the application for tax holiday was barred by limitation. The National Board of Revenue rejected the application praying for tax holiday after examining the documents produced before it and never took any decision before issuing impugned letter dated 21-12-2000 by which the NBR refused to grant tax holiday for non fulfillment of the terms and conditions as laid down in the concerned provision of law. It is further contended that after receiving the review application by the respondent No.1 it was referred to the 3-member review committee on 11-1-2001. Thereafter, on the application of the petitioner company the NBR arranged hearing for the petitioner before the 3- member review committee on 5-2-2001 which maintained the earlier orders of rejection and accordingly, informed the decision to the petitioner by letter dated 4-4-2001. Thus, on compliance of different provisions of the Ordinance and on perusal, and consideration of all the papers and documents produced before the NBR the rejection order was rightly passed, since the petitioner failed to comply with the terms and conditions of section 46A(2)(d) and 46A(2)(f) of the Ordinance.

6. During the hearing of the Rule the respondent No.2 filed a supplementary affidavit and contended that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes, Circle-3, Zone-1, Dhaka conducted the inspection of the concerned factories for the purpose of exemption and submitted his enquiry report on 19-10-2000 wherein in item No.9 it was stated that out of 139 machineries 45 machineries in total are too old and he also stated that the petitioner company failed to produce the letter of credit, bill of entry, invoice and list of the machineries. The DCT in his report further stated at paragraph Nos. 10(a) and 10(b) that the petitioner company started commercial production with the help of old machineries much earlier in 1999 but in the tax holiday application the petitioner company declared that the company started its commercial production on 1-4-2000 i.e. after about one and half years from the actual date of its commencement of commercial production. This is also reflected from the consumption of electricity bill noted in the order-sheet of the NBR. Upon perusing the electricity bill of September, 1999 to July 2001 the said Deputy Commissioner of Taxes opined that the chronological billing amount proves that the petitioner company started its commercial production with the help of the old machineries more than 6 months ago and hence the petitioner's prayer for tax exemption is barred by limitation. The said DCT also observed that huge number of old machineries are being used in the petitioners' factories. The petitioner company neither submitted all import documents in support of machineries installed in the factories nor disclosed the actual date of commercial production and hence it is observed that the petitioner company did not fulfil the terms and conditions of section 46(2)(d) and (f) of the Ordinance. It is stated in the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition that though the Second Secretary in his note No.11 dated 17-12-2000 and in note No.17 dated 19-12-2000 gave opinion to allow exemption in favour of the petitioner but their opinions were not accepted by the higher authority of the NBR and thus, the same were rejected by letter dated 21-12-2000. Relying on these statements the respondent prays for discharging the Rule since the petitioner did not comply with the terms and conditions of section 46A of the Ordinance for tax holiday.

7. Mr Mahmudul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Advocate for the petitioners in both these writ petitions, submits that during the course of hearing the respondent along with the supplementary affidavit annexed the copy of the original note sheet which will give the clear picture of this case. Relying on that note sheet, he submits that nowhere in the said note sheet it has been mentioned that 45 machineries were transferred by shifting any business concern rather, admittedly, 8 machineries were borrowed as loan from the sister concern of the petitioner company which were not old and, as such, the same does not in any way contravene the provision of section 46A of the Ordinance. He submits that the present two industrial undertakings were not formed by splitting up or by reconstruction or reconstitution or any business already in existence or by any transfer to a new business of any machineries or plant used in business which was being carried on in Bangladesh at any time before the commencement of new business. Rather, the undertakings were formed by installing new machineries and the rate of electricity consumed therein, as evident from the electricity bill, proved that the installation of machineries was made during those dates. Mr Hoque submits that the National Board of Revenue categorically discussed the electricity bills between previous dates and after the date of production and came to a conclusion, as evident from the note sheet, that the electricity consumed prior to commencement of commercial production is much lesser than chronological rise of the electricity bill after commencement of commercial. production. In addition to this, he submits that only 8 old machineries were taken as loan to meet the urgent demand of the buyer. Apart from those machineries the other machineries were completely brand new with which the commencement of the factory started from 1st of April, 2000. He submits that on the date of inspection i.e. on 19-10-2000, the machineries used in the undertakings were all brand new as it appears from note sheet No.16 dated 19-12-2000. Mr Hoque drew our attention to the said noting wherein it has been clearly stated that on 1-10-2000 eight machineries were borrowed from a sister concern for a period of 1 month only to meet the emergency supply. So, he submits that the report of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes as to use of 46 old machineries is not correct at least on the date of inspection. The note sheet shows that the petitioner supplied all necessary information to the National Board of Revenue explaining its position that no old machineries were used in the undertaking excepting eight which were borrowed on 1-10-2000 from the sister concern for a period of one month only. According to the learned Advocate, this does not in any way debar the petitioner company from getting the benefit of tax exemption under section 46A of the Ordinance. According to him, since there is no splitting up of any business, reconstruction, reconstitution of any business or transfer by shifting any machineries in the business, as contemplated in the statute, there is no bar in accepting the petitioner's contention and allow the prayer for tax holiday. In this respect he submits that the expression 'transfer' in relation to a capital asset in the Income Tax Law was held to be different from the expression 'transfer' used in the Transfer of Property Act, while the expression 'transfer' under the Transfer of Property Act includes even mortgage of the immovable property, the same connotation cannot be extended to the expression 'Transfer' in the Income Tax Law. Unless the entire interest is transferred to the transferee or assigned without retaining any interest whatsoever in the transfer or with the original owner the transaction cannot be said to fall within the meaning of transfer as defined in the Income Tax Law. Referring to the case of Alapati Venkataramiah vs CIT (1969) 57 ITR 185, the learned Advocate submits that the expression 'transfer' must be construed in a restricted way so far it occurs in the Income Tax Law. He submits that it is true that the word transfer is used in addition to the word sale but even so, in the context the transfer must mean effective conveyance of the capital asset to the transferee. Delivery of possession of immovable property cannot by itself he treated as equivalent of conveyance of the immovable property. Thus/ he submits that the new undertaking if formed through taking over the old machineries under a mortgage or under a lease for a long period forming the new company will escape the bar contained, in the provision of the Transfer of Property Act, while a new undertaking which is being formed by purchase of the machineries which has been used by others will alone be affected by the bar and that will be contrary to the object behind the section. Relying on the above contention, he submits that the provision of section 46A(2)( d) is by no means a hurdle or does not debar the petitioner to get the tax exemption because in the present case nothing was transferred as meant by the aforesaid jurist to this undertaking rather it was simply a loan of 8 machineries borrowed on 1-10-2000 from its sister concern which were required to meet the urgent need of the buyers for a period of one month only. Thus he submits that chronological calculation of the electricity consumed, clearly proved that the undertaking went into production on and from 1-4-2000 and undertaking was never run by any old machineries. This will be evident from the note sheet No.11 dated 17-12-2000 and note No.16 dated 19-12-2000. In support of his connotation, Mr Hoque relied on the case of Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay City 1 vs Asbestos, Magnesia & Friction Materials Ltd reported in ITR, Vol-106 page 286, wherein it has been held that where the old machineries utilised cannot be regarded as important or essential to the new undertaking and where its value is comparatively very small, the assessee should not be denied relief for tax exemption if it is otherwise entitled to the same on the ground of such utilisation. In this respect he also relies on the case of Commissioner of Income Tax, Bombay City -II vs Sawyer's Asia Ltd reported in ITR Vol-I22, page 259.

8. Mr Hoque then submits that the impugned order Annexure-A dated 21-12-2000 and Annexure- B dated 4-4-2001 having been issued by the same person namely, the Second Secretary (Tax Exemption-1 ), the decision in the review committee appears to have been vitiated because the same person cannot review the order passed by him earlier. In this respect he drew our attention to note No.32 of the note sheet of the Customs Authority dated 5-2-2001 wherein it appears that 3(three) members review committee passed an order considering only about 8 old machineries but there was no consideration or discussion about electricity consumption or commercial operation or filing of the application within 180 days. On that score, the 2nd order passed in the impugned letter dated 21-12-2000 remained unexplained and not interfered for which the review is not actually done. In this context, he submits that the respondents committed illegality in issuing the impugned orders which are liable to be declared without lawful authority.

9. On the other hand, Mr Kazi Waliul Islam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent, submits that the petitioner company failed to comply with the terms and conditions of section 46A and, as such, was rightly refused. the benefit. According to him, using of old machineries is not permissible under section 46A and by using such old machineries the petitioner company cannot get the benefit of tax exemption as provided in section 46A of the Ordinance. According to him, admittedly the petitioner installed old machineries which, if not 45 in number, were at least 8 in number and those machineries are prohibited to form a new undertaking as contemplated in section 46A(2)(d) of the Ordinance. He further submits that the exemption application was not made within 180 days as contemplated in section 6A which will be evident from the impugned order and the note sheet that the commercial production did not commence on 1-4-2000. In this respect, he relied on the case of Modella Woolens Ltd vs Commissioner of Income Tax. Bombay City-1, reported in ITR (1979) Vol- 120 page 726 and in the case of LG Balakrishnan and Bros Ltd, vs Commissioner of Income Tax. Madras reported in ITR (1985) Vol- 151. page 270. Relying on these two decisions Mr Islam submits that if there is a transfer of the machinery and if the transfer had taken place in the process of formation or setting up of the new industrial undertaking, then the assessee may not be entitled to claim the benefit of tax exemption Accordingly, it is to be seen whether the lease of the machineries from a third party was in the course of the formation of the new industrial undertaking and whether the lease of the machinery will amount to a transfer so as to attract the concerned provision of law. On these grounds, Mr Islam submits that there is no illegality in the impugned orders in rejecting the prayer for tax holiday against the petitioner companies.

10. Heard the learned Advocate and perused the petition along with the annexures and the decisions as well. The main questions raised in these two writ petitions are, whether an undertaking established with new machineries could be disqualified for tax holiday for reason of using some old machineries taken as loan for a particular period and whether the application praying for tax holiday was filed within 180 days from the date of commercial production of the undertaking and lastly, whether the impugned orders passed by the National Board of Revenue are legal.

11. To get the correct answer of all these questions we are to consider the note sheet of the concerned nothi of the customs authority. From the note sheet, annexed with the supplementary affidavit, it appears that the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes held inquiry upon receiving the application under section 46A from the petitioner and on the basis of such enquiry, opened nathi No.11 (302) Anu:-1/2000 and No.11(301)Anu:-1/2000. On going through the said note sheet it appears that the authority calculated the time in filing the application as 177 days and thereafter, the enquiry report of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes was considered by the official of the National Board of Revenue. From note No.10, it appears that it contained a remark as to ৪৬ এ ধারায় কর অবকাশের জন্য বর্ণিত সকল শর্তসমূহ আবেদনকারী কোম্পানী পরিচালনা করিয়াছেন” In note No. 10.06 it has been stated শিল প্রতিষ্ঠানটি সম্পূর্ণ নতুন। বিদেশ হইতে নতুন মেশিন আনয়নের জন্য ৩০-৯-৯৯, ১৭-৮-৯৯ ও ৩১-৫-৯৯ ইং তারিখ র্পবালী ব্যাংক লিমিটেড ১৯৫, মতিঝিল বাণিজ্যিক এলাকা ঢাকা শাখার মাধ্যমে ঋণ পত্র খোলা হয়। ২৬-১২-৯৯, ১২-১০-৯৯, ২৩-৮-৯৯ ও ১৮-১১-৯৯ ইং তারিখে যন্ত্রপাতি সমূহ দেশে আসিয়া পৌছায়। ১০-৯-২০০০ ইং তারিখে যন্ত্রপাতি সমূহ সম্পূর্ণভাবে স্থাপন করা হয়। এই সংক্রান্ত প্রত্যায়ন পত্র রহিয়াছে। In note No. 10.07 it has been stated বাণিজ্যিক উপাদানের ১৮০ দিনের মধ্যে জাতিয় রাজস্ব বোর্ডে আবেদন পত্র দাখিল করা হয়েছে। বাণিজ্যিক উৎপাদনে তারিখ ১-৪-২০০০ এবং আবেদন পত্র দাখিলের তারিখ ২৪-৯-২০০০। অর্থ্যাৎ বানিজ্যিক উৎপাদনের ১৭৭ তম আবেদন করা হইয়াছে।”

12. Thereafter, by note No.11 the 2nd Secretary of NBR gave a picture of the electricity consumption from September, 1999 to July, 2000. From there, it appears that after April, 2000 the electricity bills are comparatively more higher than the electricity bills of the previous months. In note No.12.06 a query was made as to use of 45 old machineries. The same has been stated in the said note at: “৪৫ টি পুরাতন মেশিন ব্যবহারের ব্যাখ্যায় বলা হইয়াছে যে, জরুরী শিপমেন্টের জন্য সহযোগী প্রতিষ্ঠান, চৈতী এ্যাপারেলস লিঃ এর নিকট হইতে সাময়িকভাবে কয়েকটি মেশিন ধার করা হইয়াছে। প্রমান হিসাবে চৈতী এ্যাপারেলস লিঃ এর শিকারোক্তির দাখিল করা হইয়াছে। By note Nos.I3 and 14 the recommendation for granting tax holiday has  been made since all the terms and conditions for availing such benefit were found to have been fulfilled by the petitioner company. From note No.15 it appears that an explanation was sought for in the following manner “সহযোগী প্রতিষ্ঠান হইতে কয়টি মেশিনারী কত সময়ের জন্য তখন ধার করা হয় সেই সম্পর্কে তথ্য প্রমান ও ব্যাখ্যা সংগ্রহ পূর্বক পুনরায় নথী উপস্থাপন করেন।” Thereafter, note No. 16 runs as follows: “নোট অনুচ্ছেদ ১৫ এর আলোকে কোম্পানী হইতে ব্যাখ্যা চাওয়া হইয়াছে। ব্যাখ্যায় দেখা যায় যে, ১-১০-২০০০ তারিকে সহযোগী প্রতিষ্ঠানের নিকট হইতে ৮টি মেশিন ধার করা হইয়াছিল ১ মাসের জন্য। অর্থাৎ কোম্পানী নিজেস্ব আমদানীকৃত মেশিনারীর মাধ্যমেই বানিজ্যিক উৎপাদন শুরু করিয়াছিল ইহা প্রমান করে। তাহা ছাড়া বন্ড লাইসেন্সের তারিখ ও দেখা যায় ৯-৭-২০০০ যাহা কোম্পানীর ঘোষিত বাণিজ্যিক উৎপাদনের সহিত সামঞ্জস পূর্ন।” By note No.17 the recommendation was made for granting tax exemption to the petitioner company. Surprisingly thereafter the note No. 18 says that “প্রত্যাখ্যান আদেশের খসড়া দিন।”

13. It appears that the respondents have done so many exercises on the entire issue of allowing tax holiday to petitioner. But suddenly, why it refused the benefit to the petitioner the same cannot be  derived from the order sheet. However, thereafter, several notes were initiated for rejecting the prayer of the petitioner for tax exemption and the impugned orders were passed one after another. It appears from Note No.32 that when the petitioner sought for review under section 46(4), of the Ordinance, the review committee, while deciding the issues, simply relied on the report of the DCT saying “সংশ্লিষ্ট ডি, সি, টি সরেজ জমিনে তদন্তকালে উৎপাদন প্রক্রিয়ার পুরাতন মেশিনের ব্যবহার দেখিতে পাইয়াছেন পুরাতন মেশিন ব্যবহার কর অবকাশের মৌলিখ শাতের পরিপন্থি। সুতরাং বিভিনিও সকল সদস্য আবেদনকারির কর অবকাশ প্রত্যাখ্যানের পক্ষেমত পোষন করিলেন।

14. On perusal of the said order of the review committee, it appears that the review committee, without coming to any independent finding and decision, mechanically relied upon the report of the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes against which the petitioner preferred the review. The review committee miserably failed to make any opinion as to whether the report of the DCT was at all objectively made. However to decide these questions raised in the Rules, we are to see the provision of section 46A which deals with Tax Holiday of newly established industrial undertakings. Section 46A (1), 2( f) reads as follows:

"46A(1)-Subject to the provisions of this Ordinance, profits and gains of an industrial undertaking, tourist industry or physical infra- structure facility (hereinafter referred to as the said undertaking) set up in Bangladesh between the first day of July, 1995 and the thirteenth day of June, 2005 (both days inclusive) shall be exempt from the tax payable under this Ordinance for the period specified below:

(a) if the undertaking is set up in Dhaka and Chittagong Divisions, excluding the hill districts of Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari, for a period of five years beginning with the months of commencement of commercial production or operation of the said undertaking;

(b) if the said undertaking is set up in Rajshahi, Khulna, Sylhet and Barisal Divisions and the hill districts of Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari, for a period of seven years beginning with the month of commencement of commercial production or operation of the said undertaking.

46A(2)- The exemption under sub-section (1) shall apply to the said undertaking if it fulfils the following conditions, namely,

(d) that the said undertaking is not formed by splitting up or by reconstruction or reconstitution of business already in existence or by transfer to a new business of any machinery or plant used in business which was being carried on in Bangladesh at any time before the commencement of the new business: (f) that the application in the prescribed form for approval for the purpose of this section, as verified in the prescribed manner, is made to the board (within six months from the end of the month) of commencement of commercial production or operation.

15. On perusal of the aforesaid provisions of law it appears that the same has been inserted in the statute to encourage the continuance of setting up of new industrial enterprises in the country upto June 1995 (sections 45 and 46 were applicable to industrial undertaking set up upto June, 1995). This section applies to industrial undertakings, tourist industry or undertaking of physical infrastructure facility set up between 1st day of July, 1995 to thirteenth day of June, 2000. However, the period has been extended by the Finance Act of 2000 from June 2000 to June 2005. To have the benefit of exemption under this section the industrial undertaking shall be engaged in the manufacture of goods or the exploration and extraction of mineral resources and producing of agricultural products. This section which is to give exemption to the newly set up industrial enterprises must be construed liberally as decided in the case of Wabbing & Belting Factory Pvt. Ltd. vs CIT (1961) 43 ITR, 234, 238 wherein the assessee petitioner set up a new factory in which about one-third of the machineries installed were used in another factory for experiment and training before April, 1948 and in that case it was held by the Supreme Court of India that the assesse petitioner was entitled to exemption on the total income from the sale of the products manufactured with the help of those machineries, including the one which had been used in another factory. With that view, the case of CIT vs Indian Aluminium Co. Ltd (1973) 88 ITR 257, 276 was decided holding that (i) the new business need not be a different kind of business, (ii) the newness of the industrial undertaking does not necessarily exclude expansion or extension of the original "business and the term reconstruction would include substantial extension or expansion of the original business, provided the extension or expansion is not by splitting up of the original business i.e. the undertaking must not be formed by transfer to a new business of any machinery or plant used before the commencement of the new business. Unless the second-hand machinery or plant is sufficiently important and essential to justify the inference that the new undertaking is formed by its acquisition, this condition should be regarded as fulfilled. The explanation to clause (B) of sub-section (i) also provides that the provisions of exemption shall also apply to the expansion of unit of an existing undertaking which has not applied for accelerated depreciation under para Nos. 7 or 7 A of the Third Schedule. In the aforesaid case it was held that "on the facts, that the assessee petitioner was entitled to get benefit by section 15C of the Income Tax Act, and the use of 35% of the machineries before April, 1948, for experimental purpose did not preclude the assessee from enjoying the concession." Relying on the aforesaid case it can very well be said that admittedly 8 machineries were used upon taking loan from the sister concern and the borrowing was made only for 1 month. So, whether the machineries were used at the time of commencement of commercial production or not or whether the same were left only as installed or' whether the same is used to meet the emergency supply of the demands of the buyers must be ignored on the principle of Wabbing and Belting's case. From the present case also we do not find that the 8 old machines used in the factory, were used on the date of commencement of commercial production of the assessee's company. The National Board of Revenue is silent about the rest of the 37 allegedly old machines when admittedly 8 machines were taken as loan from the sister concern. When explanation was called for as to use of the old machines, and for how many days the same were used, the assessee submitted its reply in that regard explaining use of 8 machineries, not 45, for one month. But the National Board of Revenue neither asked for any further clarification nor passed any opinion in this respect. Thus, it appears that the National Board of Revenue allowed the petitioner to explain his position but while passing the impugned order the NBR did not consider the same and came to a wrong conclusion that the 45 old machines are being used.

<u>16. The scheme of section 46 and 46A of the Income Tax Ordinance is to encourage establishment of new industrial undertaking provided they fulfil the conditions mentioned in various sub- sections. In order to be entitled to exemption an assessee must strictly come within the terms of the provisions under which such exemption is being claimed and the Income Tax Authority must construe the said section reasonably in the context of the purpose for which the section has been introduced. It is well settled that the provision relating to exemption must as far as possible be liberally construed and that also in favour of the assessee, provided in doing so no violation is being done of the language used. In construing the whole issue before us we thus hold that the scheme is very much for encouraging industrial undertakings and rightly it should be used as liberally as possible. We have already mentioned earlier that out of 139 machines installed by the petitioner company only 8 machines, admittedly being used as old machines, were borrowed from another sister concern for a period of one month which does not in any way affect section 46A of the Ordinance in granting tax holiday to the petitioner.</u>

17. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case it appears that the petitioner explained its position correctly and when applied for tax exemption the said 8 old machines were not in use. That being the fact the NBR could have clarified the position while endorsing note No.16 dated 19-10-2000. Having not done so the letter dated 21-12-2000 and the order of the review committee dated 4-4-2001, in our opinion, have been passed without proper appreciation of the entire proceeding and without applying any mind.

18. Now coming to the question as to whether the application was made within 180 days of the date of commencement of the commercial production, it, is to be mentioned that the review committee did not utter a single word on this issue although the order dated 21-12-2000 observed that the application was not made within the stipulated period of 180 days of the commencement of the commercial production. Having seen the calculation made by the National Board of Revenue in Note Nos. 1 and 11 and nothing being explained subsequent thereto on this point even when the petitioner raised objection to the same, it appears that the NBR did not apply its mind in deciding the matter and kept the matter unattended. It appears from the review order that it simply discussed on using of 45 or 8 allegedly old machines and nothing else. From the note sheet it has come to our notice that the explanations were sought for and the petitioner by letter on several occasions explained its position denying the allegation of using 45 old machines rather admitted that it used 8 machines upon borrowing the same from a sister concern only to meet the urgent requirements of the buyer which is of course after he commencement of commercial production.

19. So, considering the facts and circumstances, it appears that sub-section 2(d) to section 46A of the Income Tax Ordinance does not debar the petitioner from getting the benefit of tax exemption since it fulfilled all other conditions of the provision of law.

20. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove, we find merit in these two Rules and the Rules in both the writ petitions are thus made absolute. Hence the impugned orders in both the writ petitions, dated 21-12-2000, 4-4-2001 and 31-5-2001 (Annexures-A, Band B 1) are declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

21. Before parting with this judgment, we want to observe as to the notes of the NBR and the systems of holding inquiry in granting tax holiday under section 46A of the Ordinance. The policy of tax holiday encourages new undertakings to be established. The tax holiday practically does not cause any revenue loss rather, at the end of the day, this policy fetches more taxes from more and more new industrial undertakings. As such, the tax authority must apply their cautious effort in allowing the tax holiday applications. But unfortunately, the way the file of the present case have been handled proceeded and the nothings have been made, it clearly reveals that the notings have been made according to the whims and capricious mind of the Tax Authority and similarly, the NBR while passing the order did not also care to consider the entire note sheet while passing the order in accordance with law. When the finding and initiative of the note appears to be in favour of the petitioner, it is not understood why and how the NBR could simply travel within the report of the DC for rejecting the prayer without assigning any reason whatsoever of its own. Again, the impugned order dated 21-12-2000 appears to be confusing. Furthermore, the order of the review committee, in about 8 lines, appears to be more interested in other things which has no reflection about the finding of the authority, rather it simply passed the order without ascertaining the legal position which appears to have been made due to callousness/non application of mind of the official of the Tax Authority which called for interference by this court. As such the high officials, who are working in the NBR, are directed to be more careful in dealing with such matters specially while dealing with the prayer for tax holiday since the scheme and object of section 46 is to encurage more new undertakings to be established.

However, there will be no order as to costs.

End.
