Abdus Salam  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Mohammad Nurul Islam Mia and others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
In this application the pe-emptor has challenged the propriety of the order dated 15-1-1970 passed by Mr. J. C. Bhowmick, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla in Miscellaneous Appeal No.125 of 1969 reversing the order dated 31-5-1969 passed by Mr. S.D.M.N. Islam, Munsiff, 1st Court, Chandpur in Miscellaneous Case No.236 of 1963 allowing pre emotion under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950

2. The petitioner filed an application under section 96(1) of the said Act for pre-emption of the case land sold to opposite party Nos.1 to 4 by opposite party No.5 by a Kabala dated 8-5-1968. The petitioner claimed therein that the case land appertaining to the holding recorded in C S. Khatian No.26 of Mouza Deshecgaon originally belonged to Abbas Ali and Amjad Ali to the extent to 2/3 and 1/2 share respectively and that the said Abbas Ali died leaving 4 sons, namely, Md. Sami, Hafez Roshan, Abdul Karim and Abdur Rahim, the father of the pre-emptee opposite party Nos.1 to 4; 3 daughters namely, Halima, Omerenessa and another; and 2 widows Zahura Khatun and Ramjan Khatun ; and that Amjad Ali died leaving 4 sons, namely, Abdus Salam. the petitioner, Abdul Kadir, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Majid, 4 daughters namely, Sharupa the opposite party No 5, Asia, Ajmatunnessa and  Omarjan and a widow Arfaternessa ; and that the said 4 sons of Abbas Ali got the holding separated in respect of their 2/3 share by 4 separation cases bearing Case Nos.70, 71, 72 and 73 of 1963 and as such the opposite party Nos.1 to 4 are not co-sharer of the holding to which the case laud appertains but the opposite party No.5, a daughter  of Amjad Ali secretly sold the case land to opposite party Nos.1 to 4 by a Kabala dated 8-5-68 who are strangers to the holding, at a consideration of Taka 500.00 without serving any notice on the petitioner; and that the petitioner came to know about the sale from rumour and subsequently after taking a certified copy of the Kabala on 19-5-68, filed the application for pre-emption on depositing the consideration money together with legal compensation.

3.The case was resisted by the pre-emptee opposite party Nos.1 to 4, contending inter alia, that they are not strangers to the holding in question; and that the alleged separation cases were without jurisdiction and  illegal and the per-emption case is also bad for defect of parties.

4. The learned Munsiff, Chandpur accepted the case of the preemptor and by his order dated 31-5-1969 allowed the pre-emption as prayed for. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge, Comilla reversed the order of the learned Munsiff by his order dated 31-5-1969 passed in Misc. Appeal No. 125 of 1969. The decision of the learned Subordinate Judge is mainly resisted on the ground that the alleged separation of the holding under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was not valid and as such was not binding upon the co-sharers, and in the absence of valid separation of the holding, the pre-emptees continued to be co-sharer in the holding and their purchase from opposite-party No.5, a co-sharer in the holding, is not liable to be pre-empted. The pre-emptor being aggrieved by that decision moved this court when this Rule was issued.

<u>5. Mr. Aminul Huque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner finds it rather difficult to support the contention of the petitioner that the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge to the effect that in the absence of all the co-sharers the 4 separation cases were not legal and valid, and consequently the holding recorded in C.S. Khatian No.26 continued to be in existence, is bad in law. From the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that the question about validity of the separation cases was specifically raised and the same has been answered It has been noticed in the judgment that the 4 sons of Abbas Ali did not make the other daughters and widows of Abbas Ali party to the separation cases filed under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It was not disputed that Zahura Khatoon and Ramjan Banu, the two widows and Halima, Omarenessa and Gadi, the 3 daughters were not made parties in the said 4 separation case. Section of the penal Tenancy Act makes it imperative that to make a valid division of at mire of holding or a distribution of the feat payable in respect thereof there must be express consent in writing of all the co-sharers. Sub section (2) of section 88 provides that the Court, on an application made to it by one or more co-sharer tenants for a division of a tenure or holding it for a distribution of the rent payable in respect thereof, or for the annulment or modification of a previous division or distribution other than one made under this sub-section or under an agreement made between all the landlords and co-sharer tenants in conformance with the provisions of sub- section (1), may by an order in writing, direct such division of the tenure or holding or such distribution of rent as she court considers fair and equitable, provided  that no such order shall be passed without notice to the landlord or the entire body of landlords or their common agent, if any, and to the remaining co-sharer tenants; and that nothing contained in the sub-section shall be deemed to authorise a court on application for division or distribution to direct a division or distribution in respect of the share of any tenant other than an application under this sub-section or a co-sharer tenant who has been joined as a co-applicant under sub-section (2). Sub-section (3) provides that on receipt of notice of an application for division of distribution under sub-section (2) a co-sharer tenant may apply to be joined as a co-applicant, and upon such application the court shall join the said co-sharer tenant as a co-applicant without further notice to the landlord or landlord sand he remaining co-sharer tenants. Thus it appears that the above provisions do not authorise the Civil Court to allow division of holding without giving notice to all the co-sharer tenants and clause (c) of the proviso to sub-section (2) puts a limitation upon the authority of the Civil Court that nothing contained in the sub-section shall be deemed to authorise a court to direct a division or distribution in respect of the share of any tenant other than an application under this subsection or a co-sharer tenant who has been joined as a co-applicant under sub-section (3).</u>

<u>6. The pre-emptor could not adduce any evidence to show that the notice was issued upon the co-Sharers who had been left out in the application filed under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and that they applied as provided under sub-section (3) of Section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Therefore, in the absence of those co-share tenants the orders of separation passed by the Civil  Court under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act were not valid under the law, and as such the same are not binding upon all the co-sharer tenants Besides as pointed out above section 88(2), proviso (c) prohibits the court from making an order for distribution of rent in respect of the share of co-share tenants who has not joined by filing an application in the proceedings, as provided in sub-section (3), This question as considered by Henderson, J. of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Sri Rajeswar Tankur and another Vs. Lakshmi Kanta Pramanik and others, A.I.R. 1944 Cal, 287. It was argued before the Court that the proviso (c) merely means that the question will not be res judicata so far as a tenant within the terms of the provision is concerned, but the learned Judge did not accept this argument and held as follows:-</u>

<u>“In my judgment it is impossible to reconcile any such interpretation with the language actually used. The proviso does not lay down that a tenant who does not join in the application will not be debarred from re-agitation the matter in some subsequent proceeding. It goes much further than that. It prohibits a court from making an order at all with respect to the share of such a tenant”.</u>

<u>In that view of the matter the learned District Judge has rightly held that the order passed in the four separation cases under section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act were not valid in law and consequently the holding appertaining to C.S.Khatian No.26 continued as before. And as such opposite parties 1-4 were not strangers to the holding as alleged by the pre-emptor, and the disputed sale is not liable to be pre-empted.</u>

7. Mr. Aminul Huque, the learned Advocate then submits that the learned judge acted illegally is not considering about the application of section 114 (g) of the Evidence Act, to the facts of this case, although on account of non-production of dakhilas for the rents paid in respect of the original holding as claimed by the pre-emptees, were withheld. The learned Advocate further submits that since the miscellaneous cases were filed by the predecessors of the pre-emptees, and rent was paid by the co-sharers in accordance with the separation of Jama, they are estopped from raising the question of validity of the orders of separation of holding.

<u>8. In the face of the language of section 88 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as pointed out above mere presumption for non-production of dakhilas showing payment of rent of the undivided holding will not be sufficient to deprive the pre-emptess from pleading that the alleged order of separation of the holding was not valid, and as such the same was not binding upon the co-shares. I do not find any substance in the contention also. So far the question of estoppel is concerned, I do not find any substance in this point also, simple answer is that there is no estoppel against statute. Mr. Aziz, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee opposite parties referred me to a decision of the Bombay High Court, in the case of Lady Dibai Dinshaw Peti & others Vs. The Dominion of India and another reported in A.I.R 1951 Bombay 72. It appears from this decision that a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court consisting of Chagla, C.J. and bhagwati J. has held that “no person be precluded from pleading that certain orders are illegal or invalid, because the question as to whether orders are illegal or invalid or invalid is a pure question of law and there can be no estoppel against law.”</u>

<u>In the result, this application fails. The rule is discharged without any order as to costs.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 889 of 2002.
lawyer:
Mvi Md Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record-For the Petitioner. 
Md Sajjadul Hoque, Advocate-on-Record-For the Respondent.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Post Telegraph and communication and  others   ------ Petitioners
Vs
Abul Khair  ------ Respondent
case_source: (From the order dated 24th April 2002 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka in Appeal No. 57 of 2002).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The Government of Bangladesh and others seek leave to appeal against the judgment and order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal Dhaka in Administrative Appellate Tribunal Appeal No. 57 of 2000 dated 24-4-2002 allowing the appeal setting aside the impugned judgment and order dated 18-4-2000 passed by the Administrative Tribunal Dhaka dismissing AT Case No. 114 of 1998 and setting aside the punishment of compulsory retirement passed on 27-2-1997 and thereby restoring the respondent to his former post treating him on duty with all financial and other benefits as admissible under the rules.

2. The respondent filed an application under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 being Administrative Tribunal Case No.114 of 1998 stating, inter alia, that he was appointed as Postal Clerk on 7-9-1971 and subsequently he was promoted to the rank of Asstt Post Master (Non-Gazetted) on 13-11-1991. During the tenure of his service he was directly associated with the Trade Union Activities. He held the office of Secretary. Vice-President as well as the President of Dhaka District Sadar Postal Union. Mr Arun Kumar Sarker, the then Additional Director General. Bangladesh Post Office used to invite false and frivolous written allegation against the elected Union office-bearers. On the basis of anonymous petition he transferred the respondent to Dhaka GPO from Sadarghat Post Office and a number of inquiries were held to victimise the respondent. Subsequently a departmental proceeding was drawn up against the respondent bringing several charges at the instance of said Arun Kumar Sarker, ADG and a charge sheet drawn up on 6-4-1996 was sent to the respondent. The respondent submitted reply to the allegations mentioning some irregularities and mistakes for which he was not responsible and the Government did not sustain any financial loss due to the alleged irregularities Had there been really any financial loss the same could have been reported to law enforcing agencies but the authority proceeded against the respondent with the departmental proceeding by appointing Mr Abdus Sattar APMG (Security) who issued notice to the respondent on 4-7-1996 fixing 8-7-1996 for appearance and hearing. The respondent appeared before him and he was given questionnaire to which he was directed to reply in writing. The Enquiry Officer conduced enquiry is violation of the prescribed rules of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1985. The Enquiry Officer found the respondent guilty of the charges and the authority issued second show cause notice dated 28-8-96. The respondent submitted reply on 1-9-96 stating, inter alia, that he had no knowledge about the opening of more than one account in his name and he never committed any offence of temporary defalcation as alleged. Thereafter, the respondent was called for personal hearing at the office chamber of Post Master General. On appearance the respondent was again provided with a questionnaire and asked to give his written reply therein. Thereafter, the respondent received the impugned order of compulsory retirement from service dated 27-2-97 although he has still 10 years  service in his credit. The respondent preferred an appeal to the Director General Post Office on 29-5-97 who rejected the appeal on 23-12-97 most illegally upholding the Order of punishment of compulsory retirement from service.

3. The petitioners contested the case filing written statement denying material allegations stating, inter alia, that the respondent was appointed as Postal Clerk and he joined in service on 7-9-1971. Subsequently he was promoted to the post of Assistant Post Master and had been working In the said post from 14-11-1991. During the tenure of his service allegations were received against him for misappropriation of money from passbook account and Savings Defence Accounts of Post Office Branch wherein he was posted. The allegations were enquired into by the Additional Director General (Saving and Insurance) Postal Department. During enquiry it was found that one Dejindra Chandra Dutta opened Account No. RD1412 and received interest of the deposit on several occasions. Account No.4357 was opened In the same Post Office in his name against the Rules. Again, his another Account bearing No. FD 4740 was brought to the same Post Office on transfer. Respondent was acquainted with the said Dejindra Chandra Dutta and he was known to him since long and at his instance several accounts were opened illegally in the Post Office. Huge amount of Government money was unlawfully disbursed to him from" those accounts. Similarly. number of accounts were opened in the name of Himangsu Dutta and Prodip Kumar Dutta, sons of the aforesaid Dejindra Chandra Dutta most illegally causing financial loss to the Government. It was also found that the respondent tried to misappropriate Taka 6000 at the time of payment of a Defence Savings Certificate. When the occurrence of temporary defalcation came to the knowledge of the authority the respondent deposited. the amount of Taka 6000. He was found to have written excess amount by interpolation for the purpose of alleged misappropriation of Taka 6000 from Account No. FG 2091. So, in view of the aforesaid allegations charges were framed in the departmental proceeding against the respondent under rules 3(b) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1985. The respondent submitted reply to the charges and personally participated at the hearing of the proceeding case before the Enquiry Officer and the authority took the decision on the basis of enquiry report on serving second show cause notice in accordance with rules. There is no illegality in the matter of taking disciplinary action against the respondent and, as such, the case is liable to be dismissed.

4. The Administrative Tribunal dismissed the case and on appeal the same was reversed as aforesaid.

5. Mvi. Md Wahidullah, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the petitioners submitted that the enquiry officer held inquiry in accordance with rules and the respondent having legally been compulsorily retired the Administrative Tribunal rightly dismissed the Administrative Case No.114 of 1994 and thus Administrative Appellate Tribunal erred in law in disturbing the finding of facts duly arrived at by the Administrative Tribunal and, as such, the same requires Interference by this Division. The learned Advocate-on-Record further submitted that the Administrative Tribunal rightly held that rule VII and X of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1985 have been complied with and the Administrative Appellate Tribunal wrongly held otherwise. The learned Advocate-on-Record lastly, submitted that during the period of service of the respondent good amount was misappropriated out of the passbook and savings certificate and Administrative Tribunal rightly held so and dismissed the case of the respondent.

6. On perusal of the Impugned judgment it appears that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal arrived at a finding, inter alia, that:

"It further transpires from the written reply of the charges that the petitioner appellant did not admit his guilt except the irregularities with regard to a payment of Taka 6000 of Saving Defence Certificate and no charge under rule 3(d) for corruption was brought against him."

"It is evident that as per provision of Rule 10(4) of Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1985 no person was nominated to present the case in support of the charge before the enquiry officer."

"It is further evident that one GM Rafiqul Islam AFMG Central (Circle) sent notice on 15-9-1996 (Annexure 1) to the petitioner directing him to personally appear before the Post Master General OP Respondent No. 3 (appointing authority) on 6-10-1996 at 11-00 AM for hearing him in person and in the name of personal hearing some questionnaire was given to the petitioner to answer. So, the appearance of the petitioner before PMG during enquiry who happens to be the appointing authority of the petitioner is against the provisions of law. If the appointing authority OP No.3 PMG was not satisfied with the enquiry report he could easily pass an order for further enquiry on certain points with a view to arrive at the firm decision."

<u>7. It appears that the Tribunal wrongly placed onus of proof to substantiate charge against the respondent contrary to the established principles of law and natural justice inasmuch as the rules VII and X of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1985 have not been complied with thereby seriously prejudicing the respondent in his defence and accordingly, set aside the impugned order of compulsory retirement of the petitioner and restored him to his original position with all back wages and benefits as admissible under law. The authority imposing any punishment upon a delinquent staff has a duty to see that he has been dealt with in accordance with law and following the principles of natural justice.</u>

8. In the instant case the Administrative Appellate Tribunal on scrutiny found that the respondent has not been properly dealt with during the enquiry complying with the provision of law following the principles of natural justice and, as such, the impugned orders have been tainted with illegality making the same illegal and void and, as such, the same are not sustainable in law.

9. We have no reason to interfere with the impugned order of the Appellate Tribunal when apparently the respondent has not been dealt with in accordance with law following the principles of natural justice.

The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Debdas Somaddar with Dipayan Saha, Advocates------For the Petitioner. 
Md Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan  for Md Motahar Hossain Advocates------For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Abdul Mannan (Md) ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Md Faloo Munshi & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 24-5-2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 154 of 2000 reversing the judgment and order dated 22-5-2000 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dohar Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1999 dismissing the pre-emption proceeding should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party No. 1 being the preemptor filed Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1999 before the learned Assistant Judge, Dohar, Dhaka impleading the present petitioner being the pre-emptee and opposite party Nos. 2-8 as other opposite parties praying for pre-emption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act alleging, inter alia, that the preemptor is a co-sharer in the case holding by purchase and that the preemptee is a stranger purchaser. It is further alleged that the opposite parties, who are also co-sharer by purchase with the pre-emptor, by a registered kabala dated 27-8-1998 and pre-emptor learnt about the sale on 16-3-1999 and then filed the case on 11-10-1999.

3. The opposite party No. 1 contested the case by filing a written objection contending, amongst others, that the pre-emption application is hopelessly barred by limitation and that the pre-emptor had knowledge of the transfer from the date of the transfer.

4. The trial framed, necessary points for consideration and on consideration of the evidence on record' came to the finding that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by purchase but the pre-emptor could not prove his date of knowledge of the purchase and filing of the case within 4 months of the date of knowledge. Accordingly, by judgment and order dated 22-5-2000 the trial Court disallowed the pre-emption proceeding.

5. The pre-emptor then filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 154 of 2000 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. The learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka who heard the said appeal found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding and that the pre-emptor was successful in proving the date of his knowledge and filing of the case within 4 months from the date of knowledge. The learned Additional District Judge, accordingly, by judgment and order dated 24-5-2004 allowed the appeal, reversed the decision of the trial Court and allowed the prayer for pre-emption.

6. Being aggrieved thereby the pre-emptee as the petitioner moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Debdas Somaddar, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has taken me through the judgments of the courts below and submits that the pre-emptor mentioned in the application for pre-emption that he learnt about the transaction in question on 16-3-1999 but did not prove the date of his knowledge in his evidence. The learned Advocate has invited my attention to the evidence of PW 1 and submitted that PW 1 no where in his evidence disclosed that he came to know of the transfer in question for the first time on 16-3-1999. Mr Somaddar further submits that PW 2 is a close relation of PW 1 and PW 2 has disproved the petitioner's date of knowledge of the transfer and the learned Additional District Judge committed a serious error of law in not considering the evidence of PW 2 in the light of the pleadings of the parties and failed to notice that PW 2 being a highly interested person did not corroborate PW 1 on the aspect of the date of knowledge of the transfer in question. The learned Advocate also submits that section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that a preemption proceeding may be filed either within 4 months from the date of the transfer or within 4 months from the date of the knowledge of the transfer in question and, in case of knowledge of the transfer, specific date must be mentioned and proved in evidence otherwise it cannot be concluded that the pre-emptor has filed the pre-emption proceeding within 4 months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer in question. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Additional District Judge totally ignored to consider the evidence of pre-emptee who cross-examined 3 PWs in the case and, in support of his submission, has relied on a decision in the case of Abdul Mazid Howlader vs Lehajuddin Howlader and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 197=48 DLR (AD) 160.

8. Mr Md Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, on the other hand, supports the decision of the lower appellate Court arid submits, that though the preemptor as PW 1 did not disclose the date of his knowledge on 16-3-1999 for the first time, as alleged in the application for pre-emption, but has clearly deposed in evidence that "আমি নালিশী সম্পত্তি মাটি ভরাট করে ঘল কররা সিদ্ধান্ত নিয়েছি। গত চৈত্র মাসের প্রথম দিকে ঘর করা শুরু করিলে ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ আমাকে পুলিশ দ্বারা বাধা দেয় ১নং বিবাদী তখন আমাকে বলে যে সে নালিশী সম্পত্তি আমার ভাইয়ের নিকট হইতে খরিদ করেছে। তৎপর আমি নকল তুলে সম্যক বিষয়ে অবগত হয়ে অত্র মামলা করেছি।" Mr Bhuiyan has further submitted that in the cross-examination also PW 1 deposed that he filed the case in the last of Chaitra. It is further submitted that PW 1 was corroborated by PW 2 Mohibubur Rahman with regard to date of knowledge of the preemptor and the lower appellate Court, being the final court of fact, has rightly concluded that the pre-emptor has proved the date of knowledge of the transfer in question and this revisional court should not interfere with the finding of fact of the final court of fact. Mr Bhuiyan has produced a calendar ofthe Bangladesh Supreme Court published in 1999 in support of his submission that 16-3-1999 corresponds to 22nd Chaitra 1405 BS and 11-4-1999 which is the date of the filing of the case, corresponds to 28th Chaitra, 1405 BS. Mr Bhuiyan accordingly, submits that if the case is filed within 4 months from the date of knowledge, non-mentioning of the date in evidence could not defeat the claim of pre-emption. According to Mr Bhuiyan, if the case is filed within 4 months from the date of the knowledge, as deposed before the court it should be treated as due compliance of the requirement of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr Bhuiyan further shows from the evidence of PWs 1 that PW 1 and 2 reside side by side and accordingly, PW 2 is a natural and neutral witness to corroborate the evidence of PW 1. Mr Bhuiyan accordingly, submits that the lower appellate Court has recorded a finding of fact with regard to the date of knowledge of the transfer in question by the pre-emptor and has filed the case within 4 months thereof and this finding is based on consideration of the evidence on record and accordingly, may not be disturbed.

<u>9. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the impugned judgments and all other evidence on record. In the application for pre-emption, the preemptor has disclosed that he learnt about the transfer in question for the first time on 16-3-1999. This date 16-3-1999 was not proved in evidence. In evidence, the pre-emptor sought to make out a case that he learnt about the transfer in last of Chaitra which correspondents to March 1999. Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act clearly provides that a pre-emption application may be filed within 4 months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer in question. In order to calculate the period of limitation, law requires that a date must be mentioned as to the knowledge of the pre-emptor in respect of the transfer in question and not the month alone. Further, the evidence produced by PW I is contrary to his pleadings, as made out in the application for pre-emption. The right of pre-emption being a prerogative right must be applied for in terms of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and any deviation with regard to date of knowledge will debar the pre-emptor to get the relief. Apart from non-mentioning of the date of knowledge in evidence, it appears that PW 2, who is a brother-in-law of PW 1, has deposed in his cross-examination মান্নান বাধা দেওয়ার সময় আমি কাছারী ঘর বহুদুর ছিলাম বাধা দেওয়ার সময় উপস্থিত ছিলাম না।” He therefore, was not witness to prove the resistance offered ,by the. pre-emptee to the preemptor at the time of filling case on the case land. This evidence of PW 1 is therefore, not a direct evidence and at best be a hearsay witness in the eye of law. Besides, this PW 2 has clearly contradicted the evidence of PW 1. The evidence of PW 1 therefore, remains uncorroborated and thus the date of knowledge of the pre-emptor regarding transfer in question, as alleged by the pre-emptor and as deposed before the court has not been corroborated by any other witness and the evidence of PW 1 without any corroboration cannot be accepted to record a finding that the pre-emptor has proved the date of his knowledge of the transfer in question. The learned Additional District Judge has proceeded to decide that the pre-emptee could not prove that the pre-emptor had no knowledge of the date of the transfer till 16-3-1999 arid shifting of such onus on the pre-emptee has resulted in a serious miscarriage of justice. Law requires that the pre-emptor must prove his case that he filed the pre-emption application within 4 months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer in question and unless the pre-emptor proves such date of knowledge, onus does not shift on the pre-emptee to prove that the pre-emptor has knowledge from an earlier date or from the date of the transfer in question. It, therefore, appears that the learned Additional District Judge has committed an error of law in failing to hold that the pre-emptor could not prove his date of knowledge of the transfer in question and accordingly, it could not be held that the case was filed within 4 months from the date of knowledge of the transfer. It therefore appears that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal.</u>

10. The decision reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 197, as cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has no application in the facts of the present case. The present case is not a case of non-consideration of the evidence of the witnesses of the pre-emptee. In the said decision, our Appellate Division held "The judgment of the appellate Court was vitiated by total non-consideration of the evidence of all the 6 witnesses of the pre-emptees proving that the pre-emption case was barred by limitation. The High Court Division was wrong in refusing to exercise its revisional jurisdiction in the case where due to non-consideration of the material evidence on record an erroneous decision was arrived at occasioning a grave failure of justice." Their Lord- ships further held: "In the instant case, the application for pre-emption having been filed after 7 years of the disputed transfer, a heavy burden lay on the pre-emptor to discharge the onus of proof that he filed the case within the statutory period of 4 months of the date of his knowledge." The facts are quite distinguishable. In any view, the impugned judgment not being a proper judgment of reversal, I find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

11. Accordingly, this Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 24-5-2004 passed by the 3rd Court of the Additional District Judge, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 154 of 2000 is hereby set aside and those dated 22-5-2000 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dohar, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 19 of 1999 restored.

12. The order of stay as granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the LCR.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants. 
Ex Parte ----- The Respondents.
book_ref: 54 DLR (AD) 173,22 BLD (AD) 246,24 BLD (AD) 43,12 BLT (AD) 27,2 ADC 211,4 ADC 844,7 MLR (AD) 249
parties:
Santipada Datta & others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Satish Chandra Das and & others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 30th June 1993 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Order No. 1992 of 1993).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal by leave was to consider the submission that the High Court Division misdirected itself in holding that both the Courts below found that the plaintiff did not acquire title by adverse possession in that it was not noticed that the material evidence in that behalf was overlooked by both the Courts inasmuch as the same mistake was committed by the learned Judge himself and it was wrongly held that the elements constituting adverse possession are lacking in the case. The evidence of defendant No.1 DW 1 who was examined on commission and the only witness for the defendants if considered along with other evidence and circumstances unmistakably prove the plaintiffs possession for more than 12 years which was adverse to the admitted owner and as such, the plaintiff is entitled to a declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession.

2. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title to the suit land by purchase or adverse possession and further that the order dated 6-2-1989 of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Comilla declaring the suit land as enemy property is illegal and inoperative.

3. The appellant instituted the suit stating, inter alia. that the suit land originally belonged to one Raj Lakshmi Devi, who granted settlement by a registered patta dated 29-4-1903 to one Mohesh Chandra Bhattacharjee; that on the death of the said Mahesh Chandra his wife Kala Kamini Devi and his two sons, Bidhu Bhusan and Narendra Bhattacharjee, sold the same to defendant No.1 by a kabala dated 5- 2-1940 for Taka 2,500.00 and handed over possession thereof to him; that while in possession, defendant No.1 who was in urgent need for going to Calcutta sold the suit land to the appellant for Taka 5001.00 and granted a receipt therefore on 14-2-1949; that at the time of appellant's purchase there was three huts on the suit land which were in possession of the tenants and the appellant had been possessing the suit land upon realising rents from the tenants openly and peacefully over the statutory period of 12 years to the knowledge of all concerned; that one BP Mazumder filed Miscellaneous Case No. 201 of 1964-65 in the Court of SDO, Chandpur for declaring the suit property as enemy property but the said case was rejected by order dated 23-8-1965; that thereafter one Sisir Das filed another petition on 10-9-1965 which was also dismissed on contest on 9-6-1966; then Sisir Das filed another application on 16-6-1966 which was sent to SDM for disposal who upon hearing the matter by his order dated 24-2-1967 directed the Tahsilder not to realise any rent from the tenants that against the said order Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1967-68 was started in the Court of ADC, Comilla who by order dated 6-3-1969 illegally declared the suit property as enemy property; that the plaintiff by virtue of his purchase and also because of his long possession over the statutory period has acquired lawful right, title and interest in the suit land and hence the suit.

4. The respondent-defendant Nos. 2 and 3 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that defendant No.1 being the owner of the suit land was in possessing of a part of the same and in the remaining portion he inducted tenants and was possessing the same through them upon realising monthly rents; that long after partition and some time before 1965 the said defendant No.1 left for India; that after the war of 1965 the suit land became enemy property and the same vested in defendant Nos. 2 and 3. That defendant No.1 did not transfer the suit land to the plaintiff, did not accept any consideration and did not grant any receipt as alleged. The alleged receipt dated 14-2-1949 is forged and fabricated; that the plaintiff has no right or possession in the suit land and that the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court and on an appeal the same was affirmed. The High Court Division summarily rejected the application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure by the impugned order against which the aforesaid leave was granted.

<u>6. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel, submits that the High Court Division as well as the Courts below misread the evidence on record and wrongly held that elements constituting adverse possession are lacking in the case and dismissed the revisional application upon an illegal view that the plaintiff did not acquire title by adverse possession inasmuch as the evidence of defendant No.1 who was examined on commission as DW 1 and the evidence of DW 1, if considered along with other evidence on record, unmistakably prove adverse possession of plaintiff for over 12 years and the High Court Division was therefore wrong in dismissing the revisional application in agreeing with the Courts below that the plaintiff did not acquire title by adverse possession.</u>

7. It appears that the suit was filed by Satish Chandra Das on the averments, inter-alia, that:

মোকাদ্দমা নালিশী ভূমিতে বাদীর খরিদা রায়তী সত্বে এবং দ্বাদশ বর্ষের উর্ধ্বকালীয় অন্যের বিরুদ্ধে দখল জনিত স্বত্ব সাব্যস্তে দখল স্থিরিতর থাকার বাবদ দাবী মং ৬,৩০০=টাকা। এ,ডি,সি সাহেবের উক্ত আদেশ সম্পূর্ণ বে-আইনী বটে। পূর্বেই উল্লেখ করা হইয়াছে যে এনেমী প্রোপার্টি ডিকলার করার আইন আমলে আসার পূর্বেই বাদী নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে অকাট্য রায়তী স্বত্ব অর্জন করিয়াছিলেন।সুতরাং নালিশী সম্পত্তি ১ নং বিবাদীর স্বত্ব দখলীয় সম্পত্তি হিসাবে এনামী প্রোপার্টি বলিয়া ডিকলার হইতে পারে না।

এই স্থলে উল্লেখযোগ্য বটে ভাড়াটিয়াগণ মধ্যে ৪ নং বিবাদী বাদীর বিরুদ্ধে নানা প্রকার পরোক্ষ ও প্রত্যক্ষ কার্যে লিপ্ত থাকায় বাদী তাহাকে (উত্তরের ভিটির পূর্ব দিকের ঘরে ভাড়াটিয়া) ভাড়া আদায় না করার হেতুতে উচ্ছেদ করার জন্য চাঁদপুর ১ম মুন্সেপী আদালতে ১৯৬৭ ইং সনের ২৩৬ নং দেঃ মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করে কিন্তু বাদী নালিশী সম্পত্তিরর কোন স্বত্তের দলিল দেখাইতে না পারায় নিম্ন আদালতে বাদীর মোকাদ্দমা ডিসমিস হইয়া যায়|

বাদীর নালিশী সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কে কোন স্বত্বের দলিল না থাকায় বাদীর নানা অসুবিধা সৃষ্টি হইয়াছে|উক্ত অবস্থায় নালিশী ভূমিতে বাদীর খরিদা ও দ্বাদশ বর্ষের উর্দ্ধকালীয় অন্যের বিরুদ্ধে দখল জনিত রায়তী স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত করার জন্য এব্য নালিশী সম্পত্তি শত্রু সম্পত্তি বলিয়া ঘোষনা করার আদেশ বে-আইনী ও অকার্যকর বলিয়া ডিক্লারেশন পাওয়ার জন্য ওই মোকাদ্দমা করিতে বাধ্য হইল|

নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদীর খরিদা রায়তী স্বত্ব ও দ্বাদশ বর্ষের উর্দ্ধকালব্যাপী অন্যের বিরুদ্ধে দখল জনিত স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত তাহাতে বাদীর দখল স্থিরতর থাকার আদেশ দিতে-

The plaintiff accordingly led evidence as to the acquisition of title by adverse possession through PWs 1 and 2. The defendant though adduced one witness i.e, Tahshildar, who could not assail any of the assertions of the plaintiff but admitted that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and that the plaintiff and the tenants of original owner Satish have been in possession of the suit land by constructing houses thereof and that the suit land has not been leased out to anybody treating the same as vested property. The trial Court, however, simply treating the suit to be of declaration of title with prayer for confirmation of possession and without considering the evidence on record held that the plaintiff has collusively with the defendant No. 1 filed Ext. 1 to create his adverse title over adverse possession of the suit land and Satish lived in India for more than 30 years and, as such, the suit property was legally declared as the enemy property.

8. The Court of appeal below, however, on consideration of the evidence on record arrived at a finding that though the appellant could not prove his title on the basis of patta from the original owner Satish as there is no legal document conferring the title of the plaintiff but the plaintiff have been able to prove their possession over a period of 12 years thereby acquiring an indefeasible title by way of adverse possession. The defendant Satish while examining on commission as DW 2 has admitted the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. But held that the plaintiff has intelligently created the papers for acquiring the suit land and, as such, relying on the Dhakhila the possession of the plaintiff would not be supported as accordingly dismissed the appeal.

9. In the case of Mir Laik Ali vs Standard Vacuum Oil Co. reported in 16 DLR (SC) 287 it has been held that:

"When there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferor."

10. Thus when there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferee. If he continues in possession of immoveable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an in-defeasible title.

11. In the case of Abdul Jalil Miah vs Niropama Ritchil reported in 49 DLR (AD) 61:

"As to the second and the most vital aspect of the case, namely, title by adverse possession, a few facts may not be lost sight of. Adverse possession implies that it had commenced in wrong and is maintained against right. The plaintiff has claimed to have his entry into the disputed land under an agreement of purchase with defendant No. 1 who had no title thereto as found by the trial Court and which finding was not reversed by the appellate Court. In such a case when the plaintiff after getting into possessing retains the same with clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property in complete negation of any right or title of the true owner thereof ie defendant No. 2, his enjoyment would be solely in assertion of hostile title."

12. In the case of Abdul Kader vs Noor Mohammad 36 DLR (AD) 261 this Court quoted with approval the following observation of Sanderson CJ that: "the term adverse possession implies that the person against whom adverse possession is exercised is a person who is entitled to demand possession at the moment adverse possession begins."

13. In the case of Ejaz Ali Qidwai vs Special Manager; Court of wards, Bulrampur Estate AIR 1935 PC 53 the principle of adverse possession was laid when "a person who bases his title on adverse possession by clear and unequivocal evidence that his possession was hostile to the real owner and amounted to a denial of his title to the property claimed."

14. In the case of Hafiz Mohammad Fateh Nasib vs Sir Swamp Chandra Hukum Chand (1947) 52 CWN 382 the list to be applied in respect of adverse possession has been spelt out as "The Correct test to be applied in a case of this nature is, whether the claimant exercised such domain over the property as to justify the inference that he was in possession of the whole. It is not necessary for him to prove that he was in physical possession of every square inch." Thus possession under a mistaken or invalid title is as effective as that of a trespasser and If sufficient in length of time and continuity gives the holder a title.

15. The learned Counsel has further submitted with reference to the case of Mother Sowdagar vs Z Alam reported in 40 DLR (AD) 62 that the concurrent finding of fact not based on evidence on record or based on misreading thereof is not immune from interference in revision.

16. The learned Counsel has further submitted the decision in the case of Abdul Kader and others vs AK Noor Mohammad and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 261 that the finding on the basis of no evidence is of no legal consequence and the finding of the Courts below could be disturbed if there is any misreading of the evidence or misconstruction of evidence.

<u>17. From the evidence we find that the plaintiff has categorically deposed that he has been in possession on the basis of lease granted through receipt and that the lease has been supported by the receipt issued at a time when the plaintiff was present and the same has been supported by PW 2. Defendant No. 1 examined on commission stated that he has transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff on the basis of receipt which was written in presence of the witnesses and delivered the huts to the plaintiff on receipt of the consideration money and duly signed the receipt evidencing receipt of the amount on 14-2-49. Since the receipt is not a deed of title it could not confer title to the plaintiff under the provision of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act but the uninterrupted adverse and hostile possession of the plaintiff over a period of 12 years from the date of 14 February 1949 up to 1961 ie., the period prior of alleged declaration of property as enemy property, the plaintiff has acquired title by adverse possession.</u>

<u>18. Thus the Courts below on misreading of evidence on record and on misconception of law as aforesaid wrongly held that elements constituting adverse possession are lacking in the case and most illegally dismissed the suit by the impugned judgments and accordingly, the suit succeeds and the impugned judgment of the High Court Division affirming those of the Courts below are set aside and the suit is decreed without any order as to costs.</u>

In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the suit is decreed without any costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by the defendants upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against order No. 10 dated 8-10-2001 passed by Joint District Judge, Court No. 1 at Gazipur in Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 2001, which allowed a prayer for inspection of the suit land.

2. Opposite party as plaintiff on 8-8-2001 instituted Title Suit No. 145 of 2001 against the defendants for a decree of perpetual injunction. In the plaint, it is stated that the plaintiff purchased the suit lands described fully in schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' to the plaint from different vendors at various times, and got his name mutated. He has been possessing the suit land by paying rents, taxes, etc. The land in 'Kha' schedule measures about 4.28 acres and is bounded by a wall. The defendants have got a land to the east of his 'Kha' schedule land. When, the plaintiff started work to raise the height of the wall, on 4-8-2001 the defendants obstructed and beat the workers, and tried to forcibly enter into the land by breaking the eastern wall.

3. On such averments, same date the plaintiff made an application under Order XXXIX rule 1 and 2 of the Code for temporary injunction for restraining the defendants from forcibly entering into the land of 'Ka' schedule by breaking the boundary wall and/or interfering, in any way, with the peaceful enjoyment of the land including ongoing construction till disposal of the suit. He also prayed for an order of ad-interim injunction in the above terms. Hearing the application, learned Joint District Judge was pleased to issue notice upon the defendants asking them to show cause as to why they should not be so restrained, and was further pleased to grant an order of ad interim injunction as prayed for restraining them from entering into schedule "Kha" land.

4. The plaintiff then, on 20-8-2001 made and moved an application under Order XXXIX rule 2(3) of the Code for taking action against the defendants and the Officer-in-charge, Hotapara Police Post for violation of the order of injunction dated 8-8-2001. In the application, it is stated that on 9-8-2001 the plaintiff informed the officers-in-charge of Joydebpur police station and Hotapara police post in writing of the order of injunction. On 13-8-2001 the process server duly served the writ of ad-injunction upon the defendants. But on 14-8-2001 at about 11-00 AM violating the order of injunction, the defendant with the help of about 200/250 miscreants, and in presence of the police-in-charge of the Hotapara police post forcibly entered into the land of 'Kha' schedule from the east by breaking through the 593-feet long eastern wall. They took away stacked materials, rods, cement, bricks, sand chips etc worth of 5,68,289, and/or damaged. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 2001 (violation). Notice was issued upon the defendants and 30-9-2001 was fixed for SR. Same date, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 appeared and filed a joint written objection to the application for temporary injunction denying the entire case of the plaintiff, whereupon 26-8-2001 was fixed for hearing of the matter.

5. Then, on 9-9-2001 in the violation case the plaintiff made and moved an application under Order XXXIX rule 7 of the Code for appointment of an Advocate, Commissioner for inspection of the suit land of 'Kha' schedule, which was ordered to be heard on date earlier fixed i.e. 8-10-2001. On 8-10-2001, hearing the application, learned Joint District Judge by the impugned order, allowed the same being of the view that whether or not there was any violation should be ascertained by a commission, and asked the plaintiff to deposit Taka 1,000,00 only as commissioner's fees. After such order was passed, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 made and moved two applications, one for time for filing written objection to the application for violation of injunction and the other for setting aside the order allowing the prayer for inspection. The learned Joint District Judge allowed the prayer for time but rejected the latter on the view that such order for local inspection would not prejudice any of the parties to the suit.

6. Mr Ajmalul Hossain, learned Senior Counsel assails the order for local inspection on various grounds. Firstly, he submits that the order is bad since it was passed without any notice upon the defendants and behind their back. He submits that under Order XXXIX rule 8 of the Code no such order for inspection can be passed without a notice upon the defendants. He cites the decision in the case of Mohammed Mobarak Hossain vs Md Mostafa Hossain, 1987 BLD (AD) 263 = 40 DLR (AD) 20. It is true that rule 8 of Order XXXIX of the Code requires a notice to be served upon the other side before any order is passed under rule 7. But the rule does not appear to be inflexible. In an appropriate case where delay may defeat the whole purpose of the order, Court may pass such order ex parte. Of course, no hard and fast rule could be prescribed for that. In the decision, the Appellate Division confirmed the order of this Division affirming an ex parte order allowing local inspection for making an inventory.

7. In the case before us, we find on 9-9-2001 the application for local inspection was filed in Court after service of a copy thereof upon the learned Advocate for the defendants. Then, the application was taken up on 8-10-2001 the date earlier fixed for hearing, when the defendants filed hajira. But the defendants did not contest the application. Then, after the order was passed they made an application for setting aside the order, which was, of course, rejected. In such circumstances, the submission of Mr Hossain cannot be accepted that the order was passed behind the back of the defendants.

8. Secondly, he submits that the order is not a speaking one as it is not supported by any reason whatsoever. The order reads as hereunder,

“শুনলাম। প্রযালোচনা করলাম। আতি একটি ভায়োলেশনের মামলা।ভায়োশেন হয়েছে কি না,তা কমিশনের মাধ্যমেই নিরুপন যোগ্য বিধায় কমিশন দরখাস্ত মঞ্জুর করা গেল।”

9. Same date, rejecting the application of the defendants, learned Joint District Judge also observed that such order for local inspection would not prejudice any of the parties to the suit. So, it is not correct to say, no reason was given for the order. Reason may be sketchy. But whether or not the alleged violation on 14-8-2001 of the injunction order dated 8-8-2001 could be determined by inspection under Order XXXIX rule 7 of the Code is a separate question altogether, which is raised before us as the moot issue for our determination.

<u>10. Mr Hossain took us through the plaint and all other applications filed by the plaintiff. He also read Order XXVI and XXXIX of the Code. He submits that learned Joint District Judge erred in law in allowing the application for local inspection of such facts and incidents which could only be investigated under Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code. Elaborating, he submits that under Order XXXIX rule 7 of the Code neither boundary disputes can be ascertained nor any evidence could validly be collected thereon. He finally, submits that learned Joint District Judge failed to appreciate the distinction between "inspection" and "investigation', and acted illegally in allowing the prayer for local inspection, since what can only be found out by local investigation cannot be permitted to be inspected. He relies upon the case of Maulana Abdul Motin and others vs Shah Alam Bhuiyan and others, 41 DLR 244; Londa Colliery vs Bholanath. AIR 1954 Cal 233; Institution of Engineers vs Bishnu Pada, AIR 1978 Cal 296; Ministry of Industries and another vs Shaft A Chowdhury 47 DLR 443; Mahendranath vs Puranananda. AIR 1988 Orissa 248; Kazi Abdul Awal Zewar Rashid vs Dhaka Municipal Corporation and another, 45 DLR 509; Abdur Rouf Chowdhury vs Abdul Hashem and another, 53 DLR 458; Ntindra Nath Roy and others vs Subhas Ch Kar, 85 CWN 915 and Serajuddin Ahmed vs Upendra Narayan Lala and others 22 DLR 827.</u>

<u>11. Opposing the Rule, Mr Habibullah, learned Senior Counsel, submits that as the defendants violated the order of injunction by entering into the suit land of 'Kha'-schedule by breaking the eastern wall, the learned Joint District Judge was justified to order for local investigation to ascertain whether or not there was any such violation and there is no reason for the defendants to become aggrieved. He cites the cases of Amulya Kumar Samaddar and another vs Annada Charan Dab and others, 37 CWN 143. where local inspection was granted to ascertain as to whether or not certain structures were old or newly constructed; Mahmud Ibne Abbas vs Begum Momtaz Hossain and another 45 DLR 421, where local inspection was ordered to ascertain whether there was any house on the suit land; and the case reported in AIR 1989 Orissa 214.</u>

12. The question raised at the Bar so seriously that it deserves a thorough consideration and determination of the nature and extent of the power of the Court under Order XXXIX rule 7 vis-a-vis Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code, to order for an inspection. We heard the learned Counsels at length. We have also read the case as relied upon by them. In order to appreciate their submissions, we first need to refer to both provisions of Order XXXIX rule 7 and Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code. Order XXXIX rule 7 reads.

"7( I) The Court may, on the application of any party to a suit, and on such terms at it thinks fit,-

(a) make an order for the detention, preservation or inspection of any property which is the subject matter of such suit, or as to which any question may arise therein;

(b) for all or any of the purposes aforesaid authorise any person to enter upon or into any land or building in the possession, of any other party to such suit; and

(c) for all or any of the purposes aforesaid authorise any samples to be taken, or any observation to be made or experiment to be tried, which may seem necessary or expedient for the purpose of obtaining full information or evidence."

Whereas Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code reads as hereunder,

"In any suit in which the Court deems a local investigation to be requisite or proper for the purpose of eliciting any matter in dispute, or of ascertaining the market-value of any property, or the amount or any mesne profits or damages or annual net profits, the Court may issue a commission to such person as it thinks fit directing him to make such investigation and to report thereon to the Court within such time not exceeding three months as may be fixed by the Court:

Provided that the Court may, on the prayer of Commissioner and on sufficient cause being shown, extend the time."

13. Under rules 6, 7, 9 or 10 of Order XXXIX of the Code the Court is empowered to pass various orders in a given situation, which are essentially in nature interlocutory. Interlocutory order as intended by the legislature must be one passed during the course of an action and incidental to the principal object of the action, say, an action like the one taken by the plaintiff against violation of an injunction order under rule 2(3) or Order XXXIX of the Code. The provisions enable a party to take interlocutory action for the purpose of assisting him in the prosecution of his cause or protecting or otherwise dealing with the subject matter of the suit.

14. Under rule 7 of Order XXXIX of the Code, the Court may make an order for the detention, preservation or inspection of the subject matter of the suit or any question arising therein. The words detention or preservation of a property does not appear to be of any ambiguity but inspection of suit property gives rise to much controversy as to its nature and extent, particularly, vis-a-vis investigation under Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code. When the meaning and scope of the word inspection is understood, the nature and extent of the power of the Court to order for inspection would be clearer.

15. Plain meaning of the word inspection is to examine a thing or incident very closely. In Ministry of Industries vs Shaft A Chowdhury, it is observed that the word inspection cannot have a separate meaning and its meaning is restricted by the words detention, preservation, which preceded it to "inspection for the purpose of detention or preservation". One thing however, must be kept in mind that inspection can be ordered only in respect of the subject matter of the suit and any question arising thereto. The Court may authorise any person to enter upon or into land or building in the possession of any other party to such suit to collect samples or carry out observation or to do experiment, which it may deem necessary for the purpose of full information or evidence in respect of the subject matter of the suit only.

16. Whereas, under Order XXVI rule 9 of the Code where the Court believes a local investigation to be requisite or necessary for the purpose of elucidating of any matter in dispute, or ascertaining damages, etc, it may issue a commission to a person directing him to make such investigation and to report back thereon to the Court. Under rule 10(1) of the Order, after such investigation, the Commissioner shall return all such evidence he collected together with his report duly signed by him. Under rule 10(2) of the Order, the report of the Commissioner and the evidence taken by him shall be evidence in the suit and shall form part of the record. What is the evidentiary value of such evidence is not at all an issue before us.

17. Investigation however, requires examination and discovery of all facts and circumstances about any fact in issue in order to obtain the truth. Investigation leads a commissioner to go beyond what he sees on the spot and to find out the truth on behalf of the Court by collecting evidence and examination of witnesses, which from its peculiar nature can be best had from the spot. Such evidence enables the Court to understand or assess the fact in issue or which clarifies or explains any point. But the Court cannot direct such commissioner to decide any issue, which ought to be decided by Court on evidence. Assistance of the commissioner is necessary to elucidate any ambiguous or cryptic in Court. On the other hand, a person authorised under rule 7 of Order XXXIX of the Code has got no power to collect such evidence. He will go to the spot to examine the subject matter of the suit or to do anything in respect of such subject matter as the Court directs him to do, and inform back to the Court. In directing an inspection the Court must keep this distinction in mind, and it must not extend the scope of inspection to that of local investigation.

18. Now, turning to the facts of the case at hand, we find that in the application for an order of inspection the plaintiff stated that on 14-8-2001 the defendants entered into the land of 'kha' schedule by breaking the 539 feet eastern wall, and in the interest of justice, a report by inspection was sought for on the following.

“(ক) বাদীর ‘খ’ তফসিল বর্ণিত সমপত্তির পূর্ব পার্শে বাউন্ডারি ওয়াল ছিল কি না?এবং উক্ত ওয়াল ভাংগা হইয়াছে কি না এবং বর্তমানে কি অবস্থায় আছে।

(খ) দরখাস্তকারী/বাদীর ‘খ’ তফসিল বর্ণিত সমপত্তিতে প্রতিপক্ষের দ্বারা পাকা পিলার নির্মাণ হয়েছে কি না? হইলে উহার পরিধি পরিমাণ ও বয়স কত?”

19. By making the application under rule 7 of Order XXXIX of the Code, the plaintiff sought for inspection to ascertain whether or not there was any wall on the eastern boundary of 'kha' schedule land and/or such wall was broken down; or whether or not, the defendants constructed any pillars on 'kha' schedule land of the plaintiff, and if they did, then what are the present age or dimensions of such pillars. In view of the provisions of rule 7 of Order XXXIX of the Code, the Court cannot order an inspection to ascertain the facts, since finding out the truth as to the facts would require the person to be appointed to collect evidence and examine witnesses. It should not escape the notice that all such facts had to be ascertained with reference to 14-8-2001 only, the alleged date of incident. There may however be a valid order for inspection of the present position of the suit land as Mr Habibullah seriously pressed for, but such inspection would not serve any useful purpose for determination of the alleged violation on 14-8-2001 of the injunction order dated 8-8-2001.

<u>20. Learned Joint District Judge fell in serious error in allowing the prayer on the view, whether or not there was violation of the injunction order was determinable by commissioner. Whether or not there was any violation of the ad-interim order of injunction dated 8-8-2001 and/or whether or not the defendants on 14-8-2001 violated the injunction order are the pertinent issues to be determined by the Court itself in the proceeding against violation of Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 2001. The Court cannot delegate its power to any person. In the proceeding pending against violation of an order of injunction under rule 2(3) of Order XXXIX of the Code, the plaintiff would have ample opportunity to prove his case of violation by evidence.</u>

<u>21. We therefore find, in total misconception of the law and without applying his judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the law, learned Joint District Judge allowed the prayer of the plaintiff and appointed a commissioner. We have therefore no hesitation to say that the learned Joint District Judge acted illegally in ordering inspection in the case by impugned order, which has, no doubt, resulted in failure of justice.</u>

22. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. The impugned order dated 8-10-2001 ordering inspection is hereby set aside. Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule 11-11-2001 is recalled and vacated, learned Joint District Judge is directed to proceed expeditiously with the proceedings pending before him.

Communicate.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule, at the instance of the defendant-appellant-petitioner is directed against the judgment and decree dated 7-6-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Gopalganj in Title Appeal No. 37 of 2001 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2001 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge (in charge), Gopalganj Sadar, Gopalganj in Title Suit No. 120 of 1997.

2. The case of the plaintiff, in brief, is that the defendant No.1 proposed to sell the suit property to the plaintiff and the plaintiff agreed to the proposal. Thereafter on the 16th Magh 1402 BS in presence of the witnesses the sale value of the suit land was settled at Taka 14,100 and it was also settled that the plaintiff would pay Taka 13,800 to the defendant No. 1 within 5 days and accordingly, the defendant No.1 delivered possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff. Pursuant to that decision the plaintiff paid Taka 13,500 to the defendant"No. 1 on the 20th Magh, 1402 BS in presence of the neighbouring people. The defendant No.1 accordingly, delivered possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff and gave undertaking that on payment of rest Taka 600 she would execute and register the kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff. Since then the plaintiff has been enjoying and possessing the suit land by erecting hut thereupon. At the time of receiving the advance money the defendant No.1 delivered the sub-kabala deed of the suit land to the plaintiff. The defendant No.1 lives with her husband in Khulna and off and on she used to visit the village home. Subsequently, the defendant No.1 was requested on different occasions to receive the remaining amount of consideration money and to execute and register the kabala in favour of the plaintiff but the defendant No.1 on different pleas evaded to comply with the same. Thereafter, on 29-7-1997 the plaintiff in presence of the witnesses again requested the defendant No.1 to receive the rest amount of consideration money and to execute and register the kabala deed but the defendant No.1 refused to execute and register the kabala deed and hence the plaintiff has been constrained to bring the present suit for specific performance of contract.

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations brought in the plaint stating, inter alia, that the defendant No.1 never made any proposal to the plaintiff to sell the suit land to him, there was no settlement of consideration money therefor and the defendant No.1 never received any consideration money from the plaintiff as alleged. The defendant No.1 never delivered possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff and she did never give any undertaking to execute and register a kabala deed in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land as alleged. In fact, there was no agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 in respect of transfer of the suit land. The husband of the defendant No.1 and the plaintiff belong to the same kindred. The defendant No.1 used to live in Khulna with her husband but now she lives in her village home since last two and half years. There is a good relationship between the defendant No.1 and the plaintiff and because of that relationship the defendant No.1 gave the responsibility to the plaintiff through her husband to record her name in the last field survey and for this purpose she handed over the copy of the kabala deed of the suit land for the time being to the plaintiff in presence of the neighbouring people of the village, namely, Babul Kazi, Nowsher Kazi and Jaliluddin Kazi. Subsequently, the defendant No.1 requested the plaintiff to return the said original kabala deed but the plaintiff on different pleas was making delay and thereafter, with intent to grab the suit land, the plaintiff brought the instant suit on false contention and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost.

4. Three witnesses for the plaintiff and 2 witnesses for the defendant No.1 were examined in the case. The trial Court considering the evidence adduced by the parties decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff against which the defendant No. 1 preferred the appeal being Title Appeal No. 37 of 2001 before the learned District Judge, Gopalganj which was ultimately disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Gopalganj by his judgment and decree dated 7-6-2001 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2001 passed by the trial Court in Title Suit No. 120 of 1997.

5. Being aggrieved by that judgment and decree dated 7-6-2001 the defendant appellant- petitioner has preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that there was no contract for sale in respect of the suit land between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 and that the plaintiff did never pay any consideration money to the defendant No.1. also did never receive any consideration money from the plaintiff in respect of the suit land as alleged and that the plaintiff instituted the suit only with intent to grab the suit land on false and baseless allegations. further submits that the plaintiff hopelessly failed to substantiate his claim by adducing any independent and most reliable witnesses since it is a case of oral contract inasmuch as the plaintiff hopelessly failed to prove the talk of the contract and payment of the contract but in spite of the fact the trial Court by non-consideration and mis-appreciation of the material evidence on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. He further submits that the appellate Court below also by non-consideration and mis-appreciation of material evidence on record affined the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court although the appellate Court below found gross discrepancies in the evidence of the PWs regarding talk of the contract, payment of the contract and number of currency notes paid therefor. Had the Courts below closely scrutinized those evidence the result of the suit and the appeal would have been otherwise. In the circumstances the judgment and decrees passed by the appellate Court below as well as by the trial Court have resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and the same are not sustainable in law.

7. Mr Md Aminul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.1, submits that the impugned judgment and decrees passed by the appellate Court below and the trial Court suffer from no infirmity on the ground of non-consideration and mis-appreciation of the material evidence on record and there is no reason that may call for interference with the impugned judgment and decrees.

8. Heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the revisional application, the impugned judgment and decrees and the LC Records.

9. It is a case of oral agreement for sale of an immovable property. So far as the oral agreement is concerned, it should always be very closely scrutinised and taken with a grain of salt. Although an oral agreement for sale of immovable property is not barred by law, it is to be looked at with some suspicion unless it is proved by reliable evidence. Now let us see how far the plaintiff has been able to substantiate his case of oral agreement by adducing reliable evidence.

10. Plaintiff, appearing as PW 1, stated in his examination-in-chief that the talk of sale of the suit land was held in the "Kachari Ghar" of the defendant and payment was made in the house of the defendant No.1. But in cross-examination he (PW 1) stated that the talk of sale was held on 15th Magh, 1402 BS in the Bazar at the tea-stall of Nitu Mia and at that time except Nitu Mia and himself none was present. In the plaint it is stated that the talk of sale was held in the house of defendant No. 1 and the payment was made in "Baithak Khana". PW I has stated that at the time of talk Bashu Sikder, Sana Mia, Mokbul and Akhtar Kazi were present and except those none was present. Besides, PW 1 stated in his evidence that Sana Mia was present at the time of talk. But in the plaint the name of Sona Mia is totally absent.

11. In view of the above self-contradictory statements of plaintiff PW 1 regarding time and place of talk of the contract as well as payment of the consideration money of the contract inasmuch as absence of the defendant No. 1 in the evidence of PW 1 on the aforesaid occasions give rise to concoction as to veracity of the alleged oral contract for sale of the suit land.

12. PW 2 Mokbul Sikder stated in his evidence that talk of contract was held at the "Kachari Ghar" of Julhash but the plaint case is that the talk was held in the house of the defendant. PW 2 also stated that Abu Sayed was present at the time of payment of the consideration money. But in the plaint it is stated that Abu Sayed was present only at the time of talk of sale. Besides, PW 2 did not state in his evidence that defendant No.1 was present at the talk of contract. PW 2 also did not state that consideration money was paid to the defendant No.1.

13. So, from close scrutiny of the evidence of PW 2, his testimony regarding talk of the contract with the defendant No.1 as well as payment of the consideration money to the defendant No.1 look askance at to believe that there was a contract for sale of the suit land between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 as alleged.

14. PW 3 Sona Mia did not state where consideration money was paid. He stated in his examination-in-chief that Bashu Sikder, Mokbul Sikder and Abu Sayed were present at the time of payment of consideration money but neither the plaint nor plaintiff, as PW 1, did mention that Abu Sayed was present at the time of payment of the consideration money.

15. The above evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3 are contradictory to each other regarding time and place of talk of the alleged contract and date of payment of the consideration money which also do not disclose that the plaintiff had ever any talk of sale with the defendant No.1 in respect of the Suitland and the plaintiff ever paid any consideration money to the defendant No.1 as alleged.

16. Besides the above, in view of the testimony of plaintiff PW I as well as of PW 3, some Bashu Sikder, Akhtar Kazi and Abu Sayed are the important witnesses with regard to the alleged contract. But they being neighbours of both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and also being important witnesses have not been examined in this case, rather, the plaintiff examined some Mokbul Sheikh as PW 2 and Sona Mia as PW 3 who being closely related to the plaintiff belonging to different villages cannot be considered to be impartial and disinterested witnesses. Withholding of the aforesaid disinterested neighboring witnesses in the case by the plaintiff gives rise to a presumption that had they been examined in the case they would not have supported the plaintiffs case and, as such, the defendant No, 1 is entitled to get the benefit of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. Tender and refusal to accept the consideration money by the defendant No.1 has also not been proved and with this the plaintiff has totally failed to prove his cause of action in filing the suit.

17. The plaintiff must prove his own case and weakness of the defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff although the defendant No.1 has examined 2 witnesses in this case who have deliberately denied the fact of the alleged contract for sale of the suit land.

<u>18. From the close scrutiny of the facts, circumstances and evidence as above it appears that the plaintiff has hopelessly failed to prove by reliable evidence that there was ever any oral agreement for sale of the suit land between himself and the defendant No.1 as alleged. The plaintiff not having disclosed the material facts in respect of time, place, talk and the payment of consideration money of the alleged contract in the evidence adduced by him, which are the foundation of a contract, both the courts below by mis-appreciation and non-consideration of those aspects of the material evidence passed the impugned judgment and decrees which has resulted in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the same are not sustainable in the eye of law.</u>

19. In the facts and circumstances of the case when there is mis-appreciation and non-consideration of some material evidence then it is incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case.

20. I find instant support of my above views in the case of Hossain Ahmed Chowdhury @ Ahmed Hossain Chowdhury and others vs Md Nurul Amin and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 and in the case of Muslemuddin (Md) and others vs Md Jonab Ali and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 13.

21. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs.

22. The impugned judgment and decree dated 7-6-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Gopalganj in Title Appeal No. 37 of 2001 as well as those dated 31-1-2001 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge (in charge), Gopalganj Sadar, Gopalganj in Title Suit No. 120 of 1997 are hereby set aside.

Send down the LC Records at once.

End.

lawyer:
KS Zaman, Advocate------For the Appellant. 
Rafiqur Rahman with Serajur Rahman, Hasnat Quaiyum and Nasima Akhter, Advocates------For the Respondents.
parties:
Uttara Bank Ltd ------Appellant
vs
Aysha Siddiqua and others ------Respondent
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: The Uttara Bank presented the above appeal against judgment and decree dated 11-8-1999 passed by Subordinate Judge and Additional Artha Rin Adalat No. 1 at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 34 of 1998, which decreed the suit in part.

2. The appellant as plaintiff on 31-7-1997 instituted Title Suit No. 142 of 1997 in the Fourth Court of Subordinate judge and Artha Rin Adalat at Dhaka for a money decree of Taka 19,38,052. The suit was then on transfer to the above Court renumbered as Title Suit No. 34 of 1998 .

3. Plaint case, in short, is that on 27-9-1989 defendant No. 1 as proprietor of "Joypara Shipping Licence" made a prayer to the Bank for money for building a Cargo Launch at her individual entrepreneurship. On 24-6-1990 the Bank sanctioned a credit limit of Taka 15,00,000 subject to certain terms and. conditions. On her further prayer, the Bank by letter dated 17-6-1991 enhanced the limit from Taka 15,00,000 to Taka 20,00,000 and fixed installment at Taka 1,28,000 from Taka 96,000.

4. Defendant repaid some money but ultimately failed to adjust the loan. Pursuant to a legal notice, she prayed for exemption of 75% of the interest. The Bank informed the defendant that it was not possible and asked her to repay the entire loan together with interest.

5. The outstanding bank dues stood at Taka 19,38,052 as on.30-6-1997. Accordingly, the suit was instituted as the defendant refused to repay the dues.
