6. By filing a written statement the defendant opposed the claims of the plaintiff. Her case, in short, is that the defendant was doing business with good name and fame. She was operating CC A/C No. 37 with the plaintiff bank since 1981. She borrowed money thrice and on earlier two occasions she repaid the loan in time. Last time Taka 20,00,000 was sanctioned to make a cargo coaster and she received first installment on 17-10-1990. Enough time was spent in building the cargo vessel. During the political turbulence in 1990, continued hartal, strike, 'Bondh', cargo business came to a standstill. At the time, her cargo met with a serious accident and she sustained huge loss in business. While the cargo was carrying boulders from Dhaka to Chittagong, on the way at Ramgati the vessel grounded on the sand. Taking loan from other sources the coaster could be repaired. Repair of the vessel was done with the knowledge of the bank. But the bank did not come forward to help her in any way, rather asked her to deposit Taka 5,00,000 out of the FOR, which was opened and deposited with the bank out of the sanctioned loan as per term of the advance. The cheque for Taka 2,85,000 given by the Sadaran Bima Corporation as insurance claim for the accident was also adjusted against the loan. Consequently, the defendant could not square up the dues of the Bank. The defendant however deposited in total Taka 24,40,000 i.e. Taka 4,40,000 over and above the principal amount.

7. Further case of the defendant is that the Bangladesh Bank as per policy decision of the Government issued direction/circulars asking the commercial banks to reduce the rates of interest but the plaintiff bank never reduced. In 1994, the plaintiff bank fixed the rate of interest 14.5%.

On the pleadings, following issues were framed:

(a) 	whether the suit as framed was maintainable;

(b) whether the plaintiff has got any cause of action;

(c) 	whether the suit was barred by limitation;

(d) whether statement of accounts filed was in order and correct; and

(e) what relief the plaintiff was entitled to.

8. In support of its case, the plaintiff examined two witnesses and adduced number of documents, which were marked as exhibit 1, 2 series, 4 to 6 and 7 series. The defendant examined her husband as her only witness and adduced number of documents, which were marked as exhibit 'Ka' to 'Ta'.

9. By impugned judgment and decree, learned Subordinate Judge came to following findings that,

(i) 	out of Taka 20,00,000 sanctioned Taka 15,00,000 only was given to the defendant and Taka 5,00,000 was kept back with the bank by opening a FDR A/C as security;

(ii) the defendant deposited in the Bank in total Taka 24,40,000;

(iii) If the FDR amount of Taka 5,00,000 together with interest of Taka 1,41,025 in total Taka 6,41,025 and insurance claim of Taka 2,85,000 was deducted from said amount, the defendant deposited Taka 17,98,975 against Taka 15,00,000; and

(iv) Defendant deposited Taka 2,99,075 as interest.

10. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the Bank was entitled to charge interest at the rate of 8% only and calculated interest at said rate of 8% on Taka 15,00,000 for the period from 1992 to 30-6-1997 i.e. six and half years and found total interest due at Taka 7,80,000 and after deducting Taka 2,99,075 as deposited by the defendant from said amount, held that the outstanding dues was Taka 4,80,925 and decreed the suit in part for said amount only.

11. The decree was challenged on several grounds on behalf of the appellant. Mr KS Zaman, learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that the suit was brought as a mortgage suit but a decree for money was granted. Secondly, he submits that learned Subordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to reduce any amount from the substantive claim of the plaintiff nor he had got any jurisdiction to grant interest at the rate of 8%, which was against the terms of the contract. Lastly, he submits that the terms of the contract granting loan to the borrower did not entitle her to any reduction of rate of interest.

12. In the plaint, relief sought for is a decree of Taka 19,38,052 and for realisation of the decreed amount by sale of the mortgaged property and the cargo vessel described in the schedule to the plaint if the defendant fails to pay such decreed amount in time. The trial Court granted a preliminary decree for Taka 4,80,000 and asked the defendant to pay said amount within 120 days in default the plaintiff would be entitled to recover said amount with interest at the rate of 8% with effect from 1-7-1997 till realisation. The exception taken to the decree therefore, is of no substance.

13. It is not disputed that on the prayer of the defendant the plaintiff Bank first sanctioned a credit limit of Taka 15,00,000 and then enhanced the limit to Taka 20,00,000 for building a cargo launch subject to certain terms and conditions.

14. The list of terms and conditions for sanction of the loan is usually long and elaborate. Firstly, out of Taka 20,00,000 sanctioned Taka 5,00,000 was taken deposited against a fixed deposit account with the bank as a pledge. Secondly, the cargo vessel to be built had to be hypothecated to the Bank and to be registered both in the names of the borrower and the bank. The properties comprised of holding No. 51 Goalnagar Lane was mortgaged to the bank and the owner of said property had to furnish a personal guarantee for repayment of the loan.

15. It is also not disputed that out of Taka 20,00,000 sanctioned, the defendant deposited Taka 24,40,000 of course including the FDR amount of Taka 6,41,025 and the insurance claim of Taka 2,85,000. So, the claim in the suit appears to be mainly based on interest or interest on interest or capitalisation of the interest. But we could not ascertain the basis of the claim either from the plaint or so-called statement of accounts filed in Court.

16. It appears that a sanction letter was issued under the signature of one Assistant Vice President of the Head Office of the Bank to another Assistant Vice President of Johnson Road Branch, Dhaka communicating approval to the sanction of a cash credit of Taka 15,00,000 in favour of the defendant under usual terms and conditions. This letter is marked as exhibit 1. Similarly, another letter dated 17-3-1991 was issued by the Head Office communicating its approval to enhancement of the credit limit to Taka 20,00,000 to said branch office, which is marked as exhibit 2(Jha). The decision neither sanctioning the loan or enhancing the limit does not appear to have ever been brought to the knowledge of the defendant. Nor any contract executed between the bank and the defendant in respect of the loan could be produced by the Bank. Even exhibit 1 and 2(Jha) do not appear to have been ever shown to the defendant. The Bank has however produced number of usual documents and papers of the bank security with the signatures of the defendant thereon taken in the course of disbursing of the credit.

17. In said sanction letter exhibit 1 it appears that rate of interest was fixed as following interest:

"18% per annum with quarterly rests subject to any change at the discretion of the bank from time to time."

18. From other documents produced, it however appears that the bank changed/altered the rates of interest from time to time. The statement of accounts is also marked as exhibit 8. But from such statement of accounts, it could not be ascertained what was the rates of interest for what period of time. Nor we could find how the claim was calculated either in the plaint or in the depositions of the witnesses.

19. PW 1 Md Hanif Patwari, a manager of the Bank in deposing on behalf of the bank admitted that in 1994 the Bangladesh Bank directed them to exempt 75% of the accumulated interest. He also stated that at different times different rates of interest were charged but he could not say how the statement of accounts was prepared at such changed rates of interest at what time and for what period.

20. On the other hand, the defendant adduced a circular dated 9-3-1992 issued by the Bangladesh bank, exhibit 'Kha'. By the circular, the Bangladesh Bank asked all commercial banks to charge interest at the rate as shown in the schedule.

21. Mr Rafiqur Rahman submits that in case of small and cottage industries, as per the circular the interest could only be charged at any rate from 8% to 13%. But the Bank charged interest in exorbitant rate in violation of the directives of the Bangladesh Bank. PW 1, in the witness box, claimed that they were not bound to follow the instructions/directions of the Bangladesh Bank.

22. Mr Zaman submits that as the loan did not fall in the category of small and cottage industries, the defendant could not claim the bank should charge interest at the rate of 8% to 13%. No paper or document could however be produced to show what the project against which the bank financed was.

23. Fact remains the loan of Taka 15,00,000 or Taka 20,00,000 was advanced for making a cargo coaster to a proprietor at individual entrepreneurship. Why such a project could not be said to be a small and cottage industry could not be ascertained for want of necessary papers.

24. The Banking Companies Act, (Act XIV of 1991), in brief, the Act was promulgated for regulating the bank companies operating in Bangladesh and their banking transactions. Section 45 of the Act provides as hereunder,

"Where the Bangladesh Bank is satisfied that:

(a) in the public interest; or .

(b) in furtherance of monetary and banking policy; or

(c) to prevent the affairs of any bank being conducted detrimental to the interest of the depositors or prejudicial to the interest of the bank company; or

(d) to ensure the proper management of any bank companies generally; it is inevitable to issue directions to bank companies in general or to any bank company in particular, it may from time to time, issue such directions as it deems fit and the bank companies or the bank company, as the case may be, shall be bound to comply with such directions. "

25. Plain reading of the section makes it clear that in the public interest or in the interest of the depositors or the banking policy or even in the interest of the bank, the Bangladesh Bank, as a central bank of the country, is empowered to determine banking policy in relation to loan or advances to be followed by the bank companies in general or any bank company in particular, and when a policy is so determined it shall have a binding effect. In particular, the Bangladesh Bank may, from time to time, give directions with regard to the rate of interest and other terms and conditions for giving loan, advance or other financial accommodation. Such directions are always binding upon all bank companies. These powers are common and universal to all regulatory banks the world over.

26. From the evidence on record, it is clear like crystal, the Bank did not pay any heed to such directions issued time to time by the Bangladesh Bank. Ignoring such directions, the Bank prepared its statement of accounts. Had the interest been calculated at any rate within the range of 8% to 13% from February, 1992 and 75% of the interest exempted in 1994, we are afraid the Bank would not have any outstanding dues against the defendant.

27. Few points relating to the word 'interest' must be made clear. Halsbury's Laws of England; 4th Edition, Volume 3 at page 118, para 160 defines interest as follows:

"160. Interest. By the universal custom of bankers, a banker has the right to charge simple interest at a reasonable rate on all overdrafts. An unusual rate of interest, interest with periodical rests, or compound rests, or compound interest can only be justified, in the absence of express agreement, where the customer is shown or must be taken to have acquiesced in the account being kept on that basis. Whether such acquiescence can be assumed from his failure to protest at an interest entry in his statement of account is doubtful.

Acquiescence in such charges only justifies them so long as the relation of banker and customer exists with respect to the advance. If the relation is altered into that of mortgagee and mortgagor by the taking of a mortgage, interest must be calculated according to the terms of the mortgage, or according to the new relation.

The taking of a mortgage to secure a fluctuating balance of an overdrawn account, is not, however, inconsistent with the relation of banker and customer, so as to displace a previously accrued right to charge compound interest.

It is the practice of bankers to debit the accrued interest to the borrower's current account at regular periods (usually half-yearly); where the current account is overdrawn or becomes overdrawn as the result of the debit the effect is to add the interest to the principal, in which case it loses its quality of interest and becomes capital."

28. Osborn Concise Law Dictionary defines "interest" as a sum payable in respect of use of another sum of money called the principal.

<u>29. Black's Law Dictionary (7th Edition) defines "interest" as the compensation fixed by agreement or allowed by law for the use or detention of money, or for the loss of money by one who is entitled to its use; especially the amount owed to a lender in return for the use of the borrowed money. According to Strouds Judicial Dictionary of Words and Phrases (5th Edition), "interest" means, inter alia, compensation paid by the borrower to the lender for deprivation of the use of his money. When a person is deprived of the use of money which he is entitled to he has right to be compensated for the deprivation as was decided in the Secretary, Irrigation Department, Government of Orissa and others vs GC Roy, (1992) 1 SCC 508. Similarly, in Dr Shamlal Narula vs CIT, Punjab, (1967) 7 SCR 668, it was held that interest is paid for deprivation of the use of money. In Riches vs Westminster Bank Ltd (1947) 1 All ER 469, the essence of interest, in the opinion of the House of Lords, is that it is a payment which becomes due because the creditor has not had his money at the due date. It may be regarded either as representing the profit he might have made if he had the use of money, or, conversely, the loss he suffered because he had not that use. So, the main essence of interest is the compensation to be paid to the lender or creditor for the failure of the borrower to pay the money borrowed on due date. Interest is generally understood to mean the amount which one has contracted to pay for use of the money borrowed. The words 'interest' and 'compensation' may be used interchangeably. Interest is compensation allowed by law or fixed by the parties, or permitted by custom or usage, for use of money of another for the delay in paying back the money borrowed after it becomes due.</u>

30. 'Penal Interest' is not same as 'interest'. Penal interest is extra liability incurred by a debtor for committing some wrong for making the payment when it should have been made to the person wronged. It is neither related with nor limited to the damages suffered. Thus, when the liability to pay interest is founded on the doctrine of compensation, penal interest is a penalty founded on the doctrine of penal action. Penal interest can be charged only once for one period of default and therefore cannot be permitted to be capitalised.

31. The interest can be capitalised on the analogy that the interest falling due on the accrued date and remaining unpaid, partakes the character of an amount advanced on that date, yet penal interest, which is charged by way of penalty for non-payment, cannot be capitalised. Further interest, i.e. interest on interest, whether simple, compound or penal, cannot be claimed on the amount of penal interest. Penal interest cannot be capitalised. It will be against public policy.

32. When a debtor enters into a fresh agreement with the creditor and undertakes payment of the original principal amount coupled with interest by treating the sum total as principal, any contract express or implied and an express acknowledgment of accounts, are best evidence of capitalisation. This acts as novation of the original contract, which is popularly known as rescheduling in our banking parlance. Acquiescence in the method of accounting adopted by the creditor and brought to the knowledge of the debtor may also enable interest being converted into principal. It may be remembered that a mere failure to protest is not acquiescence.

33. Capitalisation method is founded on the principle that the borrower failed to make payment though he could have made and thereby rendered himself a defaulter. To hold an amount debited to the account of the borrower capitalised it should appear that the borrower had an opportunity of making the payment on the date of entry or within a reasonable time or period of grace from the date of debit entry or the amount falling due and thereby avoiding capitalisation. Any debit entry in the account of the borrower and claimed to have been capitalised so as to form an amalgam of the principal sum may be excluded on being shown to the satisfaction of the Court that such debit entry was not brought to the knowledge of the borrower and/or he did not have the opportunity of making payment before capitalisation and thereby, excluding its capitalisation.

<u>34. Capitalisation of interest charged with periodic rests is no doubt permissible. But there should be uniform banking policy in this regard and the intervention of the central bank is ,therefore necessary. When a bank claims interest in excess of what is permitted by circular/ direction of the Bangladesh Bank, the Court can always give relief to the aggrieved party. Any interest charged and/or capitalised in violation of directives of the Bangladesh Bank, as to rate of interest, or as to the periods at which rests can be arrived at, shall be disallowed and/or excluded from the capital sum.</u>

35. Modem bank is a highly organised institute. Adjudication of claims of the bank companies generally should not be time consuming provided the pleadings are more objective, clear and unambiguous and is supported by clean statement of accounts. In the pleading, averments should be clear that the interest/compound interest is charged at such and such rates, and capitalised at such periodic rest, as are permitted by, and in conformity with the directives of the Bangladesh Bank. A statement of accounts to be filed in Court must show the details and giving debit entries, and if debit entry relates to interest then setting out also the rate of interest and the period for which the interest was charged. If the case is so presented with clean picture, then in case of any controversy about the debit balance, the onus would be on the debtor to prove why the account should not be accepted. Such practice would narrow down the scope of controversy and reduce much time of everyone in suits by financial institutions.

<u>36. In such suits, the issues raised are generally capable of being determined by documentary evidence. The Court can act on presumption that the transactions or dealings have taken place and accounts maintained by bank companies in conformity with the directives of the Bangladesh Bank. Cf Central Bank of India vs Ravindra, (2001) 1 SCC 367.</u>

37. It is common experience, when a borrower needs money and comes to a bank for loan, advance or any sort of financial accommodation he finds little time to go through the cryptic security papers developed and updated by the talent of best brains over the century tendered for signature/execution. They at best want to know and settle the rate of interest. They do not care to understand the trap they are going to be entrapped and tied hands and feet by executing the security papers. At the time what mostly preoccupies their all faculties is the sanction of the loan, advance or accommodation and actual disbursement only. This is universal pattern of behaviour of the borrowers.

38. It is the duty of the bank company to safeguard its advance, loan or any financial accommodation to bring any disbursement/debiting in the account of the borrower to the knowledge of and get acquiesced by the borrowers. In Court, when the bank papers of security are produced no-body wants to go deep into them unless the bank. company could place its case simply and clearly as to the interest charged and calculated.

39. In the case before us, we could not find either from the plaint or from the evidence how the plaintiff became entitled to the money claimed as on 30-6-1997.

40. We find the terms and conditions for sanction of the loan include registering the vessel both in the name of the Bank as well as the borrower. The vessel was required to be hypothecated to the bank. The Bank thereby had acquired some sort of control and/or management over the vessel. When the vessel met with an accident, the Bank did nothing either by extending little accommodation or in salvaging the vessel. Rather, the Bank acted rudely; it debited the money received out of the insurance claim for the accident and en cashed the fixed deposit.

41. This is not modem banking. The contribution of the bank companies to the economy of a nation is tremendous. The Bank is no doubt interested in the return of its good money. But the modem banking must be distinguished from the trading of the usurers. It must be remembered, if the very project goes wrong and/or ruined and/or frustrated, chance of payment of the bank dues becomes a remote possibility. The bank companies should have overall watch and care right from the inception of a project till at least recovery of the bank finance.

<u>42. There are ups and downs in life. The credit history of the defendant does not appear to be bad. She is a woman. Earlier on two occasions she borrowed money and paid back in time. This claim of the defendant was never denied. In the circumstances, we are sorry to say, the Bank tried simply to ditch the defendant by refusing all sorts of accommodation in the matter of salvaging the vessel.</u>

<u>43. In the above view of the matter, in granting a partial decree for Taka 4,80,925 learned Subordinate Judge committed no error either on law or on facts.</u>

44. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby affirmed.

45. Send down the record at once.

Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Governor of the Bangladesh Bank for circulation amongst the bank companies for guidance.

End.

caseno: Memorandum of Appeal from Original Decree No. 33 of 1992
lawyer:
Muhammad Nazrul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Appellant. 
Mahmudul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Respondent Nos. 1 and 2.
parties:
Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd ------ Petitioner
vs
Shohag Medicine Supply and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury J: This appeal has been preferred against the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 2 Khulna in Title Suit No.33 of 1990. The Adalat by judgment dated 30-9-90 decreed the suit in part directing realisation of Taka 1, 64.925.00 from the defendant.

2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that defendant4espondent No. 1 is a business establishment, of which defendant No. 2 is the owner and defendant No. 3 is his wife. This defendant No. 2 while maintaining current account No.870 with the plaintiff bank purchased medicines worth Taka 1,75,925.00 on hire and those were sold to the defendants on the basis of sanction order dated 7-5-88. The price of medicine was Taka 1,60.000 and there was a condition that the defendant would repay the amount involved by 6-11-88. The balance of the amount was fixed as profit charged on the selling of the medicines. Out of this amount of Taka 1,75,925.00 the defendant No.2 paid only Taka 11,000.00. Then a notice was issued on 25-14-89 asking the defendant to repay the loan with profit as earlier agreed upon. But on 15-8-90 defendant No. 2 refused to pay anything. He also by signing the confirmation letter accepted the outstanding dues of the bank when the defendant refused to pay the bank's dues the plaintiff had to institute the suit claiming compensation at the rate of Taka 19.90% per annum totaling  Taka 2,20,306.00 as outstanding dues of the bank till the filing of the suit.

3. Defendant No. 2 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing written statement admitting part claim of the plaintiff. His further case is that he failed to make any profit in the business as his employee misappropriated the cash and goods of shop making the defendant a destitute. But in spite of that he managed to repay Taka 11,000.00 to the bank. His case is that due to financial stringency he was not in a position to repay the banks dues.

4. Both the parties adduced evidence before the trial Court The Artha Rin Adalat on consideration of the evidence on record and the facts and materials, particularly the agreement, by his judgment decreed the suit on 7-10-91 in part. The plaintiff on being aggrieved by this part decree preferred this appeal. The contesting defendant has not filed any cross-objection.

5. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff appellant submits that the contesting defendant No.2 entered into an agreement with the bank on the stipulation that on selling the medicines which the bank purchased at Taka 1,60,000.00 he would pay Taka. 1,75,925.00 to the bank. This amount of Taka 1,75,925.00 includes the profit of the bank. It is submitted that the advance was made under Moazzel system of banking now parts operated by the Islami Bank which is a new concept in the banking business in our country. It is submitted that the defendant on accepting the quantum of profit took the delivery of medicines but he only repaid Taka 11,000.00 and after that till date he has not paid a single farthing for which the bank suffered loss and damages. It is submitted that the trial Court illegally found that in the agreement there was no condition of giving damage to the plaintiff in case of failure of the defendant. But by Moazzel system of advance provides that such damage may be given where there is a basis of damages. The defendant accepted Taka 1,60,000.00 on condition of paying of Taka 1,75,925.00. The difference is calculated as profit. So the basis of calculation of the damages is there in the agreement. But the trial Court overlooked it.

6. Mr Mahmudul Islam the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondent, on the other hand, submits that for getting damages there must be evidence that the plaintiff suffered loss and damages which are very much absent in the present case. He submits that in the agreement as well as while deposing before the trial Court the bank official has not stated how the bank suffered damages or the quantum of the damages and unless there is proof by evidence the awarding of damages is barred under section 74 of the Contract Act.

7. There is no dispute on the transaction as alleged by the plaintiff bank. It is an admitted fact that the bank on 7L5-88 on credit sold medicines worth Taka 1,60,000.00 to the defendant on condition that he would repay the aforesaid amount with profit in all amounting to Taka 1,75,925.00 within 6-11-88. It is also an admitted fact that the contesting defendant paid only Taka 11,000.00 to the hank though it was agreed upon that the defendant would pay Taka 10,000.00 per month. It is also an admitted fact that when the defendant failed to clear up the dues the hank issued a notice on 25-4-89 and ultimately the contesting defendant refused to pay anything on 15-8-90. Thereafter the present suit was instituted for realisation of the aforesaid amount with damages.

<u>8. Admittedly, the money was advanced under Moazzel system of banking which is a new concept of Islami banking system in our country. In by Moazzel system a party is given certain properties on a contract which is as follows:</u>

<u>“১ বাই মোয়াজ্জাল চুক্তিতে বিক্রয়ঃ নগদ দাম পরিশোধ করতে অপারগ বা অনিচ্ছুক কোন গ্রাহক ব্যাঙকের আর্থিক সহযোগিতায় কোন পন্য সামগ্রী একং করার প্রস্তাব দিলে ব্যাংক প্রথমে উক্ত পন্যের কাটতি, বাজার দাম সম্ভাব্য মুনাফা, ক্রেতার বিশ্বাস যোগ্যতা, দাম পরিশোধের সময় পরিশোধের ধরন ইত্যাদি বিষয় সতর্কতার সাথে পরীক্থা করে সব কিছু অনুকুল হলে বাজার থেকে নগদ দামে উক্ত পন্য একয় করে গ্রাহকের সম্মতিক্রমে নির্ধারিত দামে ভবিষ্যতের কোন নির্ধারিত তারিখে বা নির্ধারিত কিস্তি অনুসারে মূল্য পরিশোধের শর্তে গ্রাহকের কাছে মাল হস্তান্তর করে।</u>

<u>এরূপ বাকীতে বিক্রয়ের ক্ষেত্রে ব্যাংক ক্রেতার কাছ থেকে পন্য মূল্যের চেয়ে অতিরিক্ত মূলোর সম্পত্তি আমানত হিসাবে বন্ধক রাখে।</u>

<u>গ্রাহক সময়মত দাম পরিশোদ করতে ব্যর্থ হলে ব্যাংক উক্ত বন্ধকী সম্পত্তি বিক্রয় করে পন্যের মূল্য আদায় করে। কোন অবস্থাতেই ব্যাংক একবার ধার্যকৃত পন্যের মূল্য বৃদ্ধি করে না। তবে ইচ্ছাকৃত খেলাপী গ্রাহকের বেলায় ব্যাংক ক্ষতিপুরন আদায় করে থাকে। নির্ধারিত সময়ের পূর্বে দাম পরিশোধ করলে ব্যাংক রেয়াতে (Rebate) দিয়ে থাকে বাই মোয়াজ্জাল পদ্ধতিতে বিক্রয়ের বেলায় ব্যাংক পন্যের মূল্য এবং ব্যাংকের মুনাঢ পৃথক পৃথক ভাবে জানায় না।</u>

<u>From the aforesaid it appears that Moazzel system of transaction is a simple transaction whereby the bank on credit sells certain properties goods to the customer on a fixed profit and the purchaser was required to repay the amount agreed within the stipulated time. This indicates that without any personal investment a purchaser may get some profit out of the business on the investment made by the hank. From this by Moazzal system of transaction it appears that one having no capital may earn profit by taking advantage of this system of banking. In the present case medicines worth Taka 1,60.000.00 was delivered to the defendant on condition that within the stipulated time he would pay back Taka 1,75,925:00. The difference of Taka 1,60,000.00 to Taka 1,75.025.00 was fixed as the profit of the hank. This transaction has not been denied or challenged from the side of the defence. Rather the defendant categorically admitted this. There was a condition that the amount should be repaid to the bank by 6-11-88 which has not been done excepting of course payment of Taka 11,000.00. Thereafter the bank instituted the present suit for realisation of Taka 2,20,306.00 from the defendant which included the aforesaid amount of Taka 1,75.925.00 plus consolidated damages till the disposal of the suit at the rate of Taka 19.90% as annual compensation on the aforesaid amount of Taka 2,20306.00 till realisation. The trial Court it appears found that as in the agreement Ext. there is no stipulation for damages the plaintiff hank is not entitled to any damages and decreed the suit for an amount of Taka 1,64,925.00 already paid. The bank then preferred this appeal on the ground that they are entitled to damages.</u>

9. Now the moot question is whether the hank is entitled to any damages as prayed Fir. Admittedly the amount taken was to be returned by 6-11-88 and during that period only Taka 11,000.00 was repaid.

<u>10. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the contesting respondent placing the decision reported in AIR 1927 (Sind) 49 (Abdul Ali Moosabhoy vs Gokaldas Lalji and another) submits that section 73 of the Contract Act makes it compulsory for the plaintiff to prove that he has suffered damage and the extent to which he has suffered before a court can award him damages for breach of contract, and if he does not give the best evidence, every presumption should be made against him. He submits that before the trial Court the plaintiff failed to prove the quantum of damages and none deposed that the bank actually suffered damages for which claim as prayed may be entertained. He submits that the main criterion of the damages must be proved by proper and adequate evidence which is very much lacking in the present case.</u>

<u>The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, on the other hand submits that when there are materials on record for assessment of damages the court may award compensation in such a transaction. He submits that even in the aforesaid decision placed by Mr Mahmudul Islam it has been held that even though there is no evidence but that by itself does not relieve the court altogether of the duty of assessing the damages as best it can on evidence and materials actually placed before it. He submits that the contesting defendant entered into an agreement with the bank that he should pay back Taka 1,75,925.00 to the bank within the stipulated time which amount included a profit of Taka 15,000.00 out of the advance given by the bank. So the quantum of profit is there which may be construed as quantum of damages and the damages as claimed by the bank may he calculated on the basis of this material which is an admitted fact. It is submitted that this Islami Bank is operating as a welfare oriented banking system and the share-holders of the bank are entitled to the profit on their investment. When the plaintiff took the medicines on condition of payment of Taka 1,75,925.00 he must repay the same with profit as earlier assessed and when he failed he is liable to pay the damages, the basis of which calculation is already there in the record. In support of his submission Mr Muhammad Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff appellant placed reliance in the case of Amin Jute Mills Ltd vs Arag Ltd reported in 28 DLR (AD) 76. Where it has been held that a party guilty of such breach of contract is liable to pay compensation measure of which shall be assessed on the quantum of loss sustained on account of the breach or which the parties knew to be likely to flow from the breach. It has also been held that the measure of damages is to be ascertained between the difference of the contract rate and the market rate on the fact of breach. This is the rule of law but its proof rests on the facts and circumstances of each case. It there is no marker on the due date or no direct evidence is forthcoming the court is not precluded from arriving at the real rate that can fairly be gathered from the evidence and circumstances of the case. It is submitted that the basis of assessment of compensation is already there in agreement Exhibit 1 which is an admitted document and the contesting defendant admitted that he took the medicines worth Taka 1,60,000.00 on 7-5-88 on condition of making the repayment of Taka 1,75,925.00 within 6-11-88 and within that period he only paid back taka 11,000.00. It is the case of the defence that as the medicines and other valuable properties of the defendant have been misappropriated by the Manager the defendant was not in a position to pay hack the agreed amount. But it appears that before the trial Court no evidence was led on this assertion and there is no stipulation in the agreement that in case of pilferage or any misappropriation by any 3rd party the contesting defendant will not be bound to pay back the aforesaid amount.</u>

11. It appears that relying on this stipulation made in Ext.1 the bank filed the suit for realisation of Taka 120,306.00 from the defendant which they assessed on the basis of the profit as set forth in Ext. 1 which amount is up to the date of tiling of the suit. The hank also claimed some damages at the rate of Taka 19.90% per annum till realisation of the aforesaid amount. The trial Court it appears decreed the suit in part holding that in Ext.1 there is no mention of awarding damages.

<u>12. We have considered the whole aspect of the matter and it appears that the contesting defendant was fully agreeable to pay a profit of Taka 15,000.00 to the bank on the medicines he took. He was party to the agreement. As he was a party to the agreement he was bound to pay back Taka 1,75,925.00 within 6-11-88. It is also an admitted fact that the bank entered into the transaction after purchasing medicines worth Taka 1,60,000.00 which is the money of the public. Excepting payment of Taka 11,000.00 till data the defendant has not paid a single farthing to the bank who has fully utilised the medicines and the money and now he is avoiding payment. The acts and activities of the defendant are found to be not bona fide and in such circumstances when the transaction was under by Moazzal banking system and when there is material in the agreement Ext.1 for the determination of the damages we hold that the trial Court was not correct and right in refusing to award damages as prayed for. Following the decision of our Appellate Division, reported in 28 DLR (AD) 76 we hold that when there are materials before the court for ascertaining damages the trial Court illegally refused to award damages. The same view was also taken, in the earlier decision of the Sind High Court. It cannot be said that there is no material for ascertainment of damages. It may be mentioned that PW I has not categorically stated the quantum of damages but Ext.1 is there which provides a model for assessment of compensation for which agreement is an agreed and admitted document.</u>

13. It appears that the bank filed the suit for realisation of Taka 2,20,306.00 from the defendant which they calculated as price of medicines of worth Taka 1,75,925.00 out of which Taka 11,000.00 was repaid and damages amounting to Taka 55,389.00 till the date of institution of the suit. It appears that they have calculated this on the basis of quantum of profit and clearly stated in agreement Ext. 1. In view of the system of Moazzal banking and in view of the agreement Ext.1 and in view of the fact that the contesting defendant failed to repay the agreed amount within the stipulated time and in -view of the fact that the Bank time and again requested the defendant to clear up the dues by sending letters which were marked exhibits before the trial Court and in view of the fact that the basis of ascertainment of damages is there in Exhibit 1, we hold that The learned Artha Rin Adalat committed illegality in not decreeing the suit in full amounting to Taka 2,20,306.00 as the plaintiff appellant is entitled to a decree of that amount.

14. As regards compensation for the period subsequent to filing of the suit it appears that the bank claimed damages at the rate of Taka 19,90.00 per annum which in the facts and circumstances we are not inclined to allow even though after the institution of the suit till date the defendant has not paid anything to the bank. The percentage that the plaintiff bank claimed is not there in the agreement Ext. So, this cannot be accepted. We could have ascertained the damages on the materials found in Ext.1 from the date of institution of the suit till realisation but the bank has not claimed as such. They claimed damages at the rate of 19.90% which we are not inclined to allow.

15. Having given our anxious consideration to the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides, we hold that the learned Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Khulna committed illegality in not decreeing the suit for realisation of Taka 2,20,306.00 as prayed for and the plaintiff appellant is entitled to a decree for that amount.

16. Court fees paid are correct. The appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Khulna in Title Suit No. 33 of 1990 is modified and the suit is decreed for an amount of Taka 2,20,306.00.

17. The contesting defendant is hereby directed to pay back this amount to the plaintiff within 30-4-98 without fail and in case of failure by the defendant respondent, the plaintiff bank will be at liberty to realise the amount through the process of the court.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

caseno: Writ Petition No. 300 of 1995, with Writ Petition No. 1694 of 2000.
lawyer:
Syeda Rizwana Hasan with Md Iqbal Kabir and Shakil Ahmed Khan, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
MI Farooqui with Sadiqur Rahman and Razia Sultana, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
Karunamoy Chakma, Assistant Attorney-General with Syeda Afsar Jahan, Assistant Attorney-General and Rajik-al-Jalil, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Respondents. 
Humayun Kabir Sikder, Advocate ----- For Respondent No.8.
parties:
Dr Mohiuddin Farooque being dead his substitute Syeda Rizwana Hasan and Another ----- Petitioners 
Vs
Government of Bangladesh represented by the Ministry of Communications and Others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: In Writ Petition No. 300/1995, an application under Article 102(1 )(2)(a) of the Constitution of Bangladesh was filed by Syeda Rizwana Hassan, a public interest litigant and Director (Programmers) and Member, Executive Committee of Bangladesh Environment Lawyers Association (BELA), registered under the Societies Registration Act 1860 seeking directions upon the respondents I) to take all adequate and effective measures to check pollutions caused due to the emission of hazardous smoke from motor vehicles and the use of audible signaling devices giving unduly harsh, shrill, loud or alarming noise, 2) to ensure that the exemption of motor cycle from the requirement of certificate of fitness under the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1983 be withdrawn immediately 3) to adopt and install appropriate technology for providing correct certificates of fitness 4) to set Bangladesh standard for petroleum ensuring the reduction and removal of toxic and hazardous constituents from the same 5) to require all imported motor vehicles to be fitted with catalytic converters.

2. The case of the petitioner, in brief, is that the environment and ecology of Bangladesh are being continuously endangered and threatened by various activities originating from private and public sources. Amongst the primary causes and source of environment degradation, pollution of natural resources on which the survival of life is dependent e.g. air, water, soil, etc, have exceeded standards necessary to sustain life and livelihood contrary to statutory safeguard. Such grave contamination, amongst others, has been contributed directly by the emission of hazardous smoke and noises in the air from faulty and unfit motor vehicles lacking road worthiness as required by law. As a result, an unhealthy environment has been prevailing at many places. The problem of air pollution from faulty motor vehicles has been universally identified as a major threat to human body and life by various scientific researches, studies, investigations, reports, surveys conducted by various persons, agencies, institutions, both national and international and the agencies of the Government have highlighted the issue in their various reports and publications. The major cities of the country are exposed to innumerable environmental hazards many of which are typical to urban areas. The most threatening urban centre is Dhaka which is the capital of the country. Some of the environmental hazards of the city are quite acute and incompatible with the conditions required for the growth of human life and ecology. The lives of the dwellers of the Dhaka city and its environment are subjected to many threats and injuries that originate from human actions and omissions. Amongst these, the air pollution, especially from the faulty motor vehicles, have choked the air of Dhaka city exceeding all tolerable and acceptable limits causing serious health hazards as irreparable damage to the physical environment and ecology. Such violations and the consequences are clearly visible in the Dhaka city which needs no evidence to anyone who has been to Dhaka city. The pollution from the motor vehicles has been the results of violations and non-compliance of the requirements of various laws and policies and the failures of the respondents to enforce the regulatory provisions and to perform their duties in accordancewith the laws and policies. The incessant use of high noise making horns, like pneumatic horns by the trucks, buses, minibuses, etc. and sound from the faulty vehicular engines have filled the air of Dhaka city totally disregarding laws and as an evidently flagrant violation of various regulatory prohibitions. Such excessive noise pollution are affecting the normal and safe life, especially of the students, examinees, commercial establishments, offices, hospitals, clinics, educational institutions, the children and the sick, etc. Children, aged and the sick are the worst victims. The noise pollution is more acute in some particular areas of the city disturbing the public peace creating public annoyance. Being concerned about the severity of the vehicular pollution prevailing in Dhaka city, the petitioner along with BELA conducted an investigation into the reports, publications and the regulatory system on vehicular air pollution and possibilities of preventing the same. The investigation conducted by the petitioner and BELA showed that the total number of on road vehicles till 1994 were 3.37,012 out of which the percentage of the type of vehicles were approximately Bus: 4, Mini-Bus: 3, Truck: 3, Three-wheelers: 10, Motor Car: 15, Jeep and Micro-Bus: 8, Motor Cycle: 48.6 and others 2.40. Although the largest number of vehicles is Motor Cycles, they have been exempted by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 from the requirement of regular fitness certificate. Most of these motor cycles are driven by two stroke engines. and are polluters of hazardous smoke and also of disturbing noise. The investigation of the petitioner and BELA also revealed that the number of Motor Vehicles that have come for fitness certificate till 1994 were 96,192 which indicate that excluding the number of motor cycles, about 65,000 motor vehicles on road did not come to the BRTA for obtaining fitness certificate although they were required by law to do so or to surrender their certificate of registration or the Blue Book to the authority and no effective steps have been undertaken by the respondent Nos. 1-6 to compel them to comply with the requirements of law. The issuance of certificate of fitness under the Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1983, which is issued for one year, does not entitle a motor vehicle to ply on the road even if the same becomes unfit before the expiry of the said period and, in such cases, the fitness of the said vehicle has to be cancelled by the authority.

3. The current procedure of granting fitness certificate by the respondent No. 2 is passed on human judgment which is subject to error and corruption although the technology of ensuring fitness through automation is easily available and also cost effective and, as such, measures have been adopted almost in every country. The investigation of the petitioner and BELA further revealed that many of the vehicles used by the respondents and other Government agencies including those of the Transport Pool do not have fitness certificate as per records. Some of these vehicles are hazardous polluters. The current status of the scenario clearly manifests that a large number of vehicles emitting hazardous smoke and using pneumatic and other high noise making audible signals have been playing in Dhaka city under the respondent's nose defying the laws and policies and the respondents have failed to enforce the relevant laws, policies and standards in preventing the vehicular pollution of the country, more particularly in the Dhaka city and hence failed to perform their statutory duties and responsibilities resulting in serious health and environmental hazards.

4. The degree and extent of vehicular pollution are further aggravated by the quality of petroleum products used by the vehicles containing various constituents which are too dangerous to health and may cause serious diseases like cancer, etc. The quality of petroleum is further degraded through adulteration and adding of additives in it while carrying and refining. Besides other purposeful reasons, one factor of such contamination is caused by the oil tankers which carry all different types of petroleum in the same container. The other qualitative issue is the lead- laced gas emitted because of the use of leaded petroleum severely affecting the lungs, liver, brain and the nervous system resulting in high blood pressure, IQ and memory-retention damage among children and damage to fetuses leading to deformed babies. The high sulfur content in the petroleum and hence in the smoke, causes severe damages to the ecology. Besides the introduction of lead, free petrol and consequent to the same, in many countries, catalytic converters are being installed in the vehicles to catalyse the reaction between oxygen and nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and the hydrocarbons to produce nitrogen gas, carbon dioxide and water vapour. The uses of catalytic converters have proved to be cost effective and easily implementable, particularly in countries which import rather than locally manufacture meter vehicles. The degree of vehicular pollution in the Dhaka city areas has exceeded all limits and such concerns are being raised by public and private bodies and individual repeatedly through the newspapers and the state controlled electronic media of the country. The extent of such pollution has assumed such a grave proportion that the proposed Environment Conservation Bill, 1994 which has been approved by the cabinet and is pending for placement before the parliament, has incorporated a separate and specific provision in section 6 by only this issue with higher penal sanction. All the matters pertaining to motor vehicles including smoke and noise control, road-worthiness, etc., are covered by various provisions of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1983 (Ordinance No. LV of 1983).The Dhaka Metropolitans Police Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance III of 1976), the Environment Pollution Control Ordinance 1977 (Ordinance No. XIII of 1977) and the Dhaka City Corporation Ordinance, 1983 (Ordinance XL of 1983). After the Issuance of the aforesaid Rule, the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995) was enacted by the Parliament, the said Act, empowered the Director General of the Department of Environment (respondent No. 6) to take all measures necessary to combat and arrest all kinds of pollution. The respondents in various documents admitted the ever deteriorating condition of air in the city on several occasions published from their respective offices, Considering the prevailing state of pollution, the Second Meeting of the National Environment Committee held on 4-5-97 being presided over by the Hon'ble Prime, Minister included the pollution caused by the hazardous. Omission from motor vehicles as the first agenda for discussion. In the said meeting the respondent No.5, the Ministry of Environment and Forest expressed its seriousness that pollution in the four metropolitan cities including Dhaka as caused by the motor vehicles is so acute and visible that same may adversely affect foreign investment and tourism in Bangladesh. The respondent No.5 also admitted the harmful effect of hazardous vehicular omission on human health, particularly on the mental and physical development of the children and stated that such commission was posing innumerable innocent children to a threat of continued deteriorating state. It was disclosed in the said meeting that 700/0-80% of the motor vehicles plying on the streets is not road worthy. In the said meeting of the National Environment Committee, the respondent No. 5 suggested a few measures to be undertaken to reduce hazardous air pollution caused by the motor vehicles to one third of the present state. The measures recommended by the said respondent include, among others, the following:

(3) 	Take a greater attempt regarding fitness of vehicles.

(4) 	gradually phase out two-stroked engine vehicles and ban the plying of such vehicles that are older than three years.

(5) 	direct the Eastern Refinery to -provide lead-free petrol.

(6) 	effectively implement existing laws to prevent the use of high noise making horns.

Under the above circumstances, it is evident that the respondent, although admitted the severity of the pollution from vehicles, have miserably failed to implement the respective laws, rules and regulations and also their own decisions taken in furtherance of the legal obligation and consequently vehicular pollution both in the form of emission and noise continues to persist at a much severer scale posing deadly threat to the life, health, safety and comfort of the city dwellers.

5. It is submitted that the supply, distribution and marketing of degraded quality and adulterated petroleum products are gross failure of respondent Nos. 11, 12, and 13 in the performance of their statutory and public duties which has put at stake the lives of the millions of the residents including the petitioner and his family and the visitors of the Dhaka city and its ecology. It is submitted that the aggravation of the vehicular air pollution causing and aggravating the miseries and ailments of the residents of the city and subjecting the lives of the petitioner and his family to such threats that demonstrate the failure of respondent Nos. 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 to provide environmentally sound petroleum and also require compulsory installation of catalytic converters with all the imported vehicles as necessary for implementing the National Environment Policy 1992 and for achieving the purposes and spirit of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1983 the Environment Pollution Control Ordinance, 1977 and for safeguarding the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution. It is also submitted that the respondent Nos. 12 and 13 have failed in their public and statutory duties to provide an environmentally sound Bangladesh Standard on petroleum specifying its constituents in line with national requirements and international standards.

6. The petitioner being seriously concerned and aggrieved by the failures of the respondents in the performance of their statutory obligations and the duties, issued a Notice of Demand for Justice on 17- 7-1994 upon the respondents but the respondent have failed to take any appropriate steps so far.

7. Being aggrieved the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. During pendency of the Rule the petitioner filed two applications, one seeking the following direction namely,

(i) to ensure that the decision in the fiscal year 1999-2000) banning importation of leaded petrol into the country be upheld for the following years;

(ii) ensure that all imported motor vehicles are fitted with catalytic converter from July, 2001

(iii) enforce restrictions against the use of such electric and other loud and shrill horn as provided under section 139 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1983 and Rule 114(d) of the Bengal Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 within a period of threes months from the date of issuance of the direction;

(iv) take immediate steps within eight weeks to activate the five centers with automatic computerised process that have already been constructed after providing correct certificate of fitness and thus ensure that no unfit vehicles ply on the roads and inform the Court of taking such steps.

(v) Set Bangladesh Standard for Petroleum in accordance with the international standard ensuring the reduction and removal of toxic and hazardous constituents from the same;

(vi) submit a report on compliance of the order of this court within the time-frame as may be fixed by this court.

9. Considering the urgency of the matter by subsequent application the petitioner sought for some direction upon the respondent in the following terms requiring them to;

(i) ensure that the decision to convert all Government-owned petrol/diesel driven vehicles into CNG-operated vehicles be implemented within such period as may be fixed by the Court.

(ii) ensure that new and adequate number of CNG Stations required to facilitate and promote the conversion of petrol/diesel driven vehicles into CNG are set up in the Capital city within such time as may be fixed by the Court.

(iii) prepare and submit report within four weeks in the form of an action plan setting out definite time-frame and stating the measures to be undertaken to phase out/remove the two-strokes three-wheelers from the roads of the Capital city by the year 2003.

(iv) submit a report in compliance of the order of this court within time frame as may be fixed by this court.

10. In Writ Petition No. 1694/2000 another, application under Article 102 of the Constitution was filed by Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST), represented by Staff Lawyer Mr Md Abdul Mannan Khan on similar facts. The petitioner sought the following directions from this court:

(a) pass an order or orders issuing a Rule Nisi as to why the respondents should not be directed to enforce air and atmosphere free from pollution in Dhaka by taking necessary measures including following:

(1) Two strokes, particularly baby-taxis, should use lubricating oil designed for two stroke engines; Fuel and Lubricating should meet appropriate standard at all stages from the production through distribution, to retail sale;

(2) Octane level of standard be raised to 87 R ON minimum required for baby- taxis, Motorcycles and scooters and for passenger cars a minimum 9 I to 92 R ON is ensured.

(3) Measures should be taken to reduce the level of sulfur initially to 0.5% in the long run.

(4) The unlicensed sale of fuel and low quality lubricants must be stopped.

(5) The price gap between the Kerosene Oil and Petrol be narrowed down to avoid adulteration.

(6) To phase out the existing two strokes fleet within two years and to replace it with clean transport alternatives;

(7) Ban on new licences for two stroke three-wheelers in Dhaka and cancellation of 9 years old licences of baby-taxis.

(8) Number of Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) vehicles is raised to meet the requirement and CNG stations bemaintained properly round the clock.

(9) Legal action be taken against the owners and drivers of the vehicles emitting polluted smoke into the air.

11. And as to why they should not be directed to report every six months of actions and results of the above directive to this Court. As the facts of both the Writ Petitions are almost similar we do not like to restate the case of the petitioner of this Writ petition separately.

12. The respondent Nos. 6, 8, and 10 contested Writ Petition No. 1694 of 2000 by filing separate affidavits in apposition. In Writ Petition No. 300 of 1995 the respondent Nos. 5, 6, 9 and 10 contested the Rule by filing affidavits in opposition. The respondent Nos. 2 and 4 filed affidavit of compliance and denied the material allegations made in the writ petition. The respondents contended, inter alia, that they are trying to control air pollution from faulty and arrogant vehicles, from emission of hazardous smoke and incessant use of high noise making horns, such as pneumatic horns, by the trucks, buses minibuses etc., in two ways namely (1) Monitoring and (2) Regulatory. In the monitoring programmer, samples are collected from selected places in the city and an alysed in the DOE's Laboratory. The degree and gravity of pollution is detected on the basis of the results of the analysis reports. To augment prevention, control and mitigation measures, publicity and information dissemination is undertaken through mass media for general public awareness and also by informing the concerned people. Another important regulatory function being continuously affected is the prevention of unlawful air pollution from vehicle by the summary trial and punishment on the spot of offenders through the activities of Mobile Courts. These Mobile Courts for dealing with unlawful air pollution by vehicles are a joint initiative of the Department of Environment with the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA), the Metropolitan Police and the Dhaka Metropolitan Magistracy. On average, these Mobile Courts can apprehend and take action against 20 to 30 offending vehicles every day. It is submitted that the Department of Environment has already submitted a proposal tomake petrol lead-free and for minimizing sulfur in petrol and diesel. It is further submitted that the respondents have already taken up a programme to convert vehicles for use of environmentally friendly CNG fuel instead of petrol or diesel. The Department of Environment has recommended that all Government vehicles should be converted for CNG use as a first step. In the meantime, some of the organisations have started to convert their vehicles for use of CNG. It is also stated that the Government has taken proper step to convert 450 Nos. of Government Pool Vehicles into CNG. All Government vehicles can be converted into CNG within next few months, if funding is available for the purchase of conversion kits and daily 8-10 Government vehicles can be converted after purchasing conversion kits. The Government have 6 filling stations at Dhaka and within next 2 months 2 more filling station will come up and it may be expected that another 6 filling stations could possibly be set up by December, 2002. It is also stated that for the sake of environment, appropriate measures are being taken to reduce the contents of sulfur in diesel up to 25% and the contents of it in petrol was reduced to 0.1 % from 0.5%. It is submitted that the Government itself is very much concerned with the contents of sulfur in diesel and petrol and, as such, direction may not be necessary. The decision dated 28-8-2000 of Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution shows that it is an unanimous decision to maintain the contents of sulfur up to 0.50% as the production of diesel with 0.25% sulfur contents is not at all possible with the present IRL and it is not available even by International Tender. The respondents also stated that they permitted importation of petrol driven vehicles with built in catalytic converters by SRO No. 269 Ain/2001. The respondents contended that by SRO 208 Ain/2002 dated 6-7-2002 imports of 2 stroke engines of 3-wheelers (Tempo etc.) have been banned. It is also stated that the Government have already taken various steps towards introduction of CNG system in the country and already 1575 vehicles have been converted to CNG system and this conversion process is going on experimentally. 30 Nos. of two-stroke baby-taxi have been converted to CNG under a project of theDepartment of Environment. A Non-Government Organisation CDS (CNG Distribution Company) is engaged in this area to promote the CNG system and necessary steps have been undertaken by the Government and non-Government organisations. The Government has banned the import of chassis with 2 stroke engines and 2 stroke engines-driven three-wheelers since 6-7-2000. Government is also planning to phase out 2 stroke three wheelers by 2007. It is also stated that the Government has restricted plying of 3-wheelers 9 years old or above, buses/minibuses 20 years old or above from 1st January 2002 in Dhaka city. It is submitted that BRTA is conducting trial test of vehicles in the vehicles Inspection Centre (VIC) in the 4 Metropolitan Cities namely, Dhaka, Chittagong, Rajshahi and Khulna from May, 1999.

13. We have heard Mrs Syeda Rizwana Hassan, the petitioner who appeared in person in Writ Petition No. 30 of 1995 and Mr MA Mannan Khan, the petitioner, who also appeared in person in Writ Petition No.1694 of 2000, and Mr Karunamoy Chakma, the learned Assistant Attorney-General for the respondents.

<u>14. On perusal of the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondents and on consideration of the submissions of the learned Advocates it is clear that the respondents, specially the Department of Environment, do not deny that the air pollution in the city of Dhaka is mainly due to emission of hazardous smoke and incessant use of high noise making horns such as pneumatic horn by the trucks, buses, minibuses, etc., and sound from the defective vehicular engines which have been playing in the Metropolitan city of Dhaka are threatening the lives of the city dwellers and others. It is the case of the respondents that the Government at the high level took some decisions to control the air pollution of Dhaka city from faulty and arrogant vehicles, both from emission of hazardous smoke and incessant use of high noise making horns and from faulty vehicular engines plying in the city. We, however, feel some urgent preventive measures to halt sagging environment pollution and degradation of Dhaka city, one of the worst in the world, due to audible vehicular sounds and emission of hazardous black smoke from faulty and arrogant motor vehicles is indeed, overdue. Hence, in the prevailing situation, in our view, ad-interim directions as sought for by the petitioner, are necessary. Accordingly, the following directions are given:</u>

<u>(1)	To enforce Rule 114(d) of the Bengal Motor Vehicles Rule 1940 and section 139 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance 1983, to enforce restrictions against the use of such hydraulic and other loud and shrill horns including air horn and considering the problem to control such large scale violation and considering the fact that almost all the transport vehicles are fitted with such prohibited horns. We direct the respondents to issue notice and/or notification immediately notifying to all the transport vehicles operators about the restrictions provided in Rule 114( d) and section 139 of the Ordinance directing them to remove the electric, air and other loud and shrill horns and to use bulb horn in the Metropolitan city of Dhaka giving the operators 30 days' time to change the hydraulic and air horn and to fit vehicles with bulb horn with the warning that failure to remove 'such prohibited horns from their vehicles, penal actions should be taken against them according to law and it should be notified that no such transport vehicles should be given certificate of fitness if fitted with such horns which are prohibited under Rule 114(d) of the Rules and section 139 of the Ordinance. We also direct the respondents to proceed against the vehicle operators by taking penal action if they fail to remove such types of prohibited horns after the expiry of the period of 30 days which shall be provided for change of such horns by notification or by notice to be issued by the Government giving wide publicity through print and electronic media. The respondents should also take steps for notifying such restrictions regarding the use of such types of horns in respect of vehicles which enter into the Metropolitan city of Dhaka from other Districts and Metropolitan Cities so that they may be aware of such restrictions in the matter of use of such prohibited horn in the Metropolitan city of Dhaka.</u>

<u>(2) To conduct tests of vehicles in the 5 Vehicles Inspection Centres already handed over to BRTA within 6(six) months and to issue certificate of fitness of the vehicles including motor cycles (two- wheelers)</u>

<u>(3) To implement the decision of the respondents for converting all government owned petrol/diesel driven vehicles plying in the Dhaka Metropolitan city into CNG- operated vehicles within 6(six) months.</u>

<u>(4) To implement the decision of the respondents to set up six more CNG filling stations in Dhaka city by December, 2002 and also to set up more CNG filling stations from time to time to meet the requirements of vehicles and CNG stations be maintained properly round the clock.</u>

<u>(5) To implement decision of the respondents that all motor vehicles from July 2001 be fitted with catalytic converter and diesel particulate filter by December, 2002.</u>

<u>(6) To set Bangladesh standard for petroleum in accordance with the international standards ensuring the reduction and removal of toxic and hazardous constituents from the same.</u>

<u>(7) To phase out existing 2 stroke 3-wheelers by December, 2002 and to replace it with cleaner transport alternatives;</u>

<u>(8) To impose ban on new licences for two stroke 3-wheelers in Dhaka Metropolitan city and cancellation of9 years old licences of baby-taxis with immediate effect.</u>

<u>This writ petition shall be deemed to be pending for the purpose of monitoring. The respondents are also directed to give wide publicity to the directions of this court in print and electronic media on consecutive two days twice in a week for one month.</u>

15. The respondents are directed to submit reports every six months of actions and results of the above directions to this court.

Let this order be communicated to all the respondents.

End.

lawyer:
Bashiruddin Ahmed, Advocate ----- For the petitioner. 
Md Salahuddin, Advocate ----- For the opposite party.
parties:
Foez Ahmed ------ Petitioner
Vs
Joynal Abedin and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 10-8-94 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Laxmipur in Title Appeal No.184 of 1988 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 18-7-1988 passed by the Assistant Judge, Ramgati in Title Suit No.9 of 1988 decreeing the suit should not be set aside and or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. Opposite party No.1 as plaintiff, filed the suit for declaration that the sale deed mentioned in schedule 2 to the plaint in respect of the suit property was without consideration and was not acted upon.

3. The case of the plaintiff in brief, is that he went to the house of his friend Suja Miah on 12-5-87 in between 1-00 PM and 11-30 PM and entered in to a contract with defendant. Foyes Ahmed for selling the suit land. The price for the suit land was fixed at Taka 15,000. The defendant gave the plaintiff a sum of Taka 500 as baina on the condition that he would pay the balance amount of Taka 14,500 to the plaintiff on 24-5-87 and then the plaintiff would execute and register the sale deed in his favour. At the time of agreement the plaintiff on being asked by the defendant put his signature on 3 (three) blank stamp papers. On the next date the plaintiff returned to his new house at village Maijarchar under Sudharam Police Station in the District of Noakhali. According to the terms of the contract the plaintiff went to the house of the defendant to execute and register the kabala on receipt of the balance of the consideration. The plaintiff having not found the defendant at his house, went to Ramgati Sub-Registrar's office, 22 miles away from his house. But there also the defendant not being available the plaintiff again went to the house of the defendant. This time the plaintiff met the defendant but he told the plaintiff that as he could not arrange the money it was not possible for him to give him the balance money. The defendant further told that after procuring the money he would inform the plaintiff and would obtain the kabala from him. The plaintiff came back to his house relying on the said words of the defendant and waited for the information from him. After about 2 months the plaintiff heard that the defendant created a sale deed in respect of the suit land. Then the plaintiff made a search and after obtaining the certified copy of the sale deed came to know definitely about the same. The plaintiff never executed and registered the kabala in question and the same was created in collusion with the deed writer taking the advantage of the signature of the plaintiff on the blank stamp papers. The sale deed in question was never acted upon and on behalf of the plaintiff his brother is possessing the suit land. The creation of the kabala by the defendant created cloud over plaintiffs title to the suit land and hence the suit.

4. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaintiffs case of bainapatra and the allegation of forgery in creating the sale deed and contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff himself on receipt of Taka 15,000 from the defendant as consideration for that suit land executed the kabala on 13-5-87 at the house of the deed writer at the bazar of char Larenge. The deed could not be registered on that date because of the time constraint. Thereafter, the plaintiff himself appeared before the Sub-Registrar on 21-5-87 and registered the deed. The plaintiff could not put his left thumb impression on the deed as his left thumb was swollen. The plaintiff transferred his old residential house and other immovable properties to the defendant for an amount of Taka 3,000 and executed a Nadabinama in favour of the defendant. The sale deed and the Nadabinama are genuine documents. After the transfer of the suit land and the house the plaintiff went to his new homestead in the District of Noakhali. The defendant recorded his name in the DD Khatian No. 1176 and paid rents and is in possession of the suit land.

5. The trial Court by judgment and decree dated 18-7-88 decreed the suit on the finding, inter alia, that the consideration money as mentioned in the kabala did not pass to the plaintiff and that the kabala in question was not acted upon although the trial Court found that the plaintiff executed and registered the kabala. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree defendant No.1 filed Title Appeal No. 184 of 1988 before the District Judge, Laxmipur who by the impugned judgment and decree dismissed the appeal-concurring with the finding of the trial Court on the point of passing of consideration and also on the point that kabala was not acted upon. The appellate Court did not agree with the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff executed and registered the kabala. The appellate Court on consideration of the evidence on record found that the plaintiff did not execute and register the kabala.

6. Mr Bashiruddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that both the courts below misread the evidence on record on the question of passing of consideration as well as on the question of possession of the suit land by the defendant in pursuance of the kabala in question. He submits that the appellate Court being the final court of fact also misread the evidence on record as to the execution and the registration of the kabala in question by the plaintiff and thus, committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit.

7. Mr Md Salahuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, in opposing the Rule supported the judgment .and decree of the court below. He submits that findings as to the passing of consideration and the possession of the suit land being concurrent this court sitting in revision cannot interfere with the said findings of fact.

8. Mr Bashiruddin Ahmed further argues that the court below wrongly shifted the onus upon the defendant to prove the passing of consideration, though the kabala in question clearly mentions the receipt of the consideration money by the plaintiff. To this argument Mr Salahuddin submits that except the defendant who was examined as DW 1 none of the other DWs deposed as to the passing of the consideration to the plaintiff. He further submits that when the plaintiff categorically denied the receipt of consideration it was the obligation of the defendant to prove the same. Therefore, there was no wrong in the approach of the court below.

9. It is true that when a document is registered it has a presumption under section 114( e) of the Evidence Act that the same has duly been executed and registered by the person shown to be the executor. And section 92 of the Evidence Act also prohibits admission of oral evidence for the purpose of contradicting the statements made in an instrument, here the sale deed in question, yet, the proviso to the said section clearly permits a party to prove a fact constituting fraud, want of due execution and want or failure of consideration. In this case, the specific case of the plaintiff being that he neither executed or registered the deed in question nor received the consideration money as mentioned in the kabala, he was entitled to adduce oral evidence to prove his said case. As the plaintiff adduced evidence to prove his case of non-execution and non-registration of the kabala by him and non-receipt of the consideration as well the onus shifted upon the defendant to prove that 'it is the plaintiff who on receipt of the total consideration of Taka 15,000 executed and registered the deed which he failed. In this regard, definition of sale as given in section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act is also relevant. In the said section sale has been defined as under:

"sale is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part paid and part promised"

The definition of sale as quoted above clearly shows that in order to make a sale complete consideration has to pass. Both the courts below having concurrently found that as the plaintiff did not receive consideration for the kabala in question there is no scope of interference by this court with the said finding of fact. Furthermore, Mr Bashiruddin Ahmed could not point out any particular evidence which was either misread or not considered by the court below as to the passing of consideration money.

10. It also appears that both the courts below concurrently found the kabala in question was not acted upon and it is the plaintiff who is in possession of the suit land. Mr Bashiruddin Ahmed also failed to dislodge this finding of fact with reference to the evidence on record, and, therefore, this finding also cannot be disturbed.

<u>11. The appellate Court being the final court of fact also considered the question of execution and registration of the kabala in question by the plaintiff and held that the same was not executed and registered by him. The kabala in question was marked as exhibit A-1. The kabala does not bear the left thumb impression of the plaintiff. The defendant's case is that the left thumb impression of the plaintiff could not be taken in the kabala as well as in the book of thumb impression as kept in Form No.4 in appendix X1 maintained in the Sub-Registrar's office as his said thumb was swollen. If that be the case, then the impression of the right thumb or any other digit was required to be taken as clearly provided in rule 48 of the Bangladesh Registration Rules 1973. Provision to the said rule is as under:</u>

<u>"Provided that, if the left thumb of the executant be defective or injured, the right thumb or any other digit may be used, but in that case or in the case of an executant suffering from smallpox, leprosy or other contagious disease, a note of the fact shall be made in the space reserved for impression, in the book and also on the document mentioning the particular digit used, and explaining why, in the contagious disease, no impression could be taken. When no impression is taken, no serial number should be given in the space reserved for impression in the book. But in such cases, the column meant for name and signature of the executant or the identifier in the book and also the column reserved therein for noting book number and document number, should be duly filled in for facilitating the identification of the document from the book of thumb impression and vice versa".</u>

<u>In the kabala in question neither there is any thumb impression nor there is any note in the space reserved for the left thumb impression as to why the same was not taken, which clearly shows that the instructions as contained in the said rule were not followed.
