10. The real question that falls for determination in this Rule is whether the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is maintainable?

11. We have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused the pleadings of the parties as well as the petition for temporary mandatory injunction and the impugned order of the learned trial Court and affidavit in opposition filed by the defendant-petitioner for vacating the order of stay. On careful scrutiny of the entire matters on record prima facie we find that the learned lower court while considering the case of both sides has failed to consider that for making unlawful gain the plaintiff company resorted to practising fraud by way of setting thermofluid heater in their factory and thereby consumed huge quantity of gas @ 100 cft per hour. A vigilance team of the defendant company detected this fraud of the plaintiff on 12-7- 1995. But instead of disconnecting the gas line the petitioner took a sympathetic view and asked the plaintiff to pay the prices of the huge quantity of excess gas consumed by them unauthorisedly under certain terms and conditions as laid down in the notice dated 19-11-1997. But unfortunately, the plaintiff did not pay any heed to it and continued to consume gas unlawfully till today. During this period the defendant company issued several reminders to the plaintiff for regularising their unlawful acts on payment of the arrear bills, etc. The last letter to this effect is dated 7-9-2000. So, it is not correct that the defendant has disconnected the gas line without any notice. Gas is indeed a national resource belonging to the state, being managed by the defendant company under authority of the Government. It is sold to bonafide customers on payment of price which is fixed under certain specific terms and conditions of a written contract between supplier and the consumer. So the learned court below had no jurisdiction to go beyond the terms of the contract and to grant any unjust premium to any customer under any extraneous grounds or consideration.

<u>12. In the facts, circumstances and foregoing reasons we feel inclined to hold the prima facie view that the plaintiff is under legal obligation to pay the gas bills regularly by clearing up huge outstanding bills that amounted to Taka 94,26,236.22 only up to June, 2000. The defendant company in exercise of their lawful authority has disconnected the gas line in terms of the contract. In our view, the learned trial Court committed an error of law in failing to consider that the relationship between the two contractual parties is governed by the terms of the contract mutually agreed upon by them and hence the court cannot go beyond the terms of the contract or direct the defendant company to restore the Gas line to the defaulter company and to submit Gas Bills as per meter reading though under a written bond dated 8-4-1996 the plaintiff company bound itself to pay the gas bills as per minimum charge system formulated in the 300th resolution of the Board of Directors of the defendant company.</u>

<u>13. Let us now consider the balance of convenience and inconvenience in between the parties which cannot be arbitrary. By the impugned order, the learned trial Court allowed an unjust premium to M Habib Oil Mills (BD) Ltd. The plaintiff-opposite party cannot be allowed to consume gas for an unlimited period without payment of dues and since the gas is indeed a national resource belonging to the state being managed by the defendant company under authority of the Government and it is sold to bonafide customers and not to the defaulter. Under the facts and circumstances there should have been equitable reliefs so that neither party shall suffer till disposal of the suit. The balance of convenience and inconvenience therefore, appears to us is equal. The impugned order dated 14-11-2000 is not tenable in law inasmuch as it has been passed in gross violation of the terms of the contract and to the great prejudice of the defendant company causing serious loss of revenue of the public exchequer. To meet ends of justice, at this stage, the order of the court below requires to be modified.</u>

<u>14. The order is accordingly, modified to the effect that the Titas Gas T & D Company Ltd would restore the gas connection provided the mills (M Habib Oil Mills (BD) Ltd plaintiff-opposite party pays 50% amount of the outstanding dues out of Taka 94,26,236.22 and also pays the usual gas consumption bills regularly in terms of the contract dated 1-2-1997 and undertaking dated 8-4-1996. The Subordinate Judge is directed to dispose of the suit as expeditiously as possible preferably within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment.</u>

In the result, the Rule is disposed of with the aforesaid observation without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Hamidul Haque J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the licensing agreement dated 9-3-99 signed by and between the Ministry of Information, the respondent No.1 and Mr AS Mahmud respondent No. 7 (Annexure-"F") and the subsequent approval to transfer the licence to the ETV Ltd (Annexure-"H") should not be declared to have been entered into and granted unlawfully and without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. In this Writ petition two of the petitioners (Nos.1 and 3) are professors of Dhaka University and the petitioner No. 2 is President of Bangladesh Federal Union of Journalists. The petitioners claim that the matter raised in the petition involve breaches of constitutional obligations and statutory duties by and on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 in dealing with public property in clear violation of legal mandates and public policies. So, as conscious citizens of this country, the petitioners thought it a duly to invoke the extra-ordinary jurisdiction of this Court under the Constitution in an attempt to oblige the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 to perform their public duty under the Constitution and the laws of Bangladesh.

3. Their case is that in 1998, Ministry of Information invited tenders to install and operate a Television Channel under the private ownership and accordingly, tender notice was published in a national daily. As many as 17 enterprises participated in the tender. The tenders were opened on 25-6-98 by the Technical Committee constituted for the purpose of evaluation of the tenders. The Committee was required to evaluate the tenders by taking into consideration the following factors:

a.	Balanced programmes in economic context;

b.	The concept and objective of transmitting the programmes nationally and internationally.

c.	Technical proposal for establishment of TV network;

d.	Investment proposal;

e.	Seriousness in establishing a TV network.

4. On the basis of the above criterion, the offers made by the participants were evaluated by the Technical Committee and out of 17 participants, the offer of Minard (Bangladesh) Ltd. was kept out of consideration and the other 16 participants were divided into 3 categories: the first category included those whose tenders were found to be satisfactory and 2nd category also comprised of three participants and the Committee found the tenders of the other 10 participants not acceptable at all. Accordingly, the Committee prepared an evaluation report and the same accompanied by a forwarding letter written by Convener of the Committee was sent to the Ministry of Information. This evaluation report is marked Annexure-A-I. The petitioners alleged that after the evaluation report was submitted to the Ministry of Information, the Technical Committee came under serious pressure by an interested group as a result of which the Technical Committee changed the evaluation report and in the changed report, the Committee recommended for acceptance of tenders of the following eight participants:

Serial No.5 	Ekushey Television.

Serial No.6 	Minard (BD) Ltd.

Serial No.8 	Bangladesh News Services.

Serial No.9 	Bangladesh Sky Network Ltd.

Serial No.11  Independent Media Services.

Serial No.14  Prachar Biggapani Sangstha.

Serial No.15  Multimode Transport Consultants ltd.

5. The petitioners alleged that in this changed report, Ekushey Television was placed in the top and Minard (Bd.) Ltd. who was earlier found to be not qualified at all was placed in the 2nd position Next, the petitioners alleged that subsequently Ministry of Information after discussing with the Ministry of Finance, set out number of conditions for granting licence to Ekushey Television and one of the conditions was that if the private channel transmits its programmes simultaneously when the BTV also transmitting its programmes the private channel shall pay an amount of Taka 1200 per hour but on a representation of Mr Abu Sayed Mahmud, Chairman of ETV the Finance Minister deleted the condition of charging Taka 1200 per hour. The petitioners claim that due to such an action the Government has been deprived of huge amount each year. The petitioners also claim that Mr AS Mahmud did not participate in the tender but an agreement was signed between the Government of Bangladesh and Mr AS Mahmud. According to the petitioners, at the time of signing of the agreement, Ekushey Television Ltd. was not even formed but after signing of the agreement between the Government and Mr AS Mahmud, Mr Mahmud transferred the licence to the Ekushey Television Ltd. Petitioners claim that this licensing agreement was signed in accordance with the provisions of section 4(1) of Telegraph Act 1885 and section 5 of Wireless and Telegraphy Act 1933. The petitioners alleged that as no licence was obtained from Ministry of Post and Telecommunications and no apparatus was imported by the ETV Ltd after obtaining licence and clearance from that Ministry, the licence was illegal. Next, the petitioners claim that under the Co-site agreement signed between BTV and ETV Ltd. the ETV was given the facilities of using the towers of BTV and premises of BTV but only a nominal rent was paid by ETV for such use of BTV towers and other facilities. Lastly, it is also the case of the petitioners that by allowing ETV to set up its office inside the BTV Complex at Rampura the security of BTV has been threatened because the BTV is a key point installation. So the main allegation of the petitioners is that in granting a licence for private TV Channel, the respondents though were under a legal and constitutional obligations to protect national interest, they have acted in breach of law and the policy formulated by the Government and did not act to protect national interest.

6. Respondent Nos. 6 and 8 jointly appeared by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition and opposed the Rule. Their case is that after tender notice was published in the newspaper, respondent No. 7 participated in the binding process under the name of ETV as the proprietor of the firm. A Technical Evaluation Committee evaluated all the proposals and found that proposal of eight participants merit consideration for granting licence by the Ministry and in the selection process, ETV topped the list. This evaluation report was submitted by the Chairman of Evaluation Committee on 9-7-98 to the Ministry of Information. These respondents claim that Annexure-A (1) of the Writ petition is a forged and manufactured report. According to them, after receipt of the report of evaluation on 9-7-98, the Ministry of Information prepared a summary for the Prime Minister and in that summary, it was also mentioned that under certain conditions licence would be granted to ETV under section 4(1) of the Telegraph Act 1885 and Section 5 of the Wireless and Telegraphy Act, 1933. It was also mentioned that only one of the VHF frequency could be allocated to private TV to broadcast the programmes both terrestrially and through satellite. This summary was signed by Additional Secretary, Ministry of Information and State Minister. The same was then placed before the Prime Minister for her approval which was approved by the Prime Minister on 2-11-98.

7. These respondents claim that the Secretary, Ministry of Information by an unofficial note dated 14-10-98, inquired of the DG of the BTV to confirm from the Chairman of Evaluation Committee whether the report selecting ETV and 7 other participants was the only report of the Evaluation Committee by his letter dated 14-10-98 informed that the Committee prepared several evaluation reports and confirmed that the report which was attested by the Secretary on 14-10-98 was the final evaluation report. These respondents claim that the allegation of changing the report has no basis, the report annexures A(1) is a forged one and signatures are superimposed.

8. As regards the allegation of deleting the conditions of payment of charges of Taka 1200 per hour, these respondents claimed that it was not included in the নীতিমালা under which tenders were submitted and as such this condition was deleted by the Minister of Finance.

9. As regards the transfer of licence, these respondents claim that respondent No. 7 participated in the tender as the proprietor of Messers Ekushey TV and as the ETV was neither a natural or a legal person, licensing agreement was signed by the proprietor and subsequently when the company was formed and registered, the licence was transferred in accordance with terms of the licensing agreement to the ETV Ltd. The respondents’ further claim that the licence was granted in pursuance to নীতিমালা dated 24-5-98 prepared by the Government wherein it is stated that the Government shall grant licence under both the Telegraph Act of 1885 and under Wireless and Telegraphy Act, 1933 and as the licence was granted under both the Acts as both the Ministry of Information and Post and Telecommunications are under the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, there IS no need of obtaining any fresh licence from the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications. Moreover, Bangladesh Telegraph and Telephone Board by its memo dated 30-6-90 informed the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications that BITB has no objection about setting up of broadcasting station ETV by importing necessary apparatus. The Ministry of Post and Telecommunications further by its memo dated 18-7-1999 gave permission to ETV to set up the facilities for broadcasting.

10. The respondents further claim that ETV does not broadcast its programme by using BTV facilities, it is using the space of BTV and BTTB towers for hoisting its antenna and for that purpose co-site agreement was executed between the ETV and the Government represented by BTV for use of such towers and space and ETV already made payment of Taka 27,87,394. Next, these respondents claim that BTV has not given any channel to ETV because BTV does not own any VHF channel but use a frequency allocated by the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications and such allocation is made by Frequency Board under the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications. According to these respondents previously BTV used a second channel for a short period but ultimately it was closed down and remained unused and the same VHF frequency was allocated to ETV for a fee and for that purpose, ETV has obtained necessary frequency allocation from the Frequency and Wireless Board. According to them the নীতিমালা private TV network would broadcast its programmes both terrestrially and through satellite. Accordingly, under the licensing agreement executed with the Government. ETV was granted permission to broadcast programmes both terrestrially and through satellite. The respondents also claim that for use of space of BTV grounds, ETV has obtained necessary clearance from Defence Committee of Key Point Installations.

11. The respondents claim that there are about 4 crores of viewers in Bangladesh and its prograpmrne speaks for poor and neglected people of the society. Some interested persons probably could not tolerate the popularity of ETV and as such, at a belated stage, they filed this application through the present petitioners who are acting as agents of foreign broadcasters.

12. The respondent No. 7 also appeared by filing a separate Affidavit-in-Opposition. He is proprietor of M/S Ekushey Television and as proprietor participated in the tender. His case is similar to the case of respondent Nos. 6 and 8 respondents Nos. 2, 3 and 5 also filed Affidavit-in-Opposition during the stage of hearing. Respondent No.2 is Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance. It is stated in this Affidavit-in-Opposition that decision of charging Taka 1200 and formulation of some other conditions were taken in an inter-ministerial meeting with Ministry of Information and Bangladesh TV that condition of charging Taka 1200 was deleted by the then Finance Minister on the basis of a letter written by AS Mahmud to the Finance Minister. Respondent No. 3 is Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Post and Telecommunications. In this affidavit-in-opposition it is stated that the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications did not give any permission to ETV Ltd to import wireless telegraph apparatus by the letter dated 29-11-99, that letter was issued by the Frequency and Wireless Board. It is further stated that in the import policy order 1997-2002 is schedule 1 under HS heading No. 6525 it is provided that wireless telegraph apparatus can be imported in the Non-Government sector on the basis of no objection certificate of the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications. It is also stated that neither respondent No. 6 Ekushey TV Ltd. nor respondent No. 7 Mr AS Mahrnud made any application to this Ministry for such objection certificate. It is also stated that the ETV Ltd has been granted any licence in accordance with the provisions of Wireless and Telegraphy Act, 1933. Lastly, it is mentioned that this Ministry vide its letter dated 6-9-2001 asked ETV about the licence but the ETV explained that ETV did not require any such licence. Respondent No. 5 is DG of the Bangladesh TV In his affidavit-in-opposition it is stated that ETV has been allowed to use towers of BTV and its adjacent land at Dhaka, Natore, Khulna and Rangpur TV Stations on the basis of Co-site agreement but ETV is also co-sharing Sylhet station on the instruction of Ministry of Information. This respondent admits that ETV paid Taka 17,76,498 as rent and Taka 13,93,652 as fixed security to BTV as per Co-site agreement. However, it claims that the rent paid is very nominal. Lastly, it is stated that on the basis of the contract signed between the ETV and Ministry of Finance, BTV had to allow ETV to use BTV's towers but the use of BTV's infrastructure facilities like towers in house, etc. are causing loss to BTV

13. Mr A Razzaq appeared on behalf of the petitioners, his main argument is that the Technical Committee under pressure had to change its report and as the agreement was signed by taking into consideration the changed report, the agreement cannot have any validity. In this connection, he has at first taken us through Annexure-"A (1)". He has submitted that the report at Annexure-" A(1)" was forwarded to the Secretary Ministry of Information by the forwarding letter Annexure A and in this letter it is mentioned that one set of report was enclosed. Next he referred to Annexure-"B" and has submitted that this is also a forwarding letter and this letter also bears that same memo number and in this forwarding letter it is mentioned that three sets of report were enclosed. After referring to Annexure-"A" and "B", he has argued that B was necessary because after forwarding the report through annexure-"A" the same was changed and another report was forwarded under the same memo number of the same date and these two forwarding letters, according to him, clearly prove that there was a changed report.

14. We asked the learned Attorney-General to produce the original file of BTV In the original file we have found a photocopy of annexure A at correspondence page 355. We have also perused the Peon Book of Bangladesh TV and have found that at Sl No. 38 of the Peon Book of the year 1998, the report of the Technical Committee was handed over to Secretary, Ministry of Information by hand.

15. Mr Razzaq has further argued that details of commercial financial and technical evaluation of the participants do not show that ETV's offer was responsive. In this connection he mainly gave emphasis on technical evaluation. Next he has referred to annexure B (1) and has submitted that no specific reason has been mentioned in the report as to the manner of selection. He has argued that annexure A (1) is neither forged nor the signatures in it were superimposed. In this connection, he referred to the Annexure 5(b) of the affidavit-in- opposition filed on behalf of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 and has submitted that the Convener of the Technical Committee did not say that the evaluation report পরিশিষ্ট-২ was a forged one, but he claimed that it was not the final report. Mr Rafiqul Huq who appeared on behalf of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 at a later stage of his argument, accepted the position that annexure A(1) is also a report, but according to him, it is either a draft report or a provisional one. We have also found a photocopy of পরিশিষ্ট-২. As referred to in annexure 5(b) in the file of BTV bearing No. DG প্রকৌ/০৪ আংশ-২ at page 353.

16. Now, as regards B(1) we have found that this is also a report. The report at pages 178-179 of the Affidavit-in-opposition of respondent Nos. 6 and 8 is also copy of the same report. The difference is that B (1) is not attested by the Secretary, Ministry of Information whereas report at pages 178-179 is attested by this Secretary on 14-1-1998 though the report was handed over to him on 9-7-1998. Summary to the Prime Minster was submitted on the basis of this evaluation report and ultimately after approval of the summary by the Prime Minister, agreement was signed between the Ministry of Information and Mr AS Mahmud who submitted tender papers as proprietor of ETV Annexure 3 of the Affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 show that actually tender papers were submitted by Mr AS Mahmud and such licensing agreement was made in between Ministry of Information and Mr AS Mahmud.

17. Mr Rafiqul Huq appeared on behalf of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 and Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed appeared on behalf of the respondent No. 7. They have argued that Annexure A (1) was neither the final report nor the report handed over to the Secretary, Ministry of Information. According to them, only 5(b) is the report which was forwarded to the Secretary, Ministry of Information. Mr Rafiqul Huq, after taking us through both the reports, has submitted that on 1st page of the report, names of the participants with address and the names of proposers have been mentioned whereas in Annexure-A(1) only the names of participant firms have been mentioned without mentioning any address and without mentioning the name of any proposer. Mr Rafiqul Huq has also argued that the proposal of respondent No.7 is the only proposal which had the backing of technical collaboration of BBC and no other participants submitted any such proposal backed by a foreign broadcasting company. So, according to Mr Huq, mainly on consideration of the above fact, the Evaluation Committee in its evaluation report selected ETV and placed its proposal at the top.

18. As the main point is whether evaluation report of the Technical Committee was changed we will like to decide the question at a later stage. Before that, we like to mention other arguments of the learned Advocates of both parties. Syed Istiaq Ahmed and Mr Rafiqul Huq advanced lengthy arguments on the question of locus standi. In this regard, both of them referred to the case of BRA C vs Prof Mozaffar Ahmed and others Civil Appeal Nos. 192, 193 of 2000. The decision of the Appellate Division has not yet been reported. However, both of them referred to this decision. However, both of them referred and argued that the present petitioners have no locus standi to file this Writ Petition because they do not represent the common people nor they have come for mitigating any common grievance. They have pointed out that those who participated in the tender did not move this court for any relief but the present petitioners who are not in any sense aggrieved, have come with this Writ Petition to serve the purpose of other interested persons. Both of them gave emphasis on the following observations of the Appellate Division in the above case:

"The Court in considering the question of standing in a particular case, if the affected party is not before it and if it finds no reason for nonappearance of the affected party it may refuse to entertain the application. This is a clear decision on the matters of locus standi/bonafide of a Writ Petitioner in a public interest litigation. It has been settled that expression" person aggrieved "means not only any person who is personally aggrieved but also one whose heart bleeds for his less fortunate fellow beings for a wrong done by the Government in not fulfilling its constitutional or statutory obiigations."

19. They have also referred to the case of Dr Mohiuddin Faroque reported in 49 DLR (AD) 1.

20. On the other hand, Mr Abdur Razzaq has argued that in this particular case the petitioners have come to this Court to bring to the notice of this Court the malafide exercise of power by some high Government officials and to seek intervention of this Court by way of judicial review of such malafide action. He has also argued that the action of the High Government officials should be transparent and as the main allegation in this Writ petition is that a Technical Evaluation Committee changed its evaluation report under pressure and as the Government action was taken on the basis of that changed report, the whole transaction has become malafide and, as such, any conscious citizen may come before this Court in order to ensure transparency and accountability of high Government officials. In this connection, he referred to 2002 BLD (AD) 16 = 54 DLR (AD) 88 (Paragraph 14) and also the case of Mohammad Hossain vs Quamrul Islam Siddique and others reported in 54 DLR 88.

<u>21. We have considered the arguments of the learned Advocates of both the parties. The question of locus standi does not relate to the jurisdiction of the court. To decide the question whether a petitioner has locus standi to come before this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution, we are to consider the facts and circumstances of each case. The two most important Judgments on this point of our Appellate Division are reported in 49 DLR (AD) 1 and another in 43 DLR (AD) 126 {Bangladesh Sangbadpatra Parishad vs Bangladesh. In these two cases, our Appellate Division determined some guidelines regarding the public interest litigation. But there may be various other facts and circumstances under which public interest litigations may be entertained by this Court. In the above two cases, it has been settled that there must be an explanation for non-appearance of persons who are affected. It is also settled that a person who is not personally aggrieved may also come if his heart bleeds for his less fortunate fellows for any wrong done by the Government. It is also settled that when an action concerns public wrong or injury or invasion on the fundamental rights of indeterminate number of people, any member of the public being a citizen suffering the common injury has the right to invoke the jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

22. In neither of the above two cases, the question of malafide execise of power by the High Government officials was raised, nor the question of transparency and accountability was agitated. The question of locus standi was not decided from the viewpoint of transparency or accountability. The questions are also very important questions. So, it is to be decided whether a citizen may come before this Court under Article 102 with allegations of malafide exercise of power by any high government officials specially who are responsible for decision making. There may be circumstances when a person may come before this Court against persons who are less fortunate. This Court entertained a Writ Petition (No. 6174/2000) under Article 102 for eviction of hawkers from the footpaths of the Dhaka Metropolitan area. Obviously, the hawkers are less fortunate section of the society in this Writ Petition, the Petitioner was an Advocate of this Court.

23. In another case, Dr Fostina Pareira, an Advocate of this Court, wrote a letter to the Hon'ble Chief Justice inviting his attention to the fact that 29 prisoners of different countries were languishing in Jail in Bangladesh after serving out their sentences. The Hon'ble Chief Justice referred the matter to the Bench constituted by one of us. Suo mota Rule was issued and ultimately the Rule was made absolute. In that case, writer of the letter was not an aggrieved person; in that case also, those who were languishing in the jail did not file any application before this Court for any relief. However, this court considered that keeping any prisoner in jail after serving out the sentence was gross violation of human rights and fundamental rights. We have mentioned the above cases only to show that there may be different facts and circumstances under which a person may move this Court under Article 102 though she/he is not personally affected.

24. Another case which has been cited is the case of Mohammad Hossain vs Quamrul Islam Siddiqui. In this case an Advocate of this Court moved under Article 102 when a report was published in a newspaper about some corrupt acts of a Secretary of Ministry of Works. The case is reported in 54 DLR 88. It was mentioned in the newspaper report that Registrar of this Court had also collusion with that Secretary. The Rule was opposed mainly on the ground that the petitioner had no locus standi. Both Mr Rafiqul Huq and Mr Abdur Razzaq cited this case, Mr Rafiqul Huq has submitted that the Court found the application maintainable because the petitioner as a practicing Advocate of this Court stated that he was aggrieved and shocked to read the report in the newspaper containing allegation of corruption and seeing that the corruption found its way to the premises of the Supreme Court. Under such circumstances, this Court held that in view of the allegation as reported in the newspaper, the Petitioner as an Advocate of this Court moved the application and as such filing of the Writ Petition should not be considered as not maintainable. However, Mr Razzaq cited this case to show that as there was allegation of abuse of power and of corruption against respondent No.1, a Secretary to a Government at the relevant time, this Court considered that to ensure transparency and accountability of public servants especially those who held responsible position the Court should give a direction for holding inquiry into the allegation as contained in the report published in the newspaper.

<u>25. In the instant case before us, we have found that the allegation made in this Writ Petition is that of changing an evaluation report of Technical Committee comprising of some high officials including the Chief Engineer of BTV. The petitioners allege that the report had to be changed after it was'submitted to the Ministry of Information. It is true that other participants in the tender did not move this Court for any relief, but we have found from the Writ Petition that specific allegations have been made about the malafide exercise of power of abuse of power by some high officials of the BTV and of a Ministry of the Government. Under such circumstances, we are of the view that though the petitioners are not directly affected by the action of the respondents but when they came to know from newspapers about the malafide action of a very responsible Ministry of the Government, they are entitled to move this Court for judicial review of such action of the Ministry. We may mention here that the facts and circumstances of the BRAC case are totally different from the facts and circumstances of the present case. In that case the question of the validity of a certificate of Bangladesh Bank giving no objection for incorporation of BRAC Bank Limited was raised on the ground that incorporation of BRAC bank was not consistent with section 20 of the Societies Registration Act, 1860. There was no allegation of abuse of power, lack of transparency etc. Whereas, in the instant case, the question is of malafide exercise of power by a Ministry in granting licence to a private company for telecasting programme terrestrially and through satellite.</u>

26. Both Rafiqul Huq and Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed have argued that if a Writ Petition like the present one is entertained, this Court will be flooded with such applications and the Court may not find time to perform the normal function of deciding other civil and criminal matters. We regret that we cannot agree with this view. Each of such petitions will be considered on its own merit and Rule will be issued only when some materials are placed before the Court for its satisfaction that there is reason to believe that there was abuse of power or malafide exercise of power. In the instant case before us, we find that at the time of filing the Writ Petition, the Petitioners filed some papers such as two reports of the Evaluation Committee to impress upon the Court that there was malafide exercise of power and after being satisfied, the Court issued the Rule.

27. Next argument of Mr Rafiqul Huq is that there was unusual delay in filing the Writ Petition. In this connection, Mr Huq referred to annexure 17, 17(A) of the affidavit-in-opposition dated 4-2-2002 and has submitted that at first the news about ETV was published on 1-9-1998 and then again on 22-9-1998 in “যায় যায় দিন” But the present petitioners remained silent and only at an opportune moment, that is, with the change of the Government moved this court on 19-9-2001. This, according to him, has been done with a malafide intention at the instance of some interested persons. Mr Razzaq, on the other hand, has argued that though on earlier occasions news about irregularities of ETV was published in the “যায় যায় দিন” but no detailed report was published before 11-9-2001 and some definite corrupt practices regarding ETV was referred to in that issue of the “যায় যায় দিন” Mr Razzaq has submitted that as the story was flashed in the cover page of the newspaper, the same attracted the petitioners and thereafter they managed to obtain some papers relating to granting of licence to the ETV and filed the Writ Petition on 19-9-2001 and, as such, according to him, there was no delay.

28. We have considered the arguments of the learned Advocates of both the parties on the question of delay. It is true that the Writ Petition was filed after the elected government was replaced by a Caretaker Government in accordance with provisions of our Constitution. We have noticed that besides “যায় যায় দিন” some reports were also published in the Daily Inqilab on 12-11-2001 and 13-11-2001. Weekly “যায় যায় দিন” dated 1-9-1998, 22-9-1998 and 11-9-2001 were shown to us. We find that ETV was given coverage in the front page on 11-9-2001 and in the other issues the matter did not find place in the cover page. Mr Huq has argued that the petitioner No. 2 being a Journalist was definitely aware of the report published earlier but still he remained silent'. We have perused the report as published in the three issues of “যায় যায় দিন” We have noticed that the report published on 11-9-2001 was an elaborate report touching all alleged irregularities. In view of such position, we cannot accept the explanation of the petitioners.

29. Now, let us go back to the main question, whether the report of Technical Evaluation Committee was changed or not. We have referred to arguments of both sides on this point. The definite case of the Respondent Nos. 6, 7 and 8 is that the report at page 178 annexures 5(b) is the final report. On the other hand, the definite case of the petitioners is that it is a changed report which was changed at the instance of Ministry of Information. This report (which is at P 178) is also found in another file of BTV at pages 1/18, 2/18. In this report we find names and addresses of I7 participants along with the names of proposers in the first page. In the second page, it is mentioned that the proposals were evaluated on the basis of the guidelines given by the Secretary, Ministry of Information. The guidelines are mentioned below:

ক) আর্থ সামাজিক প্রেক্ষাপটে সুষম অনুষ্ঠান।

খ) দেশব্যপী এবং বহিবর্শ্বে অনুষ্ঠান প্রচারের ধারণা ও লক্ষমাত্রা

গ) টিভি নেটওয়ার্ক প্রতিষ্ঠার জন্য কারিগরী প্রস্তাবনা।

ঘ) বিনিয়োগ প্রস্তাব।

ঙ) নেটওয়ার্ক প্রতিষ্ঠার বিষয়ে seriousness.

30. Thereafter, it is mentioned that on the basis of the above guidelines under certain conditions, the proposal of eight participants could be considered and then the names of eight participants have been mentioned. Next it is mentioned that the proposal of others were not found responsive.

31. Now, if we compare the report at annexure A(1) of the Writ Petition with the report at annexure 5(b) of affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 we find that first paragraph of both reports are same but other contents in the first page are not the same. The second paragraphs are also same and the last two paragraphs are also the same. The major difference in the two reports is found in the third paragraph. In annexure A(1) the third paragraph is as follows:

“উপরোল্লিখিত বৈশিষ্ট্যের আলোকে প্রাপ্ত প্রস্তাব সমূহ মূল্যায়ন করা হয়। ক্রমিক নং ০৬ মেসাঃ মাইনার্ড (বাংলাদেশ) লিঃ ট্রেড লাইসেন্স এবং ভ্যাট/আয়কর রেজিস্ট্রেশন উপস্থাপন করেনি বিধায় প্রতিষ্ঠানটি বানিজ্যিক ভাবে অসফল বিবেচিত হয়। নিম্ন বর্নিত ৩টি প্রতিষ্ঠানের প্রস্তাব সর্বাধিক সন্তোষজনক বলে বিবেচিত হয়।”

The three participants whose proposals were found to be most responsive were (1) Multimode Transport Consultant Ltd (2) Independent Media Services and (3) Beximco Media Ltd. Thereafter, it is mentioned that proposals of Bangladesh News Service, Bangladesh Sky Network Ltd and Prochar Biggapani Sangstha may also be accepted. Then it is mentioned that the proposals of the remaining ten participants were found to be not responsive and in that list Ekushey Television was placed in the 5th position. Now, let us see what we find at paragraph three of the other report (at page 179 of the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent Nos.(6 and 8). The paragraph is as follows:

“উপরোল্লিখিত বৈশিষ্ট্যের আলোকে প্রস্তাব সমূহ মূল্যায়ন করা হয়। কতিপয় শর্তসাপেক্ষে নিম্নলিখিত প্রতিষ্ঠানের প্রস্তাব বিবেচনা করা যেতে পারে।”

32. Then the list of eight responsive participants is given. We find that this time Ekushey Television is placed on the top and Minrad (Bangladesh) Ltd is placed in the 2nd position and Multimode Transport Consultant Ltd which was placed at top in the report at annexure A(1) is placed in the last position.

33. In may be mentioned that both these reports are signed by all the four members of the committee. From the forwarding letter at annexure A and at page 177 of the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8, it is also quite clear that both forwarding letters bear the same number and the same date and were also signed by the Convener of the Committee. We have found the photocopy of the forwarding letter Annexure-A in the file of the BTV but we have found no copy of the letter which is at page 177 of affidavit-in-opposition of respondent Nos. 6 and 8. This clearly shows that the report A(1) was given to the Secretary of the Ministry of Information by hand (as evident from the peon book of BTV and UO Note of the Secretary at page 174) and another report was again handed over by forwarding letter at page 177. It is also clear to us that though the two forwarding letters bear the same memo numbers, two different reports were handed over to the Secretary. This is evident from the fact that in the forwarding letter Annexure-A it is mentioned that one set of report was enclosed whereas in the forwarding letter at page 177, it is mentioned two sets were enclosed.

34. Now in the second report, it is mentioned that subject to certain conditions the proposal of eight participants may be considered but nowhere these conditions have been mentioned. It is also not mentioned as to who will decide these conditions. It is strange to note that it is not mentioned that on the basis of the evaluation of proposals of all the participants, the proposals of those eight participants were found responsive, rather it is mentioned that if certain conditions are fulfilled only then their proposals may be considered. We do not know actually what were noted in the relevant file where the Technical Committee recorded the minutes or deliberations. We passed two orders to produce the file but the file was not produced, even there is no explanation as to what happened to the file. We do not understand when crores of Taka are involved in the project how an evaluation of tenders could be done without maintaining a file. On the report on which the respondents have given much importance, we have found that this report is also not complete. As the conditions are mentioned in the report subject to fulfilment of which the proposals of eight participants could be considered, how this report was considered by the Ministry and ETV was found most responsive? The basic principle of any tender is that if any subsequent changes are made regarding terms and conditions each and every participant should be informed of such terms and conditions. There is nothing to show that any other participants were informed of such conditions. Still after receipt of this report, the Ministry of Information finalised the case recommending to the Prime Minister to accept the proposal of ETV to set up installations to telecast its programmes. In the summary which was prepared for the Prime Minister, there is no mention of the other report and this fact was totally suppressed. Here lies the importance of transparency and accountability. We are not technical experts. So, it may not be proper for us to say which proposal was technically responsive. We wanted to know how the Committee arrived at the decision to change the earlier report, what are the reasons for such change. It is unfortunate that none of the respondents could give answer to these questions. However, it may be mentioned that Mr Rafiqul Huq has tried to explain that the first report is the draft report and the second report is the final report and because of collaboration with BBC the proposal of ETV was finally found to be most responsive. But this is not the view of the Committee itself, rather the Committee held that only on fulfilment of certain conditions, the proposals of eight participants might be considered.

35. Now, if a report or evaluation is changed there must be some reasons for such change and these reasons should be recorded. We do not know whether any such reasons were recorded because the relevant file has been withheld. If no such reasons were recorded it will amount to arbitrary action. Had it been fact that the 1st report was forged, we would have no difficulty to arrive at a decision that report at page 178 is the correct one and the only report, but when it is admitted by both the sides including by the Convener of the Committee that more than one report was prepared, there must be some reasons for preparing more than one report. On two grounds we would like to say that the action was malafide. First, because reasons for change was not recorded in the second report nor the file was produced, second ground is that in that report it is mentioned that only on fulfilment of some conditions, the proposal of eight participants including ETV might be considered but those conditions were not mentioned in the report nor were disclosed to any of the participants. We are still in darkness as to what are those conditions which were required to be fulfilled for consideration of the proposals of those eight participants. It may be mentioned here that in the file of BTV bearing No. TV (Project) 005,07 we have found that a meeting was held on 2-7-1998 where the Committee was directed to submit report by 6-7-1998. In the same file we also found that the convenor of the Committee called meeting of the Committee on 6-7-1998 and notice was also served upon other members but thereafter when we have searched the minutes or deliberations of the meeting, we found nothing in the file.

<u>36. In view of our above discussion, it is not very much material whether Annexure-A (1) is the final report or 5(b) is the final report. Our concern is about the way, manner, and the procedure which were followed to come to a decision by the Technical Committee. It is true that this Court cannot review the merit of the decision but can review the decision making process. The process followed by the Committee is hazy and blurred, it is not transparent. In the case reported in AIR 1996 (SC) 11 (which is cited by Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed), we find that the Supreme Court of India is of the opinion that while making judicial review, the court cannot review the merits of the decision but can review the decision making process. As we have found that the process of arriving at a decision is not transparent, we are of the view that there was something wrong somewhere which the respondents, specially respondent Nos. 1 and 4, very carefully and consciously tried to keep out of the knowledge of the Court. On this ground, we are of the view that the whole transaction and evaluation is malafide.</u>

37. We are further of the view that the action taken by the Ministry of Information on the basis of that report 5(b) is also not transparent. The Ministry considered this report as final but we have found that it is not at all a final report; it is an incomplete and conditional report. The Ministry processed only the case of ETV without trying to know from the Evaluation Committee as to what are the conditions required to be fulfilled the Ministry itself determined those conditions, the Ministry did not inform the other 7 parties as to whether they are ready to fulfil the conditions. It is not known how and why the Ministry acted on that incomplete and conditional report and how the Ministry came to the conclusion that only the ETV was agreeable to fulfil the conditions and the other 7 parties were not agreeable.

38. Now, as regards, licensing agreement and other points, let us consider the arguments of both parties. The petitioners mainly raised objection on the ground that signing of the agreement by the Ministry of Information was not proper and under section 5 of the Wireless and Telegraphy Act, 1933 only the Director General of Post Office is competent to issue a licence. Mr Rafiqul Huq has argued that in the licensing agreement there is reference of both the Acts. According to him, under Rules of Business, the Prime Minister may condone any departure from the rules to the extent he deems necessary. Mr Huq also referred to the summary which was placed before the Prime Minister and has submitted that there is reference in that summary that the agreement would be signed by the Ministry of Information. Mr Razzaq has also argued that signing of the agreement was violative of Article 145 of the Constitution. On this point, Mr Huq argued that as the agreement was signed in exercise of some statutory powers given to the Ministry, provisions of Article 145 shall not apply.

<u>39. We have perused the Rules of Business provisions of Article 145 of the Constitution and the relevant provisions of Telegraphy Act, 1885 and Wireless and Telegraphy Act, 1933. We are of the view that signing of the licensing agreement in between the Ministry of Information and AS Mahmud may be considered irregular to some extent but it cannot be considered as invalid or void. We have earlier noticed that tender papers were submitted by Mr AS Mahmud on behalf of the M/S ETV because at that time ETV was not registered as a company. As the proposal was submitted by Mr AS Mahmud as proprietor of the firm, signing of that agreement with Mr Mahmud cannot be considered as illegal. But as we have found in our earlier discussion that the process followed in accepting the proposal of ETV was malafide and not transparent, we are of the view that granting of the licence was not lawful.</u>

40. As regards deleting the clause regarding charging of Taka 1200 per hour we are of the view that the decision being taken in an inter-ministerial meeting, before the change, the matter should have been sent back to that inter-ministerial committee. However, we have found that the decision was taken by the then Finance Minister, he was competent to take such decision and, as such, it cannot be said that decision of deleting the clause was illegal.

41. Another objection raised by the petitioner is that the BTV being a Key Point Installation, use of the premises of the BTV by the ETV was illegal and it endangered the security of BTV. It is true the objection was raised by the special police superintendent and chairman of Key Point Installations Survey Committee vide annexure 16(a) and 16(b) of the Affidavit-in-Opposition of the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 but we find that ultimately clearance was given by the Key Point Installations Defence Committee Annexure-16(6)

42. We have considered the arguments advanced by the learned Advocates of both the parties on all the points as referred to above. We have found from our discussion that the procedure followed by Evaluation Committee was not transparent and the manner in which the report was prepared and submitted was malafide. Of course, it is difficult to fix the responsibility but this much is clear to us that evaluation was not done in accordance with the accepted principles under which tender proposals are evaluated by an Evaluation Committee. The file was withheld and the file produced before us contains only correspondence portion and not any note sheet containing the minutes or processing the proposal of the ETV was also not transparent.

<u>43. Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has submitted with reference to section 114(e) of the Evidence Act that there is a presumption that judicial and official acts have been regularly performed. There is no doubt about this legal position, but when an action is taken or decision is taken by maintaining a file that file must be produced to show that the act was done properly. In the instant case, the relevant file has been withheld. So, we are of the view that in this case presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act shall apply. In spite of our repeated orders, the file was not produced by the relevant respondents with whom those were lying. We are very much shocked that the file was withheld and as such constrained to apply the presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act.</u>

<u>44. Now, as the process of taking decision is questionable and as the relevant respondents could not satisfy this Court how and why and on what grounds two reports were prepared what prompted the Evaluation Committee to submit a second report changing the list of responsive participants, why the participant Minard (Bangladesh) Ltd. whose proposal was left out of consideration got the second place in the second report, why the proposal which was found to be most responsive in the first report was placed in the last place in the second report and why the proposal of Ekushey Television which was found to be not responsive at all in the first report was placed in the top place. Similarly, the questions why the Ministry of Information acted on an incomplete and conditional report, how the conditions were determined, what are these conditions which the Committee did not disclose, how on such a vague report, the Ministry found that only ETV was agreeable to fulfil the conditions remained shrouded in mystery. The above actions of the Evaluation Committee and the Ministry of Information are not transparent at all. Such a view has been expressed by the Appellate Division in the case of Hyundai Corporation vs Sumikin Bussan Corporation and others which is reported in 2002 BLD (AD) 16 = 54 DLR (AD) 88 (Para 14) The relevant portion is quoted below.</u>

<u>“............... transparency 	in the policy/decision making as well as in the functioning of the public bodies is desired, for more than one reason and particularly in the matter where financial interest of the state is involved Transparency of the decision making authority is a recognised matter".</u>

<u>45. The last arguments of Mr. Rafiqul Huq was that the ETV has been registered under provisions of Investment Board Act, 1989 the provisions of that Act shall prevail over any other law and the action taken about granting of licence etc. cannot be questioned. In support of his views he cited the case of Bangladesh Telecom vs BTTB reported in 48 DLR (AD) 20 and the case of Chairman. NBR vs Beximco Infusion reported in 51 DLR (AD) 35. It is true that under section 3 of the Investment Board Act, the provisions of the Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law for the time being in force. Sub- section (5) of section 11 of the Act provides that the Board shall give its decision on all facilities that may be required for implementation of the project and sub-section (6) of the section provides that a decision given by the Board shall be deemed to be a decision given of the Government and shall be implemented accordingly. It is true that ETV obtained a certificate of registration (Annexure-12) but obtaining of such a certificate itself is not sufficient to set up telecasting installation. The proposal of ETV must be legally accepted first by the concerned Ministry. We have found that the whole process of accepting the proposal of the ETV was not transparent and, as such, was malafide. So, the provisions of section 11 shall not apply.</u>

<u>46. In view of our above discussion, we finally hold that changing of the evaluation report is malafide and the manner in which it is done is not at all transparent and acceptance of offer of ETV on the basis of the changed report and all subsequent action taken on the basis of the report including signing of the licensing agreement are also mala fide. It may be mentioned here that this Rule was issued upon the respondents to show cause as to why the licensing agreement dated 9-3-99 signed by and between the Ministry of Information and AS Mahmud and the subsequent transfer of the said licence to ETV should not be declared to have been entered with and granted unlawfully and without any lawful authority. We have found that signing of the licensing agreement itself or its subsequent transfer to ETV Ltd. was not unlawful but we have found the process followed for selecting the ETV as most responsive was not transparent and ultimately the acceptance of the proposal of the ETV was malafide and all subsequent acts including granting of licence were also malafide. So, the Rule is liable to be made absolute.</u>

47. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. It is declared that the act of acceptance of the proposal of ETV as most responsive and granting of licence to ETV by respondent No. 1 was done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

After delivery of the judgment Mr Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 6 and 8 prayed for staying the operation of the order for two weeks. Mr Razzaq opposed the prayer. However, the operation of the order is stayed for ten days.

End.

lawyer:
MI Farooqui with Ruhul Quddus and Abdul Mannan Kha, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Kader Talukder; Assistant Attorney-General with Nahid Mahtab, Assistant Attorney-General ------ For Respondent No.2.
parties:
Hanif Shaikh (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
 Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
SAN Mominur Rahman J: Rule was issued as to why the office order bearing No. Memo No. Je: Pro: Nat: //8-4/02/423 dated 4-7-2002 passed by the respondent No. 2 cancelling the declaration of "Dainik Uttarbanga Barta" evidenced by Annexure E to the writ petition, should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. The Rule has been opposed, but no affidavit-in-opposition has been filed.

3. Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner taking us through the application and the Annexures thereto, submitted that the newspaper "Dainik Uttarbanga Barta" is the only newspaper published from Natore after obtaining declaration from the respondent No. 2 on 4-5-1997 complying with the provisions of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act 1973, and that because its news items as published during the general election of 2001 appeared to be against the ideology of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, the local leaders of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, which became the ruling party, with malafide intention took opportunity of the inadvertent mistake made in the main news item published on the Independence Day issue of the newspaper dated 26-3-2002, in mentioning the names of Honourable President, Honourable Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in the Parliament incorrectly, in spite of the fact that the said newspaper has regretted for publication of such incorrect names at the first page of its issues published on 28th and 29th of March, 2002 and the respondent No.2 issued show cause notice bearing Memo No. Je: Pro: Nat/Sha:/8-4/02/194 dated 27- 3-2002 asking the writ petitioner to show cause within 3(three) days as to why the newspapers declaration should not be cancelled for such mistake. The writ petitioner submitted reply to the show cause within 30-3-2002 but after about 3 months a second show cause notice bearing Memo. No. Je: Pro: Nat: Sha: 8-4/02-402 dated 24-6-2002 was issued by the respondent No. 2 intimating that the reply to show cause dated 27-3-2002 was not satisfactory and why for non-supplying copy of the newspaper, as required under section 26 of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act 1973 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act), the declaration of the newspaper should not be cancelled under section 20 of the Act requiring reply within 29-6-2002. In response to second show cause notice the writ petitioner submitted his reply on 29-6-2002 detailing the grounds and asserting that the copies of daily newspaper were regularly supplied to the respondent No: 2 and further stating that if there be any irregularity in the delivery thereof the writ petitioner will look into and ensure that the supply of the copy of the daily newspaper. is made regularly In accordance with section 26 of the Act. But by order communicated vide Memo. No. Je: Pro: Nat/8-4/02/423 dated 4-7-2002, the declaration of "Dainik Uttarbanga Barta" has been cancelled purportedly under section 20(d) of the said Act alleging that the reply dated 29-6-2002 was not satisfactory and making further allegation that the newspaper was not being published regularly. Being aggrieved the writ petitioner moved this Court and obtained the Rule.

4. Mr Md Ruhul Quddus, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that the respondent No. 2 has manifestly exercised his jurisdiction not invested in him under section 20 of the said Act in cancelling the declaration of the newspaper by the. impugned order communicated vide Memo No. Je: Nat:/8-4/02/423 dated 4-7-2002, evidenced by Annexure 'F' in the writ petition. The learned Advocate referring to section 20 of the said Act submitted that the cancellation of any declaration subsequent to authentication of any newspaper can only be made (a) if a proprietor, the printer or the publisher of the newspaper ceased to be a citizen of Bangladesh; (b) if the printer or the publisher has been convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude or under President's Order 8/72; or (c) that if the printer or publisher has been found to be a lunatic or of unsound mind by a Court of law and (d) if a publisher ceased to have financial resource required for regularly publishing the newspaper, but in the instant case neither in the show cause notices any of such allegation has been made nor there was any occasion to attract any of the said four (4) criteria of section 20 of the said Act. It has been submitted that if there be any false news published in the newspaper action may be taken under section 31 of the Act apart from application of provisions of the Penal Code and that for non-supplying of copy of the newspapers as required by section 26 of the Act, action is to be taken under the provisions of section 35 of the said Act, which provides maximum fine of Taka 500 for every default. Learned Advocate lastly, submitted that the action of the respondent No.2 in cancelling the declaration of the newspaper is without any lawful authority and violated the right of the petitioner .guaranteed by Articles 31 and 39 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

5. Mr Abdul Kader Talukder, Assistant Attorney-General with Ms Naheed Mahtab, Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.2, submitted that admittedly the names of the Hon'ble President, Hon'ble Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition has been published incorrectly in the newspaper on 26-3- 2002 which has created confusion in the mind of the public and the newspaper issue in reference being the Independence Day issue, the writ petitioner ought to have been more cautious in the printing of such news and the same cannot be condoned on the basis of the corrigendum published in the newspaper as claimed. Learned Assistant Attorney- General however, found it difficult to show us that the allegations as made in the show cause notices and the impugned order of cancellation, evidenced by Annexure AI dated 27-3-2002, Annexure C dated 24-6-2002 and Annexure E dated 7-2-2002 respectively to the writ petition, attract any of the criteria mentioned in section 20 of the said Act.

<u>6. We have considered the statements made in the writ petition as well as the submissions made by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner and those of the learned Assistant Attorney-General, we are of the view that the impugned order of cancellation vide Memo No. Je: Pro: Nat/8-4/02/423 dated 4-7-2002, evidenced by Annexure E to the writ petition, has been passed without lawful authority inasmuch as the allegation as made in the show cause notice evidenced by Annexure AI can at best attract section 31 of the Act, that too if such publication is found to be malafide. But in the instant case, the authority regretted the mistake occurred in the news item published on 26-3-2002 in the next two issues of the newspaper on the first page published on 28th and 29th March, 2002 as corrigendum and we do not find any malafide in the mistake referred to above occurred in the issue of the newspaper published on 26-3-2002. Further, it appears that in the second show cause notice (Annexure C) a fresh allegation of non-compliance of section 26 of the Act has been made, which also has been denied in the reply. The addition of new allegation in the second show cause notice is bad in the eye of law. In the order of cancellation (Annexure E) it further appears that another new allegation as to non-publication of newspaper regularly. which was absent in the second show cause notice. has been alleged and that no opportunity has been given for reply to such new allegation and thus the impugned order of cancellation is ex facie bad. Considering the requirements of section 20 of the Act. we are of the view that no provision of section 20 is attracted to any of the allegations made in the show cause notices or in the impugned order of cancellation of the declaration and thus. the impugned order of cancellation of declaration of the newspaper appears to be not bonafide, and has been issued without lawful authority.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The order of cancellation of the declaration of the Dainik Uttarbanga Barta vide Memo No. Je: Pro: Nat/8-4/02/423 dated 4-7-2002, evidenced by Annexure E to the writ petition, is hereby declared to have been passed and issued without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

End.

lawyer:
AKM Nazrul Islam with Jabun Nahar Ayesha, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md Ozair Farooq, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party No. 5.
parties:
Shahidullah and others ------ Petitioner
vs.
Lutfur Karim and others ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
The Rule at the instance of the defendants calls in question the judgment decree dated 17-7-95 allowing Title Appeal No.88 of 1993 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali and decreeing Title Suit No,43 of 1991 for declaration that kabala deed No. 3467 executed on 28-6-1947 by Cherag Ali Pandit predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs in favour of Salamatullah predecessor-in-interest of the defendants and registered on 11-7-47 at the Sub-Registrar's office briefly SR Office, Chatkhil is forged, fraudulent, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs and for its cancellation. 

2. Plaintiffs' case is that, Cherag Ali Pandit the admitted owner of the Suit land did never execute the kabala, his signature was forged, the deed was registered by false personation by Salamatullah, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants; there was no thumb impression of Cherag Ali in the kabala; Salamatullah did not acquire any right, title and interest through the disputed kabala. The plaintiffs having come to know about the said kabala on 18-5-91 instituted the suit on 01-8-91. 

3. Defendant Nos. l, 2, 5, 6, 10, 11, 16, and 17 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying all the material assertions and allegations contained in the plaint claiming that their predecessor-in-interest Salamatullah purchased the suit land from Cherag Ali Pandit, a literate, elite, very well known and reputed person in the locality and that the said Cherng Ali was not only personally known to the then Sub-Registrar briefly SR Muzaffar Islam @ Muzaffarullah who married a niece (sister's daughter) of Cherag Ali and hence the SR dispensed with the imprinting of the mark of thumb impression of Cherag AlL 

4. Salamatullah had been owning and possessing the suit land ever since his purchase in 1947 and after his death his heirs ie the defendants have been in continued and uninterrupted possession of the suit land to the full knowledge of the plaintiffs and there had not been any forgery and false personation in the execution and registration of the kabala and the suit is also barred by the law of limitation and accordingly, the suit is liable to be dismissed with cost 

5. The learned Assistant Judge framed as many as 6(six) issues including an issue as to whether the suit was barred by limitation (issue No.4). Having heard the parties and their Counsel and having considered the evidence and materials on record, the learned Assistant Judge, Chatkhil dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 28-2-93. 

6. Strangely enough the trial Court did not discuss and consider' issue No. 4 but while discussing issue Nos. 2, 5, and 6 viz question of cause of action, the right, title and possession of the plaintiffs; discussed the question of possession and recorded a positive finding that the plaintiffs have miserably failed to prove their case. 

7. The-plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No.88 of 1992 and the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali by his judgment and decree dated 17-7-95 reversed the decision 0 of the trial Court, and thus being aggrieved, the defendants have challenged the said decision of the Lower appellate Court by this revisional application. 

8. Heard Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, learned Counsel for the petitioner- and Mr Md Ozair Farooq learned Counsel representing the plaintiff opposite party No.5 at good length. 

9. The moot question before this court is, whether the judgment of reversal passed by the lower appellate Court is a proper judgment of reversal. 

10. Both the Courts below failed to consider the question of limitation. It is worthwhile to look into that question first. The plaintiffs in this case have sought for a declaration .as to the validity of a registered deed of kabala and its cancellation. So the question of possession is of utmost importance for determination of the question of limitation. 

11. The plaintiff had -stated their knowledge about the kabala to be on 21-5-91. The Deed was executed on 28-6-47 and registered on 11-7-47. 

12. Though the cause title and the prayer have been couched in a manner to make" it look like a declaratory suit, it is in fact a suit for cancellation of a registered deed and, as such, the period of limitation is (three) 3 years under Article 91 of the Limitation Act from the date of knowledge of the fact entitling the plaintiffs to have the instrument cancelled and for a suit for declaration simpliciter the period of limitation is 6(six) years from when the right to sue accrues. Strangely enough Mr Nazrul Islam has advanced no argument on this very important point of limitation. 

13. Now in this case, the trial Court has clearly found that the plaintiffs have no possession. The plaintiffs admitted possession and payment of rent (Ext.3 series) by the defendants. The lower appellate Court having held that the question of possession is of no significance importance but did not consider it necessary to look into this question at all and, as such, the finding of fact of the trial Court as to possession stands unreversed and unrebutted. This being the position and the document having been executed and registered in 1947 and the suit having been filed on 01-8-91 the same is undoubtedly and hopelessly barred by limitation. 

14. Few relationships are as vital to man as that of possession, and we may expect any system of law, however primitive, to provide rules for its protection. Human life and human society as we know them would be impossible without the use and consumption of material things. We need food to eat, clothes to wear and tools to use in order to win a living from our environment. But to eat food we have to have land to grow on it end to do that we must first get hold of it, to wear clothes, we must have them; and to use tools, we must possess them. Possession of material things then is essential to life it is the most basic relationship between men and things. A society lacking respect for individual possession would quite clearly be unviable. Simple economics dictates that as a minimum, some measure of uninterrupted enjoyment is pre-requisite to man's deriving any benefit of value from material objects. 

15. As regards possession as evidence of ownership a rebuttable presumption of law is that of lawful origin. It lies at the root of the substantive law of acquisitive prescription. Modem possession and user, being prima facie evidence of property and right the judges attached to them an artificial weight, and held that uninterrupted, uncontradicted and unexplained, they constituted proof from which a jury ought to infer prescriptive right, coeval with the time of legal memory. (Principles of Law of Evidence of Best (12th Edition 322). 

16. The next question that comes up for consideration is on whom lies the burden of proof that the execution of the document was forged and registration was by false personation. The law is clear on 'this point Section 101 of the Evidence Act provides as follows: "Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right of liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, most prove that those facts exist When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person." Section 102 of the said Act enjoins as follows: "The burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side." 

17. In the instant case, a registered document has been challenged as a product of forgery and false personation. Here the legal presumption is in favour of the vendee and, as such, it is the vendor party who has come to court to prove that the document was not executed by the executant named in the document and it was not presented by him for registration and that it was registered by false personation. 

18. The question has been well settled by our Appellate Division reported in 39 DLR (AD) 223 (Civil Appeal No.113 of 1983). Their Lordships of toe Appellate Division have also referred to a decision reported in 33 Indian Appeal cases at page 60 wherein it was observed. "The registration is a solemn act; to be performed in the presence of the competent official appointed to act as registrar, whose duty it is to attend the parties during the registration and see that the proper persons are present and competent to act and are identified to his satisfaction; and all things done before him is in his official capacity and verified by his signature will be presumed to be done duly and in order, of course it may be shown that a deliberate fraud upon him has been successfully committed but this can only be very much stronger evidence than is for the coming here." 

19. So the trial Court rightly held that the burden of-proof lies on the plaintiff. 

2O.The next question which was agitated relates to dispensation with the thumb impression of Cherag Ali. Rule 49 (5) of the Bengal Registration Rule 1927 itself allows dispensation with the taking of thumb impression of person of position regarding whose identity there can be no doubt even if the executant is not personally known to the Sub-Registrar. 

21. In the instant case not only Cherag Ali was a person well known in the locality but also a close relation of the registering officer (SR) himself, being the husband of a sister's daughter of Cherag Ali. Not only that, it is seen from the records that Cherag Ali was also exempted previously from putting thumb impression on documents executed and registered in 1918 and 1950 and when his son PW 1 Lutful Karim was confronted with those 2 documents, he admitted that fact so the finding of the learned lower appellate Court is not acceptable on this score.

22.  Arguments were also advanced regarding presumptive value of certified copies. Public document is permissible as evidence. The trial Court accorded permission and accordingly the certified copy of the kabala of 1947 was admitted into evidence and was accordingly marked as an Exhibit and, as such, section 90 of the Evidence Act and the case reported in AIR 1984 cited by Mr Ozair Farooq have relevance in this case. 

23. Arguments were also advanced by Mr Farooq as to the withholding of the original kabala and the consequential benefit of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. In the instant case the document is of the year 1947 and the plaintiffs filed the suit in 1991 which are matters of record. 
24. Mr Nazrul Islam submits that nowhere in the evidence has it been established that the defendants had the documents in their custody or possession and they wilfully and deliberately' refrained from producing the same in court and hence the finding of the court of appeal below is erroneous and, as such, not sustainable. In support of his contention Mr Islam Cited the case of Ghulam Muhammad vs. Sher Dil reported in PLD 1967 Azad J & K 26 wherein a Division Bench held: "The presumption under section 114(g), Evidence Act is merely permissive. Court, therefore, may refuse to raise the presumption where document is an ancient one and there is possibility of its having been lost." It was further held: "Unless it is established that a document is in the possession of a party and has been willfully suppressed, a court is not entitled to presume that the contents of the document, if produced, would have been unfavourable." 

25. In the instant case I have already stated that the document is as old as 50 years and there is no evidence that the defendant had willfully suppressed the said documents from producing in court. In that view of the matter the findings of the court of appeal below as to the presumption of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act is untenable. Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act cannot be availed of by the plaintiffs. 

26. I am surprised to see that on issue No. 4 ie that the suit is barred by limitation, no discussion was made and no decision was arrived at either by the learned Assistant Judge, Chatkhil or by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali although the plaintiffs instituted the suit after a long lapse of 44 years.

27. One thing needs be mentioned here that in the instant case, the impugned kabala could not be produced before the court instead certified copies thereof were produced by both the parties ie the defendants and the plaintiffs and those were marked as Ext. 1 and Ext (ka) respectively. In this regard Mr Farooq very strongly argued that neither the alleged kabala nor the certified copies produced in court did contain any thumb impression of the executant Cherag Ali and, as such, the said certified copy has no presumptive value as regards its genuineness. Having verified the certified copy (Ext.1) I' have noticed that the Sub-Registrar Mozaffar Islam made an endorsement to the effect" Executant Cherag Ali is personally known to me." though the words the executant is hereby exempted from imprinting the mark of his left thumb on the reverse of the kabala were not there. In this connection Mr Ozair Farooq, learned Counsel for the plaintiff opposite party No.5 referred to 2 (two) registered kabala Nos.584 and 585 respectively dated 26-2-1918 admittedly executed by Cherag Ali PW Lutful Karim who is none else than the son of the executant Cherag Ali having been confronted with those two kabalas of 1918 admitted that by various deeds. His father sold out lot of properties. He was shown the kabala deeds Nos. 584 and 585 dated 26-2-18 and in those deeds his father was spared from imprinting the mark of his LTI on the back side of those deeds. Having had a close look at those two documents nowhere could I find any endorsement of the Sub-Registrar to the effect that executant Cherag Ali was exempted from putting his thumb impression. The endorsement rather was simply that the executant Cherag Ali is personally known to me and in that view of the matter, the contention raised by Mr Farooq that the certified copy of the kabala Ext. 1 containing no thumb impression of certified copy of the kabala Ext. 1 containing no thumb impression of Cherag Ali is not any exemption to that effect, kabala cannot be said to be genuine, has no force.

28.
