Mr Nazrul Islam lastly submits that in this case, the defendants in their written statements in addition to having denied all the allegations made in the plaint had stated that they were not aware as to the whereabouts of the original kabala deed and in his deposition as PWI stated that his father told him about the loss of the document and in this respect Mr Nazrul Islam, learned Counsel relied on a decision in the case of Kamod Singh vs. Khemkaran reported in AIR 1927 (Nagpur) 260 wherein it was held by his Lordships AJC that: (a) it is the duty of a court to get hold of all the relevant evidence there may be and to examine it giving of course due weight to any circumstance attending its production that might render its loss more credible, and giving the other party a fair opportunity of meeting it and no court has the right to reject evidence tendered at any stage of the trial before its close unless it is irrelevant. (b) Evidence Act section 65-Omission to plead loss of a document at the earliest stage of proceedings is not a ground for rejecting its secondary evidence. 

29. Where a document was mentioned in the plaint and the fact that it had been lost was mentioned in an oral pleading made while evidence was being given, when leave was asked to prove it by secondary evidence Held that the fact that the loss was not pleaded in the earliest stages of the case could not justify the rejection of the plea, particularly as the document was specifically mentioned in the plaint with its date." In the present case in the written statement the defendants stated that they were not aware is to the whereabouts of the original deed and in his deposition DW 1 stated that his father told him about the loss of the deed. 

30. In the case. of Bas ant Singh and others vs. Brij Raj Saran Singh and others reported in AIR 1935 (Privy Council) 132 it was held: "Evidence Act (1372) 'Section 65 Evidence- Secondary-Loss cannot be absolutely proved-Original No. seen for many years is sufficient evidence of loss can never be proved absolutely. Where there was no doubt that a document existed which purported to be a will and from which a copy was taken: Held: that the evidence of loss of the original will which was not seen for many years was sufficient to satisfy the provisions of, section 65, Evidence Act, so as to make copy admissible." It was further held: "Loss can never be proved absolutely; and although Cirraj Singh was not called as a witness, their Lordships regarded this evidence of loss of a document which has not been seen for so many years as sufficient to satisfy the provisions of section 65 Evidence Act. Accordingly, they held that the copy is admissible as secondary evidence of the original and it may therefore, as already stated, be taken as a correct copy of the original document." 

31. In the instant 'case the court of appeal below lost sight of the fact that on an application filed by the defendant petitioner, the learned Assistant Judge by order No.21 dated 28-6-92 having been satisfied with the explanation offered, allowed the defendants to produce the certified copy of the disputed kabala. 

 32. Having considered all the salient points involved in this dispute this court is of the view that the learned Assistant Judge, Chatkhil arrived at the proper decision in dismissing the suit and as such the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge reversing the decision of the learned trial Court is not a proper judgment of reversal and hence it is liable to be set aside. 

33. The Rule is accordingly made absolute. The judgment and decree of the Lower Appellate Court is thus set aside and those of the trial Court are restored.
	
34. There will be no. order as to cost. Send down the record at once. 

End.

caseno: Writ Petition No. 2644 of 1990 with Writ Petition No. 346 of 1991
lawyer:
Mainul Hosein with Md. Joynul Abedin, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners in both the writ petitions 
AK Mujibur Rahman, Deputy Attorney-General with Md. Saidur Rahman. AAG ----- For the Respondent No.2 in both the writ petitions.
parties:
Abdul Kashem, Proprietor of Lucky Engineering Works ------ Petitioner
 [In WP No. 2644 of 1990] 
Abdul Gani, Proprietor of Oriental Engineering Company ------ Petitioner 
[In WP No. 346 of 1991]
vs 
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Internal Resources Division and others ------ Respondents 
[In all the writ-petitioners]
full_judgment: Qazi Shafiuddin J: Common question of facts and law in WP No. 2644 of 1990 and WP No. 346 of 1991 being involved and the same are heard together and these Rules will now be disposed of by this common judgment. 2. Facts for the disposal of WP No. 2644/1990 are as follows: The petitioner under L/C dated 28.4.88 imported GP sheets from Japan under ITC No. 73.13 which was subsequently changed as Harmonised Code No. 72.10 and the same was carried by two vessels under 4 Bills of Lading dated 27.5.88 and 6.6.88. At that time the rate of custom duty was 50% ad valorem and the tariff value was Taka 15,000.00 per metric ton under SRO No. 115 dated 18.6.87 and sale tax was 10% ad valorem under SRO No. 114 dated 18.6.87: The consignment arrived at Chittagong port on 20.7.88 and 29.6.88. The Import General Manifest (IGM) bearing No.514/88 was submitted to the Customs and Port Authorities on 29.6.88 and 20.7.88. Four Bills of Entry were also submitted to the Chittagong Customs House on 29.1.90 and 1.2.90. The respondent No. 1, namely, Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Internal Resources Division issued Notification No. SRO 142 and SRO Nos. 114 and 115 dated 18.6.87 changing the duty structures and raising tariff value from Taka 15,000.00 to Taka 24,000.00 per metric ton on 16.6.88. By the aforesaid SRO No. 143 the concessional rate of sale tax 10% ad valorem was discontinued and the sale tax at the rate of 20% ad valorem as per Sales Tax Ordinance, 1982 was introduced. Subsequently the tariff value was also increased to Taka 26,000.00 per metric ton as per SRO No.193 dated 15.6.89. As the petitioner was required to pay custom duty and sale tax at an enhanced rate prevailing on 15.6.89 the petitioner preferred an appeal on 17.5.90 before the National Board of Revenue, Dhaka for allowing deferred payment for release of the said consignments on various grounds. No decision was communicated to the petitioner. It is stated that the petitioner had invested a substantial amount of money and imported the said consignment on the basis of that rate of duties and taxes leviable on the goods prevalent at the time of opening the L/C. As the respondent government did not pay any heed to the demand, the petitioner filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule. 3. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent Nos.1-4. The respondents denied the statements made in the petition on material particulars. It is stated that the Government enhanced the tariff value of the goods from Taka 15,000.00 to Taka 24,000.00 per metric ton by issuing SRO No.142 and SRO No.143 dated 16.6.88 in supersession of the SRO No. 115 dated 18.6.87 and also refixed the sales tax @ 20% ad valorem by issuing SRO No.143 dated 16.6.88 in supersession of SRO No.114 dated 18.6.87. The Government issued the SRO under the authority of section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969 and section 4(1) of the Sales Tax Ordinance, 1982. It is further stated that the tariff value was increased from Taka 24,000/ to Taka 26,000/ and refixed the sales tax @ 20% by issuing SRO No. 193 dated 15.6.89 and SRO No.188 dated 15.6.89 in supersession of the previous SROs in exercise of the power vested in it under section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969 and under section 4(1) of the Sales Tax Ordinance, 1982. It is stated that the petitioner was required to pay the custom duty, sale tax on the basis of the SRO 193 dated 15.6.89 and SRO 188 dated 16.6.89 inasmuch as the petitioner submitted the bills of entry on 29.1.90 and 1.2.90. It is further submitted that section 30 of the Customs Act provides for determination of the duty and sales tax at the rate prevailing on the date of submission of the bills of entry under section 79 of the said Act. 4. In Writ Petition No. 346/91 the petitioner Abdul Gani stated that he opened the letter of credit on 10.5.88 when the existing notification, namely, SRO 114 dated 18.6.87 provided sales tax at 10%, SRO 115 dated 18.6.87 providing tariff value at Taka 15,000.00 per metric ton and statutory rate of duty on import tariff value was fixed at 50%. The goods arrived at Chittagong port on 9.8.88. It is stated that SRO. 142 dated 16.6.88, 143 dated 16.6.88 and 144 dated 16.6.88 were issued by the Ministry of Finance raising the tariff value, sale tax in respect of the aforesaid goods. The petitioner submitted 3 bills of entry on 29.1.90 provisionally. The Customs have assessed the duty and sales tax at an enhanced rate on the basis of the SRO 192 dated 15.6.89, 193 dated 15.6.89 and 188 dated 15.6.89 and realised duty and taxes on 6.6.90. It is stated that the petitioner had invested considerable amount of money finding the high demand of the said goods in the local market at the time of opening the L/C. The Government did not pay any heed to the demand of the petitioner as such the petitioner moved this application and obtained the present Rule. 5. The respondents have filed an affidavit-in-opposition challenging the statements made in the petition to be untrue and incorrect and stated that the tariff value and sale tax on goods were fixed in accordance with law and no illegality has been committed. The authority vested under section 25(7) of the Customs Act, 1969 the Government issued the notification lawfully. It is further stated that the customs duty, sale tax and tariff value was determined as per SRO Nos. 192, 188 and 193 dated 15.6.89 when the bill of entry was provisionally submitted on 29.1.90 under the provision of section 30 of the Customs Act, 1969. 6. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the petitioner having imported the consignment relying on the applicable duties and sale tax on the basis of the value in the local market has acquired a vested right which cannot be taken away by subsequent notifications, as such, the notification cannot be given effect to retrospectively. It is further submitted that the Government cannot take steps and ask for duties on the basis of subsequent notifications and the Government is barred by the principle of promissory estoppel. It is further submitted that the impugned demand for additional duty and taxes on the basis of enhanced tariff value, duty and tax by virtue of SRO dated 18.6.88 and 15.6.88 vide Annexures-B 4 and E made by the Customs Authority is illegal, unconstitutional and violative of fundamental right as such, the order should be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority. In support of his contention Mr. Mainul Hosein has relied on the decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167. In that decision the Government made promise with certain terms and conditions as notified that if anybody could fulfill these terms and conditions, he would get the exemption. The importer having fulfilled the conditions and also acted upon the assurance given by the Government, it is held that the Government cannot retrace its obligations and ask for duties at the rate mentioned in the subsequent notification. It is found by the Appellate Division that the Government is estopped by the principle of promissory estopped and, as such, the impugned direction asking the petitioner to pay duty at the enhanced rate was declared illegal. Mr. Mainul Hosein also relied in the decision reported in PLD 1970 (SC) 439. In that case exemption was granted under section 12A of the Excise and Salt Act, 1942 for a period of 4 years in respect of manufacture of cigarettes in a particular place in the Chittagong Hill Tracts but subsequently included the District of Chittagong where there was no such exemption and excise duty was sought to be imposed. It was held that vested right was created in the manufacturer to have exemption for 4 years and this exemption could not have been taken away on the ground of supersession of area from Chittagong Hill Tracts. It is held in that case that the vested right cannot be taken away by subsequent notification. Mr. Mainul Hosein also placed a decision report in AIR 1963 (SC) 848. In that case the Gujrat State Financial Corporation entered into an agreement in performance of its statutory duty to advance loan to a company acting on undertaking. The company proceeded to undertake and execute project of setting up a 4-Star Hotel. It is held that principle of promissory estoppel would stop corporation from backing out of its obligation. 7. Mr. A.K. Mujibur Rahman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, submitted that the petitioner acquired no vested right as the exemption granted by the Government can as well be modified, altered or cancelled. Mr. Mujibur Rahman has placed the case of Ali Akbar Khan vs. Bangladesh and others (unreported) in WP No. 630 of 1979 disposed of on 30th July, 1979. In that case similar question also came up for consideration and a Division Bench of this Court held that no vested right had been created by virtue of grant of exemption under section 12A of the Salt and Excise Act, 1944. It is held that exemption granted by a notification by the executive in exercise of its power under section 12A of the Act could be withdrawn and reimposition of excise duty by issuing another notification in supersession of the previous one cannot be termed as without any lawful authority. In that case it is found that provision of section 21 of the General Clauses Act is applicable which reads as follows: "Where, by any Act of Parliament or Regulation, a power to issue notification, orders, rules, or bye-laws is conferred, then that power includes a power, exercisable in the like manner and subject to the like sanction and conditions, if any, to add to, amend, vary or rescind any notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws so issued." The Court held that the Government that granted exemption under section 12A of the Act has got also the power to vary, rescind the exemption. This decision and findings of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division by judgment and order dated 3.9.79 in CPSLA No. 247 of 1979. Relying on the provision of section 3(1) of the Act it is held that there shall be levied and collected in such-manner as may be prescribed duties on excise on all excisable goods other than sale which are produced and manufactured in Bangladesh and duty on salt manufactured in, or imported by land into, any part of Bangladesh as and at the rates set forth in the First Schedule. Section 12A, however, provides for exemption from levy of excise duty and the power to allow exemption has been given to the Government by the Legislature, the delegated power is to be exercised by the Government so long this power is not withdrawn. It is further held, "It is difficult to accept the proposition that once exemption had been allowed by the Government, the exemption becomes a vested right of the citizen and it cannot be modified, rescinded or withdrawn without a Finance Act. It has been rightly observed by the High Court Division that when the Executive has been granted the power to allow exemption from levy of excise duty on certain exciseable goods, the Executive has got -the inherent power to withdraw or modify the same. In so doing legislative intervention is not necessary." Furthermore it is observed in the case reported in PLD 1970 (SC) 439 which reads as follows: "It was argued by Mr. Brohi that the Notification dated the. 28th February, 1964, was without lawful authority, as the reasons on which, it was based, namely the exclusion of the District of Chittagong Hill Tracts was not relatable to the grant of exemption. The exercise of power under section 12A to grant exemption as well as the power to withdraw the exemption under section 21 of the General Clauses Act is unconditional. It is, therefore, not open to Courts to go behind the Notification of the 28th February, 1964, on the ground that the exercise of power by the Central Government was improper. However, if the grant of exemption was subject to the existence of certain conditions and the withdrawal of exemption was also made conditional on the happening of certain eventuality, then the Government could not withdraw the exemption unless the requirement of law was fulfilled. As no such conditions are provided in section 12A in the instant case, the High Court had no authority to make its own surmises as to the propriety of reasons which had motivated the issue of the notification dated the 28th February, 1964." Therefore, we are of the view that the exemption so granted or accorded does not in any way create any vested right in favour of the petitioner. Grant of immunity without any condition attached thereto can be removed or cancelled at any time but once the condition so set forth be carried out by the importer it is of course a right has been created thereby which cannot be taken away by the Government. In all the cases cited by Mr. Mainul Hosein the exemption was granted or immunity was allowed conditionally and those conditions fulfilled by the recipients and therefore, the Court held that the Government-respondent could not trace any steps and cannot ask for duties which is contrary to the promise but if the exemption or grant of immunity is without any condition, it falls within the purview of section 21 of the General Clauses Act which action can be taken at any time by the Government and such action cannot be called in question before any Court of law. In that view of the matter we hold that no vested right having been created, the principle of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked in these cases and as such provision of Section 30 of the Customs Act and section 25(7) of the said Act will be applicable and assessment could be made on the date when the bill of entry was submitted before the appropriate Customs Officer. In the premises discussed above, the Rules are discharged but without any order as to costs. End.

Shahidul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md. Fazlul Karim with Zahedul Bari, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party
parties:
Abdul Mazid ------ Petitioner
vs
Abu Zaffor Mohammad Khalil and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment: In this civil revision at the instance of the returned candidate the questions that fall for my determination are whether the Tribunal below committed error in law in holding 114 ballot papers cast in favour of the petitioner invalid and whether the petitioner stands disqualified for contesting in the election of the local Union Parishad for the post of Chairman. 2. The facts giving rise to this Rule are: Opposite party 1 instituted the Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1992 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Bogra for recounting of votes cast in Centre Nos. 1 and 2 of the local Union Parishad and for declaration that the result declaring the petitioner elected chairman was illegal and for further declaration that he was the elected Chairman. The said case founded on the allegations, inter alia. that during the counting of votes illegality was committed by the Presiding Officer as he did not separate the invalid ballot papers from that of valid ones as per Rule and there was post-election tampering with ballot papers. It was also alleged that the Chairman stood disqualified under section 7 of the Government Local Union Parishad Ordinance, 1983. 3. The election case was contested by the petitioner. His contention was that the result was declared legally and there was no tampering of the votes as alleged and that although he was a teacher of the local Secondary School he was not disqualified under section 7 of the Ordinance. 4. Mr. Shahidul Islam submits that the Presiding Officer as on counting the votes sealed the same and put into separate bags as per Rule 38 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1983 there was no violation of these Rules. It is also argued that as on counting the votes the petitioner was found to secure the highest votes he was declared elected chairman and there was no tampering with the ballot papers. He submits that the appellate Court and the Tribunal failed to consider that the gunny bags containing the ballot papers were not intact and this indicates that there was some mischief done by somebody in tampering with the ballot papers. Mr. Fazlul Karim, on the other hand, submits that the finding that 114 ballot papers were invalid based on evidence. He submits that both the Tribunal and the Appellate Court found that there was no tampering with the ballot papers. 5. Rule 38 of the Union Parishad (Election) Rules, 1983 provides for counting of votes. Clause (b) of sub-rule (3) of rule 38 provides for separation of the invalid ballot papers, Mr. Karim placed reliance upon clause (v) to contend that 114 ballot papers containing double seals have to be declared invalid, Read clause (v) of sub-rule (3) of rule 38 with R. 40(1) (a) it seems to me that 114 ballot papers containing such marks are invalid ballot papers. 6. Now let me dispose of the contention on disqualification. Section 7(2)(e) of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 provides that a person shall be disqualified for election or nomination as, or for being, a Chairman or a member if, he holds any full-time office of profit in the service of the Republic or of the Union Parishad or of any other local authority, Mr. Shahidul Islam submits that although the petitioner is a teacher of the local Secondary School but he is not disqualified for election as Chairman as contemplated in section 7(2)(e) of the Ordinance. The question is whether the petitioner holds full-time office of a "Local Authority" within the meaning of section 7(2) (e) of the Ordinance. The definition of the "Local Authority" as defined in General Clauses Act has been amended by President's Order 147 of 1972 and after amendment it stands as: "(28) local authority shall mean and include a Paura Shava, Zila Board, Union Panchayet (now Union Parishad), Board of Trustees of a port or other authority legally entitled to, or entrusted by the Government with the control or management of a municipal or local fund, or any corporation or other body or authority constituted or established by the Government under any law." Thus, it seems that the expressions "other body or authority" constituted or established by any law is local authority. As the expression "any authority" falls in the inclusive definition of the local authority it cannot be said that "any authority" does not include the school in question, specially in absence of any explicit language in the Ordinance by which the expression "school" is excluded from the definition of "any authority". Therefore, on interpretation of section 7 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 read with section 30(1) (b) of the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 I hold that the school is a local authority, Mr. Shahidul Islam, however, argues that section 30 of the Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 provides that an employee of a recognized Intermediate College or Secondary School is bound by the conditions of service as enumerated therein and there is nothing in section 30 for which the petitioner is disqualified for being a chairman of the Parishad. The contention is not correct. Section 30(1) (b) reads: (b) he shall not canvass or interfere or use his influence or stand as a candidate in any election to a local body or a legislative body in Bangladesh," Therefore, the petitioner, a teacher in the local secondary school, incurs disqualification for election of the Local Union Parishad as chairman. Mr. Shahidul Islam further contends that infringement of section 30(1) (b) is to be visited with the penalty as contemplated under sub-section (2) of section 30. Sub-section (2) provides for disciplinary action including removal for contravening the conditions of sub-section (1) of section 30. It has nothing to do with disqualification for contesting as a candidate in an election of a local body. Section 30(1) (b) and section 30(2) are independent of each other and mutually exclusive. For the aforesaid reasons, I discharge this Rule. There will be no order as to costs. End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 25-08-1999 passed by the High Court Division Dhaka in Matter No.1 06 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman CJ: I agree with the final judgment of this Court that the appeal should be dismissed. 

Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury J: I have gone through the Judgment of my learned brother Kazi Ebadul Hoque J. I agree with his conclusion that the appeal should be dismissed. But I differ from the reasonings given by him therefor. The import of Article 114 of the Articles of Association appears to me to be these. No person other than a retiring director or a nominee director shall be eligible for election to the office of the director at any General Meeting unless he is recommended by the directors. This will not apply if a member has left at the office a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of such agent signifying his assent to his candidature at least 7 clear days before the meeting. The purpose of this provision appears to be that if a general member wants to be elected as director but 'fails to give the requisite notice he will need recommendation of the directors for his eligibility for election. 

3. I am unable to agree that the word 'recommendation' occurring in the Article connotes mere scrutiny without any authority to choose. I take the simple dictionary meaning of the word 'recommendation'. I mean speaking favourably of a person for the purpose of election. 

 4. Yet I hold that the appeal must fail because the appellants have no locus standi to maintain the appeal not being themselves' aggrieved by the election, 

AM Malunudur Ralunan J: I agree with the view of my learned brother Justice BB Roy Choudhury.

Kazi. Ebadul Hoque J: This appeal by leave is from judgment and order dated 25-8-1999 passed by the Company Judge of the High Court Division in Matter No.106 of 1997 disposing of the objection raised by the respondent AM Agha Yusuf against report filed by the Chairman of the Annual General Meeting of the International Finance Investment and Commerce Bank Limited (IFIC Bank) so far as it relates to the election of directors of the said Bank. 

7. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, a Senior Advocate of this Court, was appointed Chairman to preside over the Annual General Meeting of the said Bank for the year 1997 and to submit his report by order dated 16-3-1999 passed in the said matter. The said meeting was held on 5th July 1999 presided over by the said Chairman and the said Chairman submitted his report on 4-8-1999. 

8. In the said Annual General Meeting four retiring directors of the said Bank namely, 1 Mr ASF Rahman, 2. Mr Salman F Rahman (the.appellants), 3. Mr AM Agha Yusuf, (respondent No. I) and Mr. Saiful Islam representing class 'A' shares retired and offered themselves to be re-elected directors of the said Bank for the next term. Sponsor shareholder Mr. Asaduzzaman (Folio No.0029) nominated Mr A Matin Khan as another candidate for the office of director of the said Bank representing class 'A" shares.

9. Respondent No.1 sent a, Letter to the Chairman of the Annual General Meeting on 5-7- 1999 stating that "right up to 27th Board Meeting of the Bank held on 1st July, 1999, no proposal for nomination of any director has been received by the Directors" and further stating that" there is no scope for-putting up a candidate for the directorship at the time just before the meeting." But the Chairman overruled the objection raised by the respondent No.1 in the said letter and proceeded to the election of directors of the said Bank. Five shareholders having demanded a poll election was held by the person appointed by the Chairman as Election Commissioner. After the election and counting of votes Chairman, announced the result declaring the appellants, Mr. saiful Islam and Mr A Matin Khan as directors of the said Bank. Chairman thereafter submitted his report on 4-4-1999 to the company Judge about the Annual General Meeting of the said Bank incorporating the result of the election.

10. Respondent No.1 thereafter submitted a written objection before the Company Judge against the report of the Chairman so far as it relates to the election of directors illegally overruling his objection on the ground that there has been violation of the provisions Of Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the said Bank Company in accepting the nomination of  Mr A Matin Khan as he had not left any notice in writing under his own hand signifying his assent to his candidature for the office of director at the office of the Bank after his nomination by any shareholder nor his name was recommended by the directors for such election. 

11. Appellants filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements made in the said written objection and supporting the report of the Chairman. The Chairman also filed a supplementary affidavit stating that the nomination of Mr A Matin Khan marked Annexure 'X' was not inadvertently annexed with the report. 
12. Learned Company Judge after considering the materials on record, hearing the Chairman and learned Advocates of the parties by the impugned judgment and order disposed of the objection and declared the four retiring directors elected as directors of the said Bank.

Learned Company Judge found as follows: 

"In the instant case I do not find from the record that the letter of nomination in favour of Mr A Malin Khan vide Annexure-‘X' to the supplementary affidavit was at all placed before the directors nor there was any recommendation by the directors before the AGM was held on 5th July, 1999. No paper has been filed to show that the said nomination letter was at all submitted to the directors at any time before AGM. In this view of the matter, I find that the election of Mr A Matin Khan was not held in due compliance of Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the bank and, as such, the report of the Chairman Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed with regard to the election of Mr A Matin Khan is rejected." 

13. Appellants, the two re-elected directors, obtained leave to appeal to consider the submission that the Company Judge completely misunderstood and misinterpreted Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the Bank and thereby committed illegality in declaring a defeated candidate as duly elected candidate. If this 'interpretation is accepted, then no outsider can ever be eligible to be elected as Director of the Bank in spite of having duly qualified shares unless the Board of Directors recommends his case, which goes against the concept of company law as well as principle of franchise. 

14. Following submissions of the caveator were allowed to be considered: 
"The petitioners cannot be said to be aggrieved by the impugned decision of the learned Company Judge. Neither the Bank nor Mr A Matin Khan has preferred any petition for leave to appeal from the impugned judgment. The present petitioners have, therefore, no locus standi. That a harmonious interpretation of Article 114 is that, the candidate for election to the office of Directors or his authorised agent shall leave at the office of the Bank at least 7 dear days before the meeting a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of such agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of Director and that such nomination needs to be considered by the Board of Directors to determine the eligibility of the candidate and/or his agent and also to make arrangements for holding a vote. This is what is meant by "recommendation" by the Directors. The "recommendation" is not an obstacle but a means to facilitate the election. The letter of nomination of Mr. A Matin Khan never reached the Board of Directors which held its last meeting only three days before the Annual General Meeting. The learned Company Judge, therefore, rightly came to the conclusion that the election of Mr A Matin Khan was illegal." 

15. Learned Advocate for the appellants submits that if recommendation of the Board of Directors is considered to be a condition precedent to the valid nomination of a candidate for election of a director in case of a person other than a retiring " director in pursuance of Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the Bank then no outsider could be able to be elected as director. So, the provision of Article 114 is in direct conflict with the provisions of clause (b) of subsection (l) of section 9 J of the Companies Act 1994 and, as such, interpretation of Article 114 as given by the learned Company Judge cannot be sustained. He further submits that the appellants as holders of sub-stantial shares of the Bank has right to see that election of a candidate supported by overwhelming majority of shareholders is upheld and, as such, they contested the objection filed by the respondent No.1 by filing affidavit-in-opposition before the Company Judge and so they have locus standi to file and maintain the appeal. 

16. Learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1submits• that the nomination of a candidate for election must be processed through the Board of Directors which has been authorised under the said Article 114 to scrutinize the same and place the same in the Annual General Meeting with its report for consideration of the shareholders and that does not mean that Board of Directors would exclude such nomination. He therefore, submits that there is no real conflict between Article 114 and section 91(1)(b) of the Act. He also submits that Mr A Matin
Khan having not felt aggrieved by the impugned judgment andorder the appellants as shareholders have no locus standi to challenge the same. 

17. Article 114 of the Articles of Association of the said Bank is as follows: 
"No person, not being a retiring Director, shall, unless recommended by the Directors for election, be eligible for election to the office of Director at any General Meeting, unless he or his authorised agent has at least 7 clear days before the meeting, left at the office a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of such agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of director, Provided however, this Article shall not apply to nominee Directors." 

18. From the above provision it appears that no person except a nominee director or a retiring director shall be eligible for election to the office of the director unless he or his authorised agent leaves in the office of the Bank a notice in writing under his hand or under the hand of his agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of director and unless he is recommended by the directors. 

19. In the instant case it appears from Annexure 'X' to the supplementary affidavit submitted by the Chairman on 25-8-1999 that shareholder Mr Asaduzzaman bearing folio No.000029 nominated Mr. A Matin Khan for election to the office of director of the said bank by a letter addressed to the Secretary of the said Bank purported to have been written on 24-6-1999 and at the bottom of the said letter Mr A Matin Khan made the endorsement "I agree" and put his signature under the said endorsement. So, no notice as required under Article 114 was left in the office of the bank by Mr. A Matin Khan under his own hand signifying his assent to his candidature to the office of the director. Admittedly aforesaid letter Annexure 'X' was not placed before the Board of Directors of the said Bank. If it is conceded that the said letter Annexure 'X' is substantial compliance of the requirement of notice under Article 114 the next question is whether there is any necessity of placing the same before the. Board of Directors for its recommendation. 

20. Clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 91 of the Companies Act 1994 provides that directors of the company shall be elected by the members of the company from amongst themselves in a General Meeting. According to the appellants, if recommendation by the Board of Directors under Article 114 is a must for being a candidate for the office of the director and if the Board of Directors do not recommend the name of any candidate then the mandate of the aforesaid provision would be flouted and the provision of the said Article 114 if it comes in conflict with the aforesaid provision of the said Act the same cannot stand. Learned Advocate for the appellant pointed out that in the Articles of Association of almost all the Banks relevant article is in the same language as in Article 114 of IFIC Bank. Why then Banks incorporated articles similar to Article 114 providing for recommendation of the Board of Directors for eligibility of candidature of a person' other than a nominee or retiring director for the office of the director if it is in direct conflict with the said provision of the said Act? It appears to us that such provision has been consciously made to avoid complications in the Annual General Meeting of the Bank in respect of election of directors of the Bank. If the candidature of a person for the office of director is not scrutinized by the Board of Directors before the Annual General Meeting then candidates with defective candidatures would also come to contest in the election and much time would be spent in finding out such defects and-taking decision over the same and thus complications would be created in the Annual General Meeting which has to dispose of important agenda in the meeting. If the Board of Directors scrutinizes the candidatures of such candidates then it would be possible for the Board to find out defect or infirmity in the same, if any, before the Annual General Meeting and would be able to report the same to be considered in the said Meeting. That is why there is the other requirement to submit the candidature in the office of the Bank at least 7 days before the Annual General Meeting. The power of the Board of Directors in the said Article 114 to recommend does not mean power to reject any such candidature. No such power to reject such candidature has been specifically given to the Board of Directors in the said Article or any other Article. So, under the garb of recommendation Board of Directors cannot reject the candidature of any person for the election to the office of the director of the Bank. In our considered view, the word "recommended" means power of the Board to point out defects, if any, in the candidature of a person for the office of director for consideration in the Annual General Meeting to avoid complications in such meeting and not the power to reject any candidature on the ground of -defect real or fanciful. It is for the Annual General Meeting to consider defect, if any, in the candidature of a person and to take a decision 'over the same and not for Board of Directors to do so. So, we find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants that Article 114 does not contemplate recommendation of the candidature of a candidate for the office of director of the Bank by the Board of Directors. 

21. Letter of nomination dated 24-6-1999 Annexure 'X' might have been given to the secretary but the same was not submitted in the office of the Bank. Had it been so submitted then the same would have been placed before the court with the report of the Chairman and would not have been placed before the court subsequently as an Annexure to the supplementary affidavit dated 25-8-1999 specially when respondent No.1 raised objection regarding candidature of any person at the time just before the Annual General Meeting. Moreover, no notice in writing either in the own hand of the candidate Mr A Matin Khan nor in the hand of his authorized agent signifying assent to his candidature for the office of director was left at the office of the bank except the letter of nomination Annexure 'X. left with the secretary. In any view of the matter candidature of Mr A Matin Khan was not in conformity with the requirement of the said Article 114 as regards filing of the same in the office of the Bank in writing in the hand of the candidate or his agent. Even if it is conceded that no recommendation of the Board of Directors was necessary there was no valid nomination of Mr A Matin Khan for his election as director. We, therefore, find no illegality in the impugned judgment to interfere with the same. 
	
22. It appears that the appellants filed an affidavit-in-opposition before the Company Judge to contest the written objection filed by respondent No.1 against the report submitted by the Chairman relating to election of directors. Mr A Matin Khan whose election was rejected by the' learned Company Judge by the impugned judgment has not preferred any appeal against the same. But the two elected directors who filed the said affidavit-in-opposition preferred the appeal. They are not directly affected by the impugned judgment but it appears that they are indirectly affected by the rejection of election of Mr A Matin Khan who appears to belong to their group holding majority shares. Otherwise they would not have filed affidavit-in-opposition before the Company Judge against the written objection of the respondent No.1. A voter cannot prefer an appeal against setting aside of the election of a successful candidate in an election. But that analogy will not hold good in respect of the election of directors of a company including a Bank Company. In the facts and• circumstances of the case appellants representing majority shares having contested the written objection filed by the respondent No.1 challenging election of Mr A Matin Khan before the Company Judge have locus standi to file this appeal. So we find no merit in the objection raised by the learned Advocate of the respondent No.1 regarding locus standi of the appellants. 

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. 

End.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha J: In this Rule the judgment and decree dated 16-1-95 (decree signed on 21-1-95) pased by the learned Additional District Judge, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 486 of 1988 reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 32 of 1983 have been called in question. By the impugned judgment the learned Additional District Judge reversed the judgment of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. 

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for specific performance of contract in the 2nd Court of the Subordinate Judges Chittagong being Other Suit No. 32 of 1983, alleging, inter alia, that the defendants entered into an agreement with him for sale of the suit land measuring 44 decimals of land at a consideration of Taka 55,000.00 and in pursuance of the said agreement the defendant duly executed a bainapatra dated 18-5-80 in his favour on receipt of Taka 50,000.00 as earnest money on the stipulation that they would execute and register a sale deed in respect of the suit property on receipt of the balance of the consideration money. In spite of demands the defendants did not perform their part of the contract and hence the suit for specific performance of contract. 

3. Defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit by filing written statements admitting the plaintiffs’ case and the execution of the bainapatra and expressed his willingness to execute and register the promised sale deed as prayed for. 

4. Defendant No.2 contested the suit by filing written statements denying all the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that he never entered into any agreement for the sale of the suit property to the plaintiff at any point of time. It has also been contended in the written statement that defendant No. 1 is his elder brother and they were in the same mess for 3 years and he depended upon defendant No. 1 for managing the joint properties and it was in connection with those properties he signed some blank papers at the instance of defendant No. 1 for managing the affairs of his family. It was further asserted in the written statement that the plaintiff happens to be a Bhaira of plaintiff No. 1 and they in collusion with each other have created the bainapatra for depriving him of his valuable properties. It was apprehended that the plaintiff in collusion with defendant No.1, might have converted same blank papers into the alleged bainapatra, although he never agreed to sell the property to the plaintiff on any date on receipt of any consideration money. It was further asserted that the plaintiff is simply a benamder of defendant No. 1 and it was defendant No. 1 who was pulling the curtain from behind the scene for making illegal gains at his cost and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

5. At the trial the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses and the contesting defendant also examined 4 witnesses in support of their respective cases.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned judgment dated 17-9-88 was pleased to decree the suit Thereafter contesting defendant No.2 took an appeal before the learned District Judge, Chittagong and the learned Additional District Judge, who heard the appeal, has been pleased by the impugned judgment to reverse the judgment of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. It is against this judgment the plaintiff petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Mostafa Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned Court of appeal below on a wrong view of section 114(g) of the Evidence Act dismissed the suit and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

8. Mr Mostafa Kamal Pasha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the learned Court of appeal below was perfectly justified in passing the impugned judgment on the basis of the evidence on record, after adverting to the reasons assigned by the learned trial Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Court of appeal below on due consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary, reversed the findings of the trial Court and, these being well supported by the evidence on record, cannot be interfered with in revision and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

9. We have heard the learned Advocates at length and perused the impugned judgments. It appears from the impugned judgment passed by the learned Court of appeal below' that he duly considered the material evidence of the respective parties, both oral and documentary, and reversed the findings of the trial Court on assigning cogent reasons. The learned Additional District Judge as of fact found that bainapatra Ext. 4 was allegedly executed at the residence of Arifur Rahman in the city of Chittagong whereas the three witnesses in the said bainapatra came from distant places. PW1stated in his evidence that he did not know whether the attesting witnesses would depose in the case in favour of the plaintiff. The learned Court of appeal below also noticed that the stamp of bainapatra Ext. 4 was purchased on 27-4-76 whereas the bainapatra was executed on 18-5-80 ie after a lapse of 4 years. The plaintiff did not offer any explanation whatsoever on this point. The learned Court of appeal below also found that the attesting witnesses in the bainapatra viz; PW s 2-4 are not natural witnesses and disbelieved the bainapatra and found it to be a fabricated piece of paper. The learned Additional District Judge also found that the learned trial Court totally ignored the evidence of the 4 DWs and on that count also the judgment of the trial Court could not be sustained. 

10. It appears from the perusal of the judgment of the trial Court that the learned Judge did not at all consider the evidence of the 4 DWs and the legal incidence that flows therefrom. Law requires that when the contending parties adduce evidence in support of their respective cases, whether oral or documentary, a duty is cast upon the Court to consider the same and thereafter to arrive at its conclusions with reference thereto but it has no right to ignore the evidence of a party irrespective of the value that it may carry. Applying the correct principle regarding the appreciation of the evidence the Court has the right to believe or disbelieve a witness or a number of witnesses but it has no right to ignore the evidence of a party in coming to his decision. Non-consideration of a material witness or a material piece of evidence of the witnesses of a party or any important document is a serious legal infirmity which renders the impugned decision unsustainable in law. In the instant case, while decreeing the suit the learned trial Court totally ignored the evidence of the 4 DWs without assigning any reason. The findings of the learned appellate Court on this point are fully supported by evidence and reasons. 

11. We have also carefully examined the alleged bainapatra Ext 4. On the face of if it is evident that it was typed on one page of a stamp paper. It is in the evidence of PW I that one Advocate drafted this bainapatra and it was typed by a professional typist. The draft of the bainapatra has not been produced before the Court Neither the learned Advocate who drafted it nor the man who typed it has been examined in this case and no explanation has been furnished. It is an admitted fact that the 3 attesting witnesses who deposed in the suit in favour of the plaintiff are coming from distant places and appear to be unconnected with the alleged transaction. Their presence at the time of execution of the bainapatra has rightly been found to be doubtful by the learned appellate Court. In paragraph 3 of, the plaint it has been stated that the defendant entered into an agreement for the sale of the suit land to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 55,000.00 but nothing has been stated in the alleged bainapatra as to who were the persons allegedly present at the time of finalisation of talk. It has never been alleged that any of the attesting witnesses was present at the time of finalisation of talk. It has been clearly asserted in paragraph 1 of the written statement that the plaintiff is not the real plaintiff of the suit and in his garb defendant No. 1 started this proceeding for making illegal gains. It appears that at no point of time the plaintiff appeared in the Court, although his presence was consistently demanded by the defendant from the very beginning. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the absence of the plaintiff in the Court appears to be a mystery and that mystery has not been solved by any cogent explanation. There is nothing on record to find any justifiable reason for the absence of the plaintiff in the suit although his bonafide was seriously challenged from the very beginning. Under such circumstances, the learned Court of appeal below appears to be justified in drawing an adverse presumption against the plaintiff under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. 

12. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, refers to the case of Gokal Chand and others vs. the Firm of Hukam Chand Nathumal reported in 34 IC page 714. The learned Advocate also refers to the case reported in AIR 1981 (SC) page2235 and the case of AD Koshal vs. Balakrishna Eradi reported in 1981 AIR (SC) page 2235 in-support of his submissions.

 13. In this case nowhere in the plaint it has been stated that any of the attesting witnesses was present at the time of finalisation of talk for entering into the alleged agreement by the parties. The attesting witnesses appeared on the scene at a subsequent stage only at the time of execution of the alleged bainapatra, which is just a follow up of the earlier proceedings. So, the earlier part of the proceedings remains totally unexplained for reasons best known to the plaintiff. The conspicuous absence of the plaintiff from the scene without any justifiable reason appears to be a mystery that has not been solved by any cogent explanation and on that count the learned Court of appeal below was perfectly justified in drawing an averse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. The cases cited by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner do not help him at all as the facts and circumstances of the present case are quite distinguishable from those of the cited cases. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the material on record, we are of the view that it was incumbent upon the plaintiff to come to the dock to prove the alleged agreement for sale. 

14. It also appears that the alleged bainapatra dated 18-5-80 was marked as an exhibit although the contesting defendant duly objected to its admissibility in evidence. None of the plaintiff’s witnesses exactly proved the contents of the bainapatra. The very appearance of the alleged bainapatra Ext. 4 renders it a suspicious paper. Usually the name of the typist is written at the bottom of the sheet but in this case even space measuring 16/1 of an inch has not been left to accommodate even the name of the typist. It is only one sheet of stamp paper that has been used for writing the bainapatra. The name of the typist has been set on the left hand margin of the stamp paper. This is also a strikingly unusual feature. It appears to us that only the person who drafted the bainapatra or the typist who typed it or the plaintiff himself allegedly present at the time of execution of the alleged bainapatra was the most competent person to prove the bainapatra but that having not been done, the bainapatra itself became a highly doubtful piece of paper. Moreover, there is no explanation why the stamppaper was purchased 4 years before the alleged bainapatra came into existence. In the face of Ext, 4 it appears that it contains two L Tis of two persons named Abdur Rahman and Arifur Rahman totally unconnected with the transaction in question. It remains totally unexplained why and how these LTIs appeared in the bainapatra Ext 4. The appearance of these LT is in the bainapatra lends support to the defence case and makes the plaintiffs case still more suspicious. This stamp paper might have been purchased for some other purpose but it was surreptitiously used in making the alleged bainapatra with oblique motives. The submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner do not appear to have any substance surreptitiously used in making the alleged bainapatra with oblique motives. The submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner do not appear to have any substance. 

15. The scope of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is now well settled. Consistent pronouncements by the highest court of the country have made it abundantly clear that a court of revision under section 115(1) CPC can interfere with the findings of fact, as the final court of facts, only in exceptional circumstances when the, findings are shockingly perverse or these are vitiated by non-reading and mis-reading of the material evidence or mis-construction of any important documents affecting the merit of the suit. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has not been able to point out any such legal infirmity in the impugned judgment which calls for our interference.

16. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, we are of the view that the learned Court of appeal below on proper consideration of the evidence on record and after adverting to the reasons assigned by the trial Court reversed the judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. The findings recorded by the learned Court of appeal below are well-supported by the evidence on record and are based on correct principle of the appreciation of the evidence. We find no .illegality in the impugned judgment to call for any interference by this Court exercising revisional power. 

17. In the result, this revision fails and the Rule is discharged with costs. 

Send down the lower Court records at once. 

End.

full_judgment: Latifur Rahman J : This appeal by leave by the defendant is against the judgment and order dated 26.6.94 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 668 of 1989, affirming the judgment and decree dated 25.6.89 passed by the SCC Judge and 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in SCC Suit No. 31 of 1984 for eviction of a monthly tenant. 2. The suit was filed by the respondents and their father Mirza Murshal Hossain against the defendant-appellant for his ejectment and for realisation of arrear rent. The plaintiffs' case, inter alia, is that Mirza Murshal Hossain and his wife Begum Shamsun Nahar, inducted the defendant in the disputed premises under an agreement dated 14.8.69 with effect from 1.8.69 at a monthly rental of Taka 135.00 as per English Calendar month and subsequently the said Begum Shamsun Nahar died on 17.1.83, leaving husband Mirza Murshal Hossain and a son and a daughter, the respondents; that the defendant is a defaulter and he has defaulted to pay rents of the disputed premises from September1975; that the plaintiffs required the suit premises for construction of the undone part of their multi-storied building, construction of new gas, water and sewerage lines and for keeping a passage for going to and coming from the back staircase of the building and that after serving notice upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, on 16.6.84 terminated the tenancy and claimed eviction of the defendant along with the recovery of arrear rents of Taka 4,860.00. 3. The defendant by filing a written statement denied that he is a defaulter and the premises is required for reconstruction and for taking new gas, sewerage, water lines and for keeping passage in the back staircase. The defendant's positive case, inter alia, is that he paid Taka 3,500.00 as advance and the rent was payable in advance on or before the 10th day of each month and in default the defendant should bear interest at the rate of 50% per annum upon the rent; that the defendant has been running his business of confectionery, tea, milk, etc.; that plaintiff No.1 took rents from the defendant and he confirmed that payment of rent upto June, 1977 by granting a receipt on 4.7.77; that plaintiff No. 1 from 3.7.77 to 31.5.78 bought milk on credit worth Taka 1203.00 and plaintiff No. 1 promised to adjust the same with the rent of the disputed premises; that plaintiff No.1 during the construction work of extension of the disputed holding took an advance of Taka 17,500.00 from the defendant by cheque and also in cash with a promise to allot another shop in the holding after the completion of the construction work and in default to allot another shop to the defendant the aforesaid advance of Taka 17,500.00 would be treated as an advance rent of the disputed premises; that plaintiff No. 1 agreed in writing for adjustment of the aforesaid amount; that since July 1977 upto the month of December, 1984 the total rent for 90 months at the rate of Taka 135.00 per month would be Taka 12,150.00 and the remaining Taka 10,053.00 would be at the hands of the plaintiffs which could easily be adjusted towards the rents of the disputed premises for some more years would be treated as an advance rent of the disputed premises; that plaintiff No.1 agreed in writing for adjustment of the aforesaid amount; that since July 1977 upto the month of December, 1984 the total rent for 90 months at the rate of Taka 135.00 per month would be Taka 12,150.00 and the remaining Taka 10,053.00 would be at the hands of the plaintiffs which could easily be adjusted towards the rents of the disputed premises for some more years with effect from 1.1.85 and accordingly, the defendant is not a defaulter from September, 1975 and the question of construction as claimed in the plaint does not arise: that the defendant on 22.4.89 by filing an additional written statement disclosed that the aforesaid amount was adjusted upto the month of December 1988 and then there was balance of advance money of Taka 70.00 with the plaintiffs and the defendant sent the rent through money order and after refusal of the same by the plaintiffs, he deposited rents to the Premises Rent Controller (4th Assistant Judge), Dhaka on 30.3.89 by filing House Rent Case No.12 of 1989 and since then he has been depositing the rents to the Court and the question of default does not arise at all. 4. The learned Subordinate Judge found on consideration of the materials on record, both oral and documentary, that the defendant paid rent upto August, 1975 and filed rent receipt of the same. The trial Court found that the defendant did not file any rent receipt in assertion of his claim of payment of rent from September, 1975. For non-filing of any rent receipt after August, 1975 the trial Court disbelieved the defendant's case of payment of rent from September, 1975. The trial Court on consideration of the documentary evidences found that the plaintiff, in fact, admitted the payment of money by the defendant. The trial Judge found that under section 13 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance the tenant is entitled to get rent receipt from the landlord and in the event of the failure of the landlord to grant rent-receipts to the tenant, the tenant can start a proceeding under section 27 of the Ordinance before the Rent Controller but in the present case the defendant took no such proceeding. The trial Judge further found that the plaintiff requires the premises for reconstruction of his multi-storied building and for setting up other utility services such as, installation of new gas, water, sewerage lines. On the the above findings the suit was decreed 5. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division affirmed the decision of the trial Court both on the question of default and bonafide requirements. 6. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division acted wrongly in affirming the decision of the SCC Judge when the latter on misreading of the evidence both oral and documentary on record held that the defendant was a defaulter and that the plaintiffs required the suit premises for their bonafide requirements. Leave was also granted for considering the vital aspect of the case, that admittedly the plaintiffs had in their hands unadjusted amount of money paid by the defendant which could be easily adjusted towards the payment of rent and whether on these facts the defendant could be termed as a defaulter. 7. In view of the leave granted by us we are called upon to re-appraise the oral and documentary evidences on record. In this case, the plaintiff examined one witness and the defendant examined four witnesses and some documents were filed by both the parties. 8. PW 1 Masud Hossain, son of plaintiff No. 1, deceased Mirza Murshal Hossain, deposed that the defendant did not pay any rent from September, 1975. He also denied the fact of defendant's paying rent upto June 1977. This witness admitted the acceptance of Taka 3,500.00 as security from the defendant. He denied the defendant's suggestion of adjustment of price of milk of Taka 1203.00 towards the rent. He admitted acceptance of Taka 17,500.00 from the defendant but denied the defendant's case of adjustment of the same towards rent. He further deposed that they required the shop premises for reconstruction of staircase, gas and sewerage lines. DW 1 Monoranjan Barua, the defendant filed the account book which was marked as Exhibit "Kha" and this witness proved the signature of plaintiff No. 1 Ext. Kha(1). He stated that Murshal Hossain (plaintiff No. 1) after acceptance of rent upto July 1977 has written the account book in his own hand. He also stated that from July 1977 upto 31.5.78 the plaintiff took milk on credit by coupon and wrote the same in his own hand in exhibit 'Kha', He also deposed that he paid Taka 17,500.00 to plaintiff No. 1 by cheques and cash with an agreement that in the event of plaintiffs failure to provide another shop room in the said market the amount will be adjusted towards the payment of rent and the same was written in the diary by the plaintiff himself after putting his signature. The defendant filed the said diary which is marked as Exhibit 'Gha', According to the testimony of DW 1, supply of milk of Taka 1203.00 on credit was agreed to be adjusted towards the payment of rent. He deposed that even after adjustment of rent upto February, 1989 there will be some more money in the hands of the plaintiffs. He also testified that the construction of first floor is completed and the second floor is about to be finished. According to this witness in the said holding there is a staircase, gas, water and sewerage lines from before 9. DW 2 Saleh Ahmed, an officer of Pubali Bank, has proved the payment of Taka 3000.00 on 14.12.76 and Taka 10,000.00 on 21.12.76 by cheques Ext. 'Chhah' and 'Chhah(1)' issued by the defendant in favour of plaintiff No. 1. DW 3 Samar Krishna Roy, Advocate Commissioner, proved his report Ext. 'Umma' showing that the first floor has been constructed on the top of the disputed shop with a tin roof. He deposed that second floor is under construction in other portions of the holding. 10. DW 4 Md. Raisuddin has a shop 10/15 cubits away from the disputed shop. He testified that on the eastern side of the disputed shop there is a staircase and on the top of the disputed shop first floor has been constructed. According to this witness, sewerage and water lines are already in existence. This is all the material oral evidence on record. Along with this oral evidence, we will mention about the documentary evidences produced in this case by the defendant. Exhibit 'Kha' is the account book which shows payment of rent upto June, 1977 and reads as follows: "In this exhibit, we find several coupon numbers containing different dates (for supply of milk) with the signature of plaintiff No.1 by the side of each coupon. A reference to Ext. 'Gha' shows payment of Taka 17,500.00 by three cheques and by cash for allotment of a new shop room measuring 12' x 8' by the side of the existing disputed shop. There is a clear recital in the said Exhibit." From the documentary evidences particularly, Ext. "Kha" we find that rent upto June 1977 was paid and in Ext. "Kha" we find the signature of plaintiff No. 1 by the side of each coupon. From Ext "Gha" we also find that there has been a payment of Taka 17,500.00 to plaintiff No. 1 with a clear stipulation that the same will be treated as advance rent in the event of failure of the plaintiff to allot a new shop room. From these exhibits it is clear that money was already in the hands of the plaintiffs when the suit was filed. 11. Thus, the trial Judge on a misreading of the oral and documentary evidences on record and without considering the effect of those documents held the defendant to be a defaulter. The trial Judge also failed to notice another important aspect of the case that there is assertion in the plaint that the defendant is a defaulter from September, 1975, whereas from the admitted documents filed by the defendant and believed by the trial Court and the learned Single Judge rent was paid upto June, 1977. 12. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff- respondents, submitted that in Ext. "Kha" account book, there is no signature of plaintiff No. 1 by the side of the writing 'rent paid upto June 1977' and hence the document is false. 13. We have seen the entire document and we find that in all other places by the side of each coupon there is the signature of Mirza Murshal Hossain. For the first time, Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed pointed out before us that this document is not genuine, whereas the trial Court accepted this document. There was no argument of any interpolation either before the trial Court or before the High Court Division. This document was not doubted by the trial Court at all. The trial Judge having believed this document Ext. "Kha" the argument of Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed cannot be accepted now. 14. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed further argued that as no rent-receipt has been filed from September, 1975 nor any case has been filed by the defendant under section 27 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance for violation of section 13 of the said Ordinance the trial Court including the learned Single Judge rightly held that the defendant is a defaulter. He also cited the case of Mosammat Rahima Khatun vs. Abdur Rashid Bhuiyan and another reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 520. 15. Section 13 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance provides that a tenant who makes a payment of rent to the landlord is entitled to obtain rent receipt forthwith from the landlord. Section 27 of the Ordinance provides that if a landlord wilfully refuses or fails to deliver a receipt to the tenant in accordance with the provision of section 13, a tenant may file a complaint before the Rent Controller. Section 27 of the Ordinance provides for a penalty. In the present case no such proceeding was taken by the tenant under section 27 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, because there was no wilful refusal or failure to deliver the rent receipt by the landlord as is evident from the oral and documentary evidences on record, DW 1 stated in his deposition that he has been regularly paying rent to the landlord and submitted those rent receipts granted by the landlord. He has further testified that the relationship with plaintiff No.1 was so cordial that at the time of realisation of rent he used to give receipts at times and at times he did not give any rent receipt. Exhibits "Kha'' and "Gha" are indicative of good relationship between the parties. Hence non-filing of the rent receipts by itself will not be so material as from the evidence on record admittedly the unadjusted amount remains in the hands of the plaintiffs. It may be mentioned here that the filing of the rent receipt in support of the claim of the defendant of payment of rent up to June, 1977 would have been the best evidence in the case but the defendant having actually proved the payment of rent by oral and documentary evidences the trial Court including the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division wrongly held the defendant to be a defaulter. 16. In the case of BCR 1984 (AD) 520, cited by Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, this Division while considering the case of eviction of a tenant on the ground of default in payment of rent did not consider the question of adjustment of the rents for the months for which default has been made by the respondents against the security money deposited by them as no proceeding was taken under section 14 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance within six months before the House Rent Controller. As no application under section 14 of the Ordinance was made praying for adjustment against the security money that question was not gone into. This Division further held in the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed vs. Mohd. Hassan and others, 31 DLR (AD) 155, has no application in the facts of the case. Hence this case is not very relevant for our purpose. 17. I will now consider the case cited by Mr. TH Khan to show that there being admitted unadjusted money in the hands of the plaintiffs the same could be adjusted towards the rent. 18. In the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed vs. Mohd. Hassan and others, 31 DLR (AD) 155, this Division while holding that taking of advance rent for more than one month as contemplated in section 10 of the Ordinance is illegal, observed that the tenant could not be said to be a defaulter in payment of rent within the meaning of section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance as long as the money in the hands of the plaintiff-landlord could be adjusted towards the payment of rent. In the present case we find that the amount of Taka 17,500.00 was not paid to the landlord in consideration of the grant, renewal or continuance of the tenancy and hence section 10 of the Ordinance is not attracted. 19. Thus it is clear that in this case the learned Subordinate Judge wrongly held that the defendant is a defaulter by misreading the oral and documentary evidence on record. 20. With regard to the question of bonafide requirements, in paragraph 4 of the plaint the plaintiffs stated that the suit premises is required for construction of undone part of their multi-storied building and for installation of new gas, water and sewerage lines and for keeping passage from going to and coming from the back staircase of the building. From the evidence on record we have already found that the construction of second floor in other portions of the holding was almost completed. From the evidence on record we have already found that in the holding there is existence of sewerage, water and gas lines from before. There is also a staircase by the side of the shop room through which one can go to the first floor and second floor. Hence, the finding on the question of bonafide requirements is also not tenable on a proper reading of the entire evidence on record. 21. For the foregoing reasons, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and the suit is dismissed. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. End.
