full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of judgment and decree dated 8-5-86 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Bagerhat in Title Appeal No. 38/8 affirming the decree of the final Court in a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession and permanent injunction.

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs brought Title Suit No. 631/1 in the Court off Munsif Moralganj seeking reliefs as aforesaid. The plaint case, in brief, is that schedule land belonged to Olimuddin and Alimuddin, the two brothers. They settled 4.41 acres of land to Safaruddin Faraji, Alimuddin settled 2.71 acre of land to Olimuddin who died leaving a son Mahajuddin, daughter Laxmi Bibi and wife Shajal Bibi. During CS operation the said 2.71 acres of land was recorded in the name of Menhajuddsi and Laxmi Bibi in CS Khatian No. 689.Plaintiff No.Iisthe son of said Menhajuddin. The name of Safaruddin Faraji was recorded in CS Khatian No. 688 in respect of 4.41 acres and the said 2.71 acres of land was recorded in Khatian No. 689 in the name of the plaintiffs’ father and his Fufu maternal aunt as Kolkorsha. The plaintiffs father purchased the land of plot Nos. 1822 and 182412134 of CS Khatian No. 688 from Safaruddin Faraji and entered into possession and accordingly in the remark column of the said Khatian the possession of Menhajuddin as purchaser was recorded. Laxmi Bibi and Shajal Bibi gifted their portion of the property to Menhajuddin by the registered deeds of gift dated 14-6-1926 and put him in possession and Menhajuddin became the owner of the land of CS Khatian No. 689 and possessed the same. Thus Menhajuddin became the owner of the land measuring 2.71 acres in CS Khatian No. 689 by dint of and also by inheritance and he acquired title in the land to the extent of 0.92 decimals comprising plot No. 1822 and 1824/2134 of CS Khatian No. 688 and thus Menhajuddin became the owner of the suit land measuring 3.63 acres and had been in possession of the same. The plaintiff No.1 further pleaded that for nonpayment of rent by the under tenants of CS Khatian No. 688 under original CS Khatian No. 687 and the heirs of Alimuddin having 8 annas share in the CS Khatian No. 687 having failed to pay rent for their portion of the land, the landlord brought Rent suit for realization of arrear rent and in execution of the rent decree the land of the said Khatian was auction sold which was purchased in the benami of Asmat Ali Howlader the maternal uncle of the plaintiff with the money of the plaintiff given by the defendant No. 19 and that Asmat Ali the predecessor of the defendants Nos. 1-14 had not paid the bid money for the auction purchase. It is the case of the plaintiff that after the auction purchase the plaintiff did not get possession in the land as the under tenancy which is an encumbrance against the certificate purchase had not been annulled according to the provision of Bengal Tenancy Act. The plaintiff further averred that during the plaintiffs minority the said maternal uncle managed the auction purchased land and the rent was paid in the name of Asmat Ali who is the benamder of the plaintiff. The plaintiffs’ father possessed the suit land as mentioned in schedule Kha during his life time. By amicable settlement amongst the co-owners the plaintiff became the absolute owner of the suit land and he has been possessing the land sometimes cultivating by his own labour and sometimes by borgaders for more than 12 years. During the SA and RS settlement operation the name of Asmat Ali Howlader was recorded as per advice of the plaintiff. After the death of Asmat Ali the defendant Nos. 1-12 the successors of Asmat had no title and possession and sold the said land to the defendant No. 15 who in collusion with the defendant Nos. 1-12 threatened to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land on 25-3-84 which led the plaintiff to launch the suit.

3. The suit was resisted by the defendant No. 15 on the ground, inter alia, that the suit is barred under section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure and then the defendant averred that the land measuring 4.41 acres comprising CS Khatian No. 689 belonged to Rashid Howlader and Menhajuddin Howlader. The superior landlord Laha Babu and others for realisation of rent instituted rent suit in the year 1930 and in execution of rent decree No. 860/31 auction sold the land of CS Khatian No. 687 and Asmat Ali Howlader auction purchased the land with his own money and got possession in the land. While Asmat Ali had been proceeding to annul the encumbrance as regards under tenancy of Khatian Nos. 688 and 689 there had been an amicable arrangement by which the original tenant Safaruddin made over 0.62 decimals of land of plot No. 1822 and 0.30 decimals from plot No. 1824/2134 comprising Khatian No. 688 in favour of Asmat Ali and in respect of land with an area of 3.49 acre of the said Khatian to the three sons of Safaruddin remained as sub-tenants under Asmat Ali and RS Khatian was prepared accordingly. Thus Asmat Ali by auction purchase acquired 2.71 acres of land of Khatian No. 689 and 0.92 decimals of Khatian No. 688 and owned and possessed 3.63 acres which is the suit land. After the death of Asmat Ali the defendant Nos. 1-14 being his heirs got the suit land. Further case of the defendant is, that the defendant Nos. 1-6 and 9-12 entered into agreements for sale with the defendant No. 15 by two registered sale deeds dated 7-9-83 and the defendant has been in possession and enjoying the land on payment of rent.

4. The parties adduced evidence to the best of their ability. The learned Assistant Judge upon considering the averments put forward in the plaint found that the plaintiff No. I at the same time claimed the .suit land by inheritance and also founded his claim on tenants transaction i.e. he claimed to be the real owner and his maternal uncle Asmat Ali is the benamder but the plaintiff failed to prove the plea of benami. After assessment of the oral evidence of the plaintiff witnesses and also considering the documentary evidence such as record of rights in the name of Asmat Ali, the rent receipt showing payment of rent in the name of Asmat Ali he opined that the plaintiffs claim both for title and possession is not supported by any valid and cogent evidence. Then the learned Assistant Judge proceeded to determine the maintainability of the suit in view of the provision of section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure and his clear conclusion, considering pleading, is that the suit is barred under the aforesaid provision of law and dismissed the suit, From the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff appealed to the District Judge Bagerhat and the appeal having been heard by the learned Subordinate Judge was dismissed and the trial Court's decree was upheld.

<u>5. Mr. Sk Razzaque Ali the learned Advocate, has appeared in support of the Rule and he has in the first place contended that the learned Appellate Court failed to consider the documentary evidence adduced by the plaintiff in coming to a conclusion with regard to the real controversy between the parties in the suit. He has pointed out particularly from Exhibit 7, the kabala dated 28-3-1923 showing transfer of 0.92 decimals of land by Safaruddin Faraji to the father of the plaintiff and Exhibit 6(a) which indicates that Menhajuddin had been in possession of that portion of the land as purchaser and he had the under raiyati right which was inherited by him. He further contended that the document No. 6(a) having presumption of correctness has not been evaluated and the rent receipts Exhibit 3 series have not been considered along with the oral testimony in arriving at a finding of possession of plaintiff in the suit land and, consequently, there has been total misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence occasioning failure of justice. The 2nd branch of submission of Mr.Sk Razzaque Ali is that Kha schedule land which is the suit land comprises CS Khatian Nos. 688 and 689 constituted under- tenancy under CS Khatian No. 687 and there having no khas land, the auction purchaser Asmat Ali could not have acquired any title and interest in the land of Khatian Nos. 688 and 689 unless the under tenancy is annulled by service of notice as contemplated under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and he says that there is no proof of annulment of under tenancies and the tenant having Kolkarsha or Dar karsha right continued to be the tenant in the holdings and the plaintiff got title not on the basis of auction purchase but by way of inheritance and purchase from the original tenants. The courts below having not considered this aspect of the case committed error of law occasioning failure of justice and in this regard reliance has been made on different cases of Indian jurisdiction. First case is the case of Nibaran Chandra Ghosh and others vs Pratap Chandra Chowdhury and others reported in 44 CWN 141. In that case it has been held:</u>

<u>"A sub-lease not valid against the sub-lessor's landlord under section 85 of the Bengal Tenancy Act (now repealed) is nevertheless valid against the sub-lessor as also against a third party who purchases the sub-lessor's interest at a certificate sale and transferees from him".</u>

6. The principle laid down in the case of lanaki Nath More vs Prabhasini Dasee reported in ILR 43 Cal178 was followed which is to the effect that under raiyati created by such a sub-lease by a raiyat is thus an encumbrance against a transferee from the certificate purchaser of the raiyati and must be duly annulled before the under raiyat can be rejected.

7. In the above cited case in a suit for declaration of title and ejectment of the under raiyat brought by transferee from certificate purchaser the question was raised that an under raiyati created by sub-lease by a raiyat is thus an encumbrance against a transferee from the certificate purchaser of the raiyat and must be duly annulled before the under raiyat can be ejected. In the facts of the case prayer for ejectment was refused for not having annulled the encumbrances by notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Next case that has been referred to is AIR 1937 (All) 176, Biahan Dayal vs Kesho Prasad and another, In that case section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure came under consideration and it was held that where a person purchases some property at an auction sale solely for himself and if another person claims that the purchases in fact was made by the auction jointly on his behalf (auction purchaser's) and the claimant's predecessor such claim is barred under section 66,Code of Civil Procedure. The substantial thing to be considered is that auction purchaser who is resisting the claim, claims title to the property under a purchase certified by the court, and if the property in dispute is part of the property so purchased auction purchaser is protected. A distinction should not be drawn between the cases where the whole of the property purchased is claimed and where the claimant says that he purchased only a share in the property mentioned in the sale certificate In other case the auction purchaser claims title under a purchase certified by the court and the claim comes within the mischief of section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Following the pronouncement of their Lordships of the Privy Council it was further held that the primary object of the section seems to be that the certified purchase should be deemed to be conclusive arid no one should be allowed to challenge it, unless he comes within the exceptions mentioned in the section itself. The next case referred to is AIR 1937 (Patna) 324 Naji Rajob Ali vs SkAktar Ali. In that case the applicability of section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure was considered in deciding a case under Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (VI of 1908) and under the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act clause I of section 265 provided that Chotanagpur Tenancy Act by implication renders the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure inapplicable to matters before the Deputy Commissioners except insofar as, the provision of the Code are applied to such matters by rule.

8. In 1931 Calcutta Law Journal vs 63 page 512, as has been cited by the learned Advocate, it is seen that a suit for enhancement of rent was brought by a purchaser of tenure against Osat Talukder. The facts being that the plaintiffs are the owners to Touji No. 1342 of the Noakhali Collectorate, in which a permanent tenure was held by one Basanta Kumar Mukharjee. The tenure was recorded in the record of rights as a permanent tenure the rent of which was liable to be enhanced. The plaintiff brought a suit against Basanta for enhancement of rent, that suit was compromised and in execution of the decree the plaintiffs purchased the tenure in 1913. It appears that in 1900 Basanta had granted permanent Mokarari lease to some of the defendants, in 1925 the plaintiffs brought the suit for enhancement of rent of the defendant who are Osat Talukders and for recovery of arrears of rent at an enhanced rate.

Both the Courts below held that the plaintiffs, are not entitled to claim enhanced rent from the defendants for the Osat Taluk, but have allowed a decree to the plaintiffs, in respect of arrears of rent at the old rate of rent. The plaintiffs appealed and two points were raised on their behalf. In the first place it was argued that the Mukarari Osat Taluks created by. Basanta are not binding upon the plaintiffs inasmuch as Basanta who was a non Mukarari tenure holder could not create a Mukarari under tenure or, in other words, he could not confer upon his tenants a higher right than what he himself possessed. Courts below relied upon section 179 of the Bengal Tenancy Act in support of their view that a permanent tenure holder is entitled to create a Mukarari under tenure which will be binding upon the purchaser of the tenure unless annulled under section 167 of the Act. The view taken by the courts below was upheld. That was a case for enhancement of rent. The case before me is to be decided in the context of the plaintiffs claim as founded in the plaint. It is evident from the plaint case that after the sudden purchase the plaintiff did not get possession in the land as the under tenancy which is an encumbrance against the certified encumbrances against the certified purchaser had not been annulled and further asserted that during the plaintiffs minority the said maternal uncle Asmat Ali managed the auction purchased land and rent was paid in the name of Asmat Ali. It is also admitted in the plaint that during the SA and RS settlement operation the name of Asmat Ali was recorded as per advice of the plaintiff.

9. Admittedly the auction sale took place in 1931 after the CS record was prepared and the purchase was made by the plaintiff in the name of Asmat Ali Howlader. Be it noted that the plaintiff has not made out any case in the plaint that even after the auction purchase in the name of Asmat Ali whom he designates as benamder, the predecessor of the plaintiff being in possession of the land for a long period exceeding 12 years or by custom had acquired the occupancy right in the land sold in rent decree which he inherited independent of the benami purchase and that right having not been annulled under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act the plaintiff became the tenant under certificate purchase and continued to remain so on payment of rent and that subsequently the plaintiff became tenant under the Government after the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into being. It is the admitted case of the plaintiff that the purchase in the court was made in the benami of Asmat Ali, rent was paid although in the name of Asmat Ali and the principal plaintiff has averred in the plaint that he being the real purchaser had not annulled the encumbrances and in the SA operation the record of right was prepared in the name of Asmat Ali under his advice, such being the position the cases cited would be of no assistance to the plaintiff. Rather the principle laid down in Bishan Dayal vs Kesho Prasad and another reported in AIR 1937 (All) 176 would support the plea of the defendant.

<u>10. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmad, the learned Advocate representing the opposite party No. 15, submitted that the suit is barred under section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He has contended that reading the plaint cannot be said that the claim of the plaintiff has been made otherwise than the benami purchase. He has referred to a case reported in AIR 1962 Andhra Pradesh at page 40 Chilakanarti Ketaiah vs Addanki Venkata Subaish. Here also it was decided that any suit founded upon the averments that the auction purchase was not intended to benefit purchaser he being only a benamder but the beneficial owner was the plaintiff falls within the range of section 66, Code of Civil Procedure irrespective of the fact that the certified purchaser happened to be the agent of the plaintiff even before the particular transaction took place. It has been held in that case that it is immediately plain that section 66 is widely worded and if literally construed it would take in every claim based on benami purchase. Be it noted that the expression used in the purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff or on behalf of someone through whom the plaintiff claims. Thus all cases of purchase made in a court's auction on behalf of or on account of the plaintiff fall within the mischief of the section. This section does not exclude from its purview benami purchases made for the benefit of a plaintiff by a defendant in his own name who was already acting as the agent of the plaintiff. The capacity which the defendant filed prior to the purchase cannot enter the judicial verdict. The only test is whether the court auction purchase was made on behalf of the plaintiff or of someone of whom the plaintiff traces his title. In other words, if the suit is founded on the averments that the real purchaser was the plaintiff and the certified purchaser had no beneficial interest therein section 66 Code of Civil Procedure comes in the operation. This doctrine is embodied in some of the decided cases.</u>

11. He has further argued that even if the documents filed by the plaintiffs had been discussed and considered by the appellate Court below no different conclusion as regards possession and title in the suit land could be drawn and, as such, no failure of justice has been occasioned.

12. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that the learned Assistant Judge having discussed the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties and particularly the oral testimony of the plaintiff came to a clear conclusion that the title and possession of the plaintiff appears to be clearly not proved, rather the defendant's right, title and possession has been established. Main consideration of the trial Court was whether the suit is maintainable and considering the pleadings the trial Court held that the suit is not maintainable in view of the provision of section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

13. The learned Subordinate Judge being the appellate Court question of benami purchase upon considering and having regard to the fact that the defendant No. 19 who is deemed to have been the vital witness in the case having not been examined as witness to prove the benami purchase in the name of Asmat Ali disbelieved the benami transaction as claimed by the plaintiff. The learned Subordinate Judge however failed to take notices as to what would be the legal consequence if the benami purchase in the name of Asmat Ali is held to be correct. Whether the suit is barred under section 66, Code of Civil Procedure or not that this escaped the notice of the appellate Court but the decree of the trial Court has been upheld by the appellate Court, Consequently, the view taken by the trial Court on that Court has been approved. So far as the muktipatra executed by the defendant Nos. 13-14, the heirs of Asmat Ali is concerned that was held to be not a document of title in support of the plaintiffs claim and the view taken by the appellate Court on that is maintained. The learned Subordinate Judge upon assessment of the oral testimony of the plaintiffs witness found that the plaintiffs have not been in possession of the suit and further held that the plaintiffs have failed to prove the title and possession over the suit land. The suit is for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. Both the Courts below considering the evidence on record found possession with the defendants. The finding of possession being concurrent there is hardly any scope to reject the evidence in revisional jurisdiction and to give different finding. He has however not discussed the documentary evidence in detail to arrive at a finding on question of possession and Mr. Razzaque Ali has argued on that score in order to assail the judgment of the appellate Court. Having perused all the documents my opinion is that even if the appellate Court had discussed and considered the entire documents adduced by the plaintiffs there would not have been any different conclusion and no support could have been found from these documents and the plaintiffs would not get any benefit out of that. Therefore there has not been any failure of justice for not having discussed all the documentary evidence. It is further held that the suit is barred under section 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

I have gone through the judgments of both the courts below and perused the records and I am of the view that the Courts below appear to have committed no illegality in dismissing the suit and consequently no interference is called for by this Court. The result, therefore, is that the Rule is discharged. However, there will be no order as to costs.

End.
